title: Russia dusts off its prewar demands as the US raises discussing European security at Ukraine talks
summary: After nearly five years of fighting in Ukraine, the Kremlin is eagerly embracing a U.S. offer to discuss postwar European security
story: After nearly five years of fighting in Ukraine, the Kremlin is eagerly embracing a U.S. offer to discuss postwar European security

After nearly five years of fighting in Ukraine, the Kremlin is eagerly embracing a U.S. offer to discuss postwar European security, and Moscow is using that diplomatic opening to reaffirm the tough demands that President Vladimir Putin put forward before the start of his full-scale invasion.

The proposal to discuss broader security arrangements for Europe was floated by U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoys, and that has worried Ukraine and its Western allies, who fear it will play into Moscow’s hands and weaken NATO.
The Kremlin strongly backed the U.S. idea, describing a review of the broader European security framework as vital for a settlement of Europe’s most devastating conflict since World War II.

Putin discussed the Ukrainian conflict with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, their first trilateral meeting. That encounter had fueled fears in Ukraine that they could discuss a possible settlement without Kyiv's participation.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wants a ceasefire to include a security framework to ensure that Russia does not attack his country again, and European leaders argue that such an architecture already exists in the form of NATO.

In draft agreements submitted to the U.S. and NATO in December 2021, two months before the invasion, Russia demanded that Washington and its allies pledge to exclude NATO’s expansion to Ukraine, Georgia or any other nation that was once part of the Soviet Union.
Moscow also demanded that the U.S. and its allies make a commitment to not deploy weapons or conduct any military activities in Ukraine and other ex-Soviet nations.
The documents also obliged the alliance not to station any troops in areas where they weren’t present in 1997 — before NATO moved to incorporate former Soviet bloc countries and ex-Soviet republics.

They also suggested a freeze on patrols by Russian and U.S. warships and bombers near each other’s borders. In addition, they called for efforts to reduce the risk of incidents involving Russia and NATO warships and aircraft, primarily in the Baltic and the Black seas; a reduction in the scope of military drills; and greater transparency and other confidence-building measures.
NATO allies have rejected the Russian demands as a nonstarter.

Putin described the West's refusal to consider these proposals as the main reason behind his decision to send troops into Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022, arguing that he had to act to fend off a major threat to Russia's national security. Ukraine and its allies denounce the invasion as an unprovoked act of aggression.
Speaking after the meeting with Xi and Trump, Putin reaffirmed his criticism of the West for failing to take Moscow's complaints about NATO's expansion into account.
"They just spat at our opinion,” he said.
Putin bluntly rejected the European response to Moscow's plans. He called it “political diarrhea” and “nonsense,” saying that “everybody understands that we don't strive for a war with Europe.”
He said Russia is open to discussing the continent's security arrangements with the Europeans as the U.S. has suggested, and scoffed at “hysterics in some European capitals" over Washington's offer.

“We understand that it makes no sense to discuss issues related to security in Europe without the Europeans,” Putin declared. He said Moscow invited a European delegation to visit and state its negotiating position before deciding on the date and format of Ukrainian talks.

Russia is ready to search for compromise, he said, but will not budge on its key demands. He has sternly warned that Russia will not accept the deployment of any European troops into Ukraine after the hostilities end and see them as a legitimate target.

Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said that during talks with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on Nov. 12 in the Kremlin, Putin reminded them of Moscow's 2021 security proposals, noting that they envisioned the pullback of NATO forces from Central and Eastern Europe.
Ushakov said the Kremlin would now update them with “fresh considerations.”

While Putin appears adamant on keeping Kyiv out of NATO and blocking any Western troops on Ukrainian soil, some observers say Moscow could be open to concessions on its other demands, including the rollback of NATO troops from Central and Eastern Europe.
Alexei Naumov, a pro-Kremlin political commentator, argued that Russian demands represented an initial bargaining position that could become more flexible during talks.

“Between maintaining the current status quo and the full realization of Russia’s demands, there is a vast space for compromise: mutual arms limitations, agreements regarding the deployment of military infrastructure, the parameters for a future Ukrainian military, security guarantees, and mechanisms to monitor their implementation,” he said in a commentary.
“Russia is currently negotiating from a position of strength, but that does not at all mean there will be no compromises.”

Tatiana Stanovaya, an expert at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, said that “for the first time since 2022, Moscow sees a concrete opening for negotiations that could address what it calls the ‘root causes’ of the war.”

“The Kremlin thinks the opportunity is worth pursuing, even though its expectations for this round are low,” she said. “If the talks fail, Russia is prepared to keep fighting until another opening presents itself.”

Russia expert Mark Galeotti, who heads the Mayak Intelligence consultancy, said Moscow’s set of demands could reflect “the classic attempt to start with a very, very exaggeratedly ambitious list of proposals with the expectation that you get haggled down.”
Putin could be searching for a face-saving way to end the war without achieving the land gains in Ukraine that he had sought, Galeotti noted in a recent podcast.
European leaders fear that Putin could persuade Trump to support a peace settlement that would weaken not only Ukraine but broader European security.
The European Union’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said Europe must insist on a ceasefire before taking the negotiations further — the opposite of what Putin demands.

“If we start to talk about what Russia is asking regarding the security architecture, we actually walk into the traps that Russia is setting us,” she said at a meeting of the European Political Community in Dublin earlier this month.

Zelenskyy also has warned that the U.S. proposal to discuss a new security framework for Europe before the war’s end could be dangerous, arguing that Moscow could use such discussions to weaken NATO and reshape the continent’s borders.

Kushner, meanwhile, said after meeting with Zelenskyy and European leaders on Thursday in Berlin that Trump wants to make a deal with Europe “by his side” and is not looking to impose a unilateral agreement. He also emphasized that Trump is “open” to NATO-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine, added that he believes Russia is “comfortable” with the allies offering such assurances to Kyiv.
Trump called into the Berlin talks following his meeting with Putin, Kushner said.

Stanovaya noted that Putin wants Europe to accept that Russia will have to be part of any negotiation on European security and predicted that the prospective talks will fuel differences among the allies.
“I expect the process to deepen divisions within Europe, with little prospect of concrete results,” she said in a post on X.

title: Russian attacks on Kyiv kill 3, cripple bridges and cut power
summary: Russia has launched missiles and drones across Kyiv, killing three people and injuring nine
story: Russia has launched missiles and drones across Kyiv, killing three people and injuring nine

KYIV, Ukraine -- Russia launched missiles and drones across Kyiv overnight that killed three people, injured nine others and damaged bridges and transport infrastructure, local authorities said Friday.

The attacks came hours after President Vladimir Putin vowed to retaliate against Ukraine for three aerial attacks this week on the vital Kerch Bridge, which links occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland.

“We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that,” Putin told reporters Thursday in China, where he attended a summit with the Chinese and U.S. presidents. Putin said the road side of the bridge had been “seriously damaged” and vowed to rebuild.

The Kyiv City Military Administration said the attack struck four districts of the capital. The attack caused widespread electricity disruptions. Energy provider DTEK said parts of the Pecherskyi, Solomianskyi, Holosiivskyi, Dniprovskyi and Darnytskyi districts were without power following the strikes.

Non-residential buildings were damaged in the Obolonskyi and Holosiivskyi districts, while transport and logistics infrastructure was hit in the Podilskyi and Darnytskyi districts, it said in a statement.
Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a ballistic missile attack damaged the Podilskyi Bridge, forcing authorities to close traffic from the right bank to the left bank of the Dnipro River.
The Darnitskyi Bridge was also damaged, he said.

A further strike hit the Southern Bridge, where traffic remains restricted. Only vehicles weighing up to 10 tons traveling from the left bank to the right bank, and public transport weighing up to 18 tons, are being permitted, he said.
Klitschko urged residents to avoid traveling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary. He asked businesses and institutions to arrange remote working wherever possible.

title: Denmark accuses Russian intelligence of plotting to kill American Ukrainian on its soil
summary: Authorities thwarted the attempted killing of an American Ukrainian citizen on Danish soil in a plot allegedly orchestrated by Russian intelligence services
story: Authorities thwarted the attempted killing of an American Ukrainian citizen on Danish soil in a plot allegedly orchestrated by Russian intelligence services

COPENHAGEN, Denmark -- Authorities thwarted the attempted killing of an American Ukrainian citizen on Danish soil in a plot allegedly orchestrated by Russian intelligence services, the Danish prime minister’s office said Friday.

The Russian defense attaché has been expelled from Denmark in response, Danish broadcaster DR reported. Two alleged members of the outlawed Danish gang “Loyal to Familia” have been arrested in connection with the attempted killing, police said.

The Danes’ announcement came as tensions between Europe and Russia heightened again Friday. Two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland in what its prime minister said was likely a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine.

title: France probes suspected leaks of confidential information to Le Pen’s far-right party
summary: French authorities are investigating whether a former Interior Ministry official leaked confidential information to Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally
story: French authorities are investigating whether a former Interior Ministry official leaked confidential information to Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally

PARIS -- French authorities are investigating whether a former Interior Ministry official leaked confidential information about judicial investigations to Marine Le Pen' s far-right National Rally, adding to the party's legal troubles ahead of next year's presidential election.

Hugues Moutouh, a former general secretary in the ministry, is suspected of sharing information about investigations relating to the financing of the National Rally’s 2022 and 2024 election campaigns, according to Le Monde newspaper.
Moutouh now serves as prefect of the Centre-Val de Loire region, representing the central government there.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez confirmed Friday that a judicial investigation has been opened, and summoned Moutouh for a meeting.

The Paris prosecutor’s office confirmed to The Associated Press it opened a judicial investigation “into alleged breaches of professional confidentiality, breaches of investigative secrecy, and the handling of information obtained through these offences.” It said no one has been formally handed preliminary charges at this stage.
It added that investigators conducted searches at the party’s headquarters on Nov. 9.
Le Pen has not commented on the case.
“If the facts are confirmed, they are obviously very serious,” Nuñez told BFM TV.

Less than six months before next year’s election, it’s the latest controversy to hit Le Pen’s party following accusations in September that her running mate, Jordan Bardella, made antisemitic remarks as a young party member.

The 31-year-old Bardella, who Le Pen says will be her prime minister if she wins the presidency in May, vigorously denied authorship of the comments about supposed Jewish banking monopolies and other antisemitic conspiracy theories that investigative website Mediapart attributed to him.

Le Pen will run for the French presidency next year despite being sentenced in July to wear a court-ordered electronic monitor for embezzlement. The decision by the 57-year-old veteran of three presidential races set up a fourth campaign like no other: potentially seeking votes while subject to monitoring and with a judge possibly deciding how, and for how long, the punishment is applied.
Le Pen has appealed the ruling to France’s highest court and she believes she won’t be subjected to monitoring at all.

According to opinion polls, the nationalist Le Pen is the front-runner to replace Emmanuel Macron, ahead of hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Other aspirants include two former prime ministers of Macron. Candidates from the moderate left and right, the Green party and conservatives are also running, among others.

title: El Salvador President Nayib Bukele seeks third term while attacking gangs in Haiti
summary: El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele has officially launched his bid for reelection in the February elections
story: El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele has officially launched his bid for reelection in the February elections

SAN SALVADOR -- SAN SALVADOR (AP) — El Salvador President Nayib Bukele on Thursday night officially launched his candidacy for a third term in office after years of paving the way to stay in power indefinitely.

With virtually no political opposition, the highly popular leader is positioned to coast easily into a third term in office in the February elections. Recent polls put his approval ratings around 90%, largely due to his war on the country’s gangs. The crackdown, which began in 2022, has largely debilitated the criminal groups and sharply reduced violence but fueled accusations of mass human rights abuses.

The firebrand populist submitted his presidential candidate paperwork to the country’s Supreme Electoral Tribunal. His New Ideas party, which holds a supermajority in the country’s congress, cleared the way for him to be the party’s candidate in July and remain in power.

Crowds carrying “Bukele 2027” signs cheered his arrival in a fleet of police cars at the electoral tribunal building, where candidates for 60 congressional seats and 44 municipal council seats also submitted documentation ahead of the Thursday night deadline.
“In El Salvador there is total, complete open democracy,” an impassioned Bukele told roaring supporters. “We’re sending a message to the world that El Salvador will never return to the past.”

The reelection bid comes as Bukele has taken his crime offensive to Haiti. He deployed around 2,500 troops to fight gangs after the disappearance of four Salvadoran aviation technicians in an October gang attack.

Critics have described the offensive as a way to offset international scrutiny, rally domestic support ahead of elections and solidify Bukele’s long-term political project. But Bukele, a former communications strategist, often seems to relish political spectacles.

Democratic concerns hang over the February vote. El Salvador’s Constitution has long prohibited consecutive reelection, in part because of the Central American nation’s fragile democracy. But a ruling by the Supreme Court stacked with Bukele loyalists allowed him to seek a second term in 2024.

Bukele has spent years whittling away checks and balances and concentrating power. The country's congress, dominated by his party, pushed through a congressional reform in 2025 that eliminated presidential term limits and moved up national elections from 2029 and 2027.
His government also has gone after the opposition, watchdog groups and journalists, fueling the greatest exodus of civil society since the Salvadoran civil war decades before.
Political opposition figures and international observers have said Bukele's plan to continue in office is illegal, but don't deny the leader's popular support.

“Bukele is running for a third consecutive term after packing the court, rewriting the constitution to his liking and jailing or forcing into exile those who dare criticize him. The absolute concentration of power in his hands has been the defining feature of his administration,” said Juan Pappier, Human Rights Watch deputy director of the Americas.

The country's political opposition has been rendered virtually irrelevant, in part because of years of corruption and political failures by traditional parties, which helped catapult Bukele into office in 2019.
Many Salvadorans have said they prefer giving up democratic freedoms to suffocation by the gangs.
Janetsky reported from Mexico City.

title: Rohingya in Bangladesh welcome UN court's genocide verdict but say they want to go home to Myanmar
summary: Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh have welcomed the ruling by the United Nations' top court in the Netherlands that held Myanmar responsible for genocide
story: Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh have welcomed the ruling by the United Nations' top court in the Netherlands that held Myanmar responsible for genocide

COX’S BAZAR, Bangladesh -- Hundreds of Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh sat in front of a big screen at their sprawling camp in Cox’s Bazar, watching the news from the Netherlands, where the U.N.'s top court ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation.

For many, the historic verdict on Thursday represented a “small victory” — offering a glimmer of hope that someday they would be able to return safely to their homes in Myanmar, across the border from Bangladesh.
Only then, some said, will they be “fully satisfied.”
It was a landmark judgement, finding Myanmar responsible for the crime against the country’s ethnic Rohingya — the first time the court ruled that a state committed genocide.

The Hague-based International Court of Justice also ordered Myanmar’s military-supported government to allow the Rohingya to return home safely, pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide.

But it remains to be seen how much of the ruling can be implemented. The court’s rulings are final and legally binding, but it has no way to enforce them beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council.
There was no immediate reaction to the ruling from the Myanmar delegation in The Hague or from the government in Myanmar.
At the refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Rohingya refugees told The Associated Press of their concerns.

Mohammad Rofik, a Rohingya community leader at the camp, said the verdict was “a victory” for them as it recognized the genocide and the sufferings of their minority in the Buddhist-majority nation, but that it was “not an end” to their ordeal.
“Justice has started,” Rofik said, adding that the Rohingya still have “a long way to go.”
For Sayed Ullah, another Rohingya community leader, the verdict was a historic recognition that the Rohingya are a distinct ethnic group.
“Myanmar denies the existence of the Rohingya, but now the (U.N.) court made it clear," he said.

“The Rohingya have their own distinct culture, their own language, their own land and everything else that defines an ethnic group,” Ullah said. “We, the Rohingya, have all the characteristics of a distinct ethnic group.”
Other refugees reacted sharply, saying that the international community should punish Myanmar authorities.

“The court has stated and established that genocide was committed against the Rohingya people," said Mohammad Osman, a Rohingya refugee. "Based on this ruling, the entire Rohingya community is calling on ... (the world) to impose severe punishment on Myanmar.”

In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched what it called a clearance campaign in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. The campaign led to accusations that security forces committed mass rapes and killings and burned thousands of homes.

The Hague-based court said that evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya. Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred, the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part.”

About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Bangladesh has been urging the international community to help repatriate the refugees.
Associated Press writer Julhas Alam in Dhaka, Bangladesh, contributed to this report.

title: Myanmar dismisses the UN court's ruling on its responsibility for Rohingya genocide as 'unfair'
summary: Myanmar’s government has dismissed a landmark judgment by the United Nations’ top court finding the country guilty of genocide against its Rohingya minority as “unfair.”
story: Myanmar’s government has dismissed a landmark judgment by the United Nations’ top court finding the country guilty of genocide against its Rohingya minority as “unfair.”

BANGKOK -- Myanmar’s government on Friday dismissed a landmark judgment by the United Nations’ top court finding the country guilty of genocide against its Rohingya minority as “unfair,” while opponents called upon the international community to follow through to ensure justice is done.

Khine Khine Soe, spokeswoman for President Min Aung Hlaing, noted that judges had only voted nine-to-six on Thursday to find Myanmar committed genocide against the Muslim minority Rohingya in a brutal 2017 military operation.
“Not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” she told reporters in the capital Naypyitaw. “So it was not a decision made unanimously. I would say that it was unfair.”

The ruling by The Hague-based International Court of Justice, or ICJ, was the first time the court has ruled that a state committed genocide. Myanmar’s government has denied the allegation, claiming it acted against insurgents in the 2017 military operation in northern Rakhine state.

The case focused on the military's so-called “clearance operations” in Rakhine state in 2017 when the democratically-elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi was in power. Min Aung Hlaing, who was commander in chief at the time, seized power from Suu Kyi in 2021 and has since consolidated his control of the government, being elected president earlier this year in a vote critics said was neither free nor fair.
The country is now embroiled in a bloody civil war, with pro-democracy and other militias fighting against the military.

The militant Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, or ARSA, whose attacks in 2017 against government outposts in Rakhine State were the trigger for the Myanmar military’s devastating crackdown, called the ruling an “important step towards justice" in a statement on Telegram.
The court said that evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya in the campaign in which the military was accused of committing mass rapes and killings, and razing thousands of homes.

About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.

Nay San Lwin, an activist with the Arakan Rohingya National Council, who now lives outside Myanmar, said this was just the “first victory on our path to our final one: returning to our homeland and living there in peace and dignity.”
“Without action and support from the international community, the court’s order will remain only a declaration,” he told The Associated Press. “Every country must help in whatever way it can.”
ARSA stressed that refugees have to be allowed to return home safely and that those responsible must face justice.

“We call upon the United Nations and the international community to ensure that Myanmar complies with the Court’s judgment and that justice is not left on paper,” the group said in a statement signed by “Ustad Khalid Junun,” described as its chief of general staff.
The Rohingya Solidarity Organization, or RSO, a rival militant group, issued a similar statement.

ARSA and the RSO have been marginalized since 2017, by suppression from Myanmar authorities and infighting. They are now involved in three-way fighting in Rakhine, where the Arakan Army, a Buddhist-dominated group seeking autonomy for the state, is battling the Myanmar military but has also been accused of targeting the Rohingya.
The Arakan Army did not respond to a request for comment on the court decision.

In its ruling, the court ordered Myanmar to commit to allowing Rohingya “safe, voluntary and dignified return to their place of residence.” It also ordered Myanmar to investigate, prosecute and punish people found to have committed genocidal acts and to pay compensation to Rohingya. The amount will be decided in later court proceedings.
Khine Khine Soe did not address those demands, but it was widely seen as unlikely that Myanmar would comply. She said Myanmar would reply once it reviewed the lengthy court documents.
"Since this is an international case, we will make our position known,” she said.

She also questioned the court's jurisdiction to impose conditions, and referenced a declaration on Thursday by U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at their historic trilateral meeting in China, in which they said “ the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction.”

“The main point is that the ICC and similar international institutions should not abuse their judicial authority,” Khine Khine Soe told reporters. “Given that three (of the) world’s leading nations have issued statements on this matter ... you can think about it for yourselves.”

China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Friday that while the country stood ready to “play a constructive role in advancing the repatriation of displaced people from Rakhine state, ”China has concerns over issues such as jurisdiction overreach and broad interpretations, and we believe such practices are not conducive to resolving disputes."

Myanmar’s shadow National Unity Government, the main organization coordinating opposition to military rule in Myanmar since the 2021 army takeover, welcomed the ICJ ruling, saying it respected the authority of the court and its judgment.
It also stressed that the pursuit of justice for the Rohingya must be accompanied by efforts to end the military’s ongoing violence against civilians across Myanmar.

title: All 146 Air Niugini plane passengers and crew safe after an emergency landing in Philippines
summary: An Air Niugini plane carrying 146 passengers and crew from Hong Kong to Papua New Guinea has safely made an emergency landing in a southern Philippine city due to a warning of a possible engine fire
story: An Air Niugini plane carrying 146 passengers and crew from Hong Kong to Papua New Guinea has safely made an emergency landing in a southern Philippine city due to a warning of a possible engine fire

MANILA, Philippines -- An Air Niugini plane carrying 146 passengers and crew from Hong Kong to Papua New Guinea safely made an emergency landing Saturday in a southern Philippine city due to an indication of a possible engine fire, Philippine aviation officials said.

There were no reports of injuries among the 137 passengers and nine crewmembers, who disembarked through emergency slides of the Boeing 767-383ER after it diverted from its route and landed at the Davao International Airport, the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines said.

The pilots reported that they detected, through an indicator, possible sparks or fire in the right engine. They undertook safety procedures and requested to make an unscheduled landing in Davao shortly after midnight, Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines spokesperson Eric Apolonio said without elaborating, adding that an investigation will include the accounts of the pilots.
The passengers and crew were taken to the airport terminal and provided assistance and hotel accommodation. There were no immediate reports of damage to the plane.

The Davao airport was closed to other flights to allow emergency response, causing two incoming domestic flights to be canceled. It was reopened later after safety checks were completed on the main runway, according to the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines.

title: Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, former South Africa deputy president and UN Women chief, dies at 71
summary: Former South African Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka has died at 71
story: Former South African Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka has died at 71

JOHANNESBURG -- JOHANNESBURG (AP) — Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, South Africa's first female deputy president and a United Nations under-secretary-general, has died at age 71, the South African government announced Friday.

Mlambo-Ngcuka, a former anti-apartheid activist and lawmaker in the South African Parliament, was deputy president from 2005 until 2008. She also served as minister of minerals and energy and deputy minister of trade and industry. She served as under-secretary-general and executive director of U.N. Women from 2013 to 2021.
The exact date and location of her death were not immediately shared by the government or her political party, the African National Congress.

Mlambo-Ngcuka was part of South Africa's first democratic Parliament for the ANC after the end of apartheid and white minority rule in 1994 when Nelson Mandela was elected the country's first democratically elected leader.

Tributes following her death lauded her contribution to South Africa's struggle for liberation and new democracy and the role she played at the U.N., where she championed women's rights and gender equality.

“Mama Phumzile was a distinguished leader of our movement and a dedicated servant of the people. She made history as the first woman to serve as Deputy President of South Africa,” the ANC said in a statement Friday.
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres expressed condolences and called her “a lifelong champion of the rights and empowerment of women and girls.”

“Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka’s fight began long before she entered the world stage. As a young teacher in KwaZulu-Natal and an activist against apartheid, she learned that freedom is never complete until it reaches every woman and every girl,” he said in a statement Friday.
U.N. Women said her courage inspired people around the world and her leadership helped shape a global movement.

“From her early days as an anti-apartheid activist to becoming South Africa’s first woman Deputy President, and later leading U.N. Women from 2013 to 2021, she devoted her life to justice and equality,” the agency said in a statement.

Mlambo-Ngcuka was appointed deputy president during a volatile era in South African politics and for the ruling ANC, which was experiencing infighting and a bruising succession battle. She replaced former Deputy President Jacob Zuma when he was fired after being implicated in a corruption scandal involving an arms deal.

Despite her known history as a political activist and experienced lawmaker, her appointment drew criticism over her marriage to Bulelani Ngcuka, the country's lead prosecutor who was pursuing corruption charges against Zuma.
She is survived by her husband and their five children.

title: Magnitude 6.7 earthquake shakes Peru's Andes
summary: A magnitude 6.7 earthquake has shaken the Andes in central Peru with no immediate reports of damage or casualties
story: A magnitude 6.7 earthquake has shaken the Andes in central Peru with no immediate reports of damage or casualties
LIMA, Peru -- A magnitude 6.7 earthquake shook the Andes in central Peru on Friday with no immediate reports of damage or casualties.
The U.S. Geological Survey said the earthquake struck at 7:09 p.m. local time. Its epicenter was in the Andes, 34 kilometers (21 miles) north of Junín, at a depth of 108 kilometers (67 miles).

Peru’s Geophysical Institute said no damages or casualties had been reported. And the mayor of Carhuamayo near the epicenter, Abdel Vega, also told a local television station that there were no reports of victims or material damages.
The earthquake was felt in the Peruvian capital, prompting residents to rush into the streets.
Peru lies along the “Ring of Fire,” a 40,000-kilometer (25,000-mile) arc of volcanoes and fault lines around the Pacific Basin, where most of the world’s earthquakes occur.

In August, a 6.7 magnitude earthquake in the Peruvian Andes left two people injured and damaged several homes, health centers and schools, while in July, a 5.5-magnitude quake in the Junín region resulted in six deaths and 30 injuries.

title: Workers and students protest across Europe as a strike in Italy disrupts services
summary: Workers and students are protesting across Europe on Friday as a nationwide strike disrupted transport and school services in Italy and demonstrators gathered in several countries to press demands on issues ranging from wages and living costs to educat...
story: Workers and students are protesting across Europe on Friday as a nationwide strike disrupted transport and school services in Italy and demonstrators gathered in several countries to press demands on issues ranging from wages and living costs to educat...

ROME -- Workers and students protested across Europe on Friday as a nationwide strike disrupted transport and school services in Italy and demonstrators gathered in several countries to press demands on issues ranging from wages and living costs to education and military spending.

In Italy, the 24-hour strike called by the CGIL trade union brought demonstrations to more than 100 cities, from Milan and Turin in the north to Naples, Palermo and Rome. Protesters denounced stagnant wages, rising living costs and what organizers described as the government’s failure to strengthen public services and worker protections.

The labor action coincided with an International Day of Student Mobilization, with organizers planning demonstrations in more than 45 Italian cities. Student groups joined workers in calling for greater investment in education, measures to ease the cost-of-living crisis and policies aimed at reducing inequality.

The protests were part of a wider wave of labor and student activism across Europe. In Croatia, students boycotted classes and staged protests in about a dozen cities, demanding greater investment in education, housing and public services rather than military spending.

In Austria, several hundred people gathered outside the University of Vienna for a youth-led protest calling for more spending on education and less on weapons. Police dispersed the event after reported disturbances, saying officers used pepper spray and made several arrests.

Meanwhile in Germany, demonstrators gathered to call for greater education funding and to oppose a possible return to compulsory military service. The rallies came weeks after protests on Oct. 31 that drew thousands into the streets, descending into violent incidents in some cities.
Despite their different focuses, the protests across European countries reflected common concerns about living standards, public investment, education and government spending priorities.

The strike in Italy covered both the public and private sectors. Public transportation services were reduced or disrupted in several cities, while schools and some health facilities were also affected. Planned strikes by air transport workers were canceled for Friday, though separate walkouts involving airport personnel remain scheduled for Sunday at Milan and Venice airports.

Authorities deployed additional police in several Italian cities where multiple demonstrations took place. Alongside the CGIL action, grassroots unions including Cobas organized separate strikes and marches, adding to the scale of the nationwide mobilization.
The protests also took on a political dimension, with opposition leaders joining demonstrations and criticizing Premier Giorgia Meloni’s government over wages and social spending.
Speaking at the conclusion of a rally in Rome, CGIL Secretary-General Maurizio Landini said more than 1 million people had participated in demonstrations across the country.
“The squares are full, and all generations are in the streets,” Landini told supporters. “It is a day that does not divide but unites.”

Organizers said the common thread linking the labor and student protests was a call for policies that put jobs, public services and living standards at the center of government priorities. Many demonstrators were carrying banners calling for peace and increased investment in welfare, schools and health care.
— AP journalists Geir Moulson in Berlin and Relja Dusek in Zagreb contributed to this report.

title: Athlete swims in Strait of Hormuz to highlight Iran war's impact on wildlife
summary: British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh has swum the Strait of Hormuz to highlight environmental threats during ongoing conflict
story: British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh has swum the Strait of Hormuz to highlight environmental threats during ongoing conflict

LONDON -- British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh has swum in the North Pole and Antarctica to draw attention to environmental causes. But battling freezing waters and extreme conditions hasn't prepared him for his latest challenge: swimming the Strait of Hormuz while tankers are attacked and blown up nearby.
Pugh, who is a United Nations Patron of the Oceans, spent three days this week swimming parts of the dangerous waterway to highlight how the war with Iran threatens the area's habitat and wildlife.

Wearing only swimming trunks, goggles and a cap bearing the U.N. logo, the athlete started from the Musandam peninsula, on the southern tip of the strait, and ended by rounding the Cape of Hormuz, completing about 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) in total. Pugh is believed to be the first person to undertake a long-distance swim there since the war started.
The swimmer said that minutes after he entered the water on Monday, he heard two loud explosions that rocked the sea.

“I looked up and I could see that an oil tanker about four kilometers away had been hit,” he told The Associated Press after he returned to London. “The explosion was so loud, two booms, and then fighter jets coming in. And at that moment I realized we have to get out of here right now.”
Pugh, 56, managed to finish his feat after more stops and starts, including passing another vessel that sent fireballs into the sky after it was attacked.

“Most people, when they think about the Strait of Hormuz, they think of a shipping lane,” he said. “But it is also one of the most beautiful places I have ever been … it's one of the treasure troves of the natural world.”
“With all these ships being sunk, this area is under severe threat,” he added. “It’s going to take years, decades for this area to recover.”

Iran has in recent weeks increased attacks on vessels that it claimed traveled along unauthorized routes in the strait as it seeks to impose its control on the crucial waterway, where a fifth of all oil traded passed through before the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28.
Several tankers have also struck sea mines laid by Tehran, in some cases exploding and bursting into flames, among them one that was carrying over 2 million barrels of oil last month.
Pugh warned of how oil leaking from the dozens of tankers damaged since February could create lasting problems for the region's animals, as well as its coastlines, coral reefs and mangrove forests.

He described seeing large numbers of dolphins following his boat as he sailed in, as well as turtles and ospreys. He also marveled at the hundreds of turtles he saw during a swim along the Omani coast before the war.
“When oil gets in there, when chemical pollution gets in there, it becomes very, very difficult to clean up that type of mess,” he said. “It lasts for generations.”
Pugh has had plenty of experience facing extreme temperatures and predators, including great white sharks. But swimming in a conflict zone presented entirely new dangers.

To stay safe, the challenge was done in sections over three days, with a total of about six and a half hours of swimming. The athlete recalled seeing a gas carrier being struck as he returned to the harbor on the second day.

“I’ll never ever forget going past that gas carrier, the smell of the chemicals and then the flames, they were literally like fireballs going up into the sky. Around the ship, the water was on fire,” Pugh said.
“And to think of the impact which a casualty like this has on nature — it was very, very acute.”

Pugh has spent much of the past 40 years swimming in places from Antarctica to the Red Sea and the English Channel to urge more action to protect marine environments from climate change, pollution and loss of biodiversity.

He was the first athlete to swim across the North Pole and complete a long-distance swim in every one of the world’s oceans. In 2023, he swam all 315 miles (507 kilometers) of the Hudson River to highlight the importance of clean rivers.
His foundation says the challenges have helped secure official agreements to protect more than 3.5 million square kilometers (about 1.35 million square miles) of vulnerable ocean.
Some have dubbed Pugh’s blend of epic swimming and political outreach as “Speedo diplomacy.”
“Sport opens doors, it creates dialogue, it enables people to start thinking about these important issues,” Pugh said.
“My message is very simple,” he added. “We’ve got to stop the war. We’ve got to open the strait, and we’ve got to clean up the pollution.”

title: Heavy fighting erupts in Haiti as armed forces fight gangs to regain control of key corridor
summary: Armed forces in Haiti have launched an aggressive operation to remove powerful gangs long entrenched in a key corridor that connects the country’s capital to its western and southern regions
story: Armed forces in Haiti have launched an aggressive operation to remove powerful gangs long entrenched in a key corridor that connects the country’s capital to its western and southern regions

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Armed forces in Haiti launched an aggressive operation on Thursday to remove powerful gangs long entrenched in a key corridor that connects the country’s capital to its western and southern regions.
It is the first significant operation in the five years since violent gangs seized control of Martissant, located in the western tip of Port-au-Prince.

Haiti’s National Police posted a video on X stating that at least 34 suspected gang members were killed in Martissant during a fight with police officers working with a task force composed of members from Vectus Global, a private security firm founded by former U.S. Navy SEAL and Blackwater founder Erik Prince.
Local media reported heavy gunfire and explosive drones in the area as Haiti’s police posted a video of armored vehicles rumbling through the community.

Martissant is located along Route 2, the main road that leads out of Port-au-Prince to important western and southern cities. Thousands of people would travel through Martissant every day before gangs seized control of the area more than five years ago, disrupting the country’s economy as they prevented goods from entering or leaving the capital. Gangs have since charged tolls or randomly opened fire on cars or buses that dare cross through.
Ever since gangs seized absolute control of Martissant, aid workers and Haitian civilians have been forced to take alternative transportation or use rural back roads.

The fight to control Martissant began in June 2021, when gangs from Grand-Ravine and Village-de-Dieu attacked the Ti-Bois gang. Armed men set fire to homes, killed families, destroyed businesses and seized control of Martissant’s police station.
The clashes forced at least 19,000 people to flee their homes and affected some 800,000 people overall, according to a July 2022 United Nations report.
Several years ago, gangs operating between Tabarre and Carrefour would demand some $380 from those transiting through Martissant, according to a 2023 U.N. report.

Last year, Haiti’s Center for Analysis and Research in Human Rights noted that ever since Martissant fell, hundreds of public and private institutions were relocated and more than one million people were forced to flee their homes.
As the fight in Martissant continues, a U.N.-backed gang suppression force also has made recent inroads against gangs in a push to not only displace them but prevent their return.
“Operations are entering a new phase: increasing pressure on gang networks, dismantling more strongholds, and extending control over strategic areas,” the force wrote Thursday on X.
The gang suppression force said it’s working in places including Tabarre in Port-au-Prince and in Haiti’s central Artibonite region, which has come under repeated violent attacks by armed men.
The force said it has come under fire as it advances along Route 5, “removing obstacles established by gangs to isolate communities and control key routes.”
The force said it also cleared and secured a church and school that gangs had been controlling north of Gros-Morne.

“It is about restoring freedom of movement, reopening access to public institutions, and re-establishing State presence for communities that have endured years of gang control,” the force wrote Sunday on X.
Also fighting gangs are some 2,500 troops deployed by El Salvador last month when four of their own went missing after an Oct. 18 attack in Haiti’s capital.

Following orders by Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, the troops have attacked the main homes of two of Haiti’s most powerful gang leaders, Jeff and Lanmò San Jou, this month. Neither one was killed.

Thousands of Haitians poured into the streets of Port-au-Prince and beyond this week in support of Bukele, but experts have criticized the unilateral operations of Salvadoran troops and noted that the use of explosive drones has claimed a growing number of innocent victims.
A small group of Salvadorans are separately working with the gang suppression force.

In late September, El Salvador’s legislature passed a law authorizing the participation of that group in Haiti for another 12 months until October 2027. The law was championed by Bukele and overwhelmingly approved by the country’s congress, controlled by Bukele’s party.
The ongoing clashes with gangs continue as Haiti prepares for its first elections in more than a decade. The country hasn't had a president since Jovenel Moïse was killed in July 2021.

title: A cyberattack using artificial intelligence targeted the EU in October, official says
summary: An official in Brussels says a cyberattack using software powered by artificial intelligence targeted the European Union in October
story: An official in Brussels says a cyberattack using software powered by artificial intelligence targeted the European Union in October

BRUSSELS -- A cyberattack carried out with artificial intelligence targeted the European Union in October, an official in Brussels said on Thursday, and some of the bloc's digital tools remain offline.
The official did not elaborate on the cyberattack, or say who could have been behind it. It was the first time the 27-member bloc reported a cyberattack using an AI tool.
“AI-assisted tools can be used and especially misused to detect vulnerabilities," said Thomas Regnier, spokesperson for the European Commission, the executive body of the 27-nation EU.
"Indeed we can confirm that this was done with AI tools," he added. "We have seen many global cyberattacks recently, and of course no one is immune to this.”
Regnier said the EU first detected the incident on Oct. 22 and that authorities launched an investigation while also imposing “preventative measures."

Politico first reported the incidents. The news site said the attack lasted at least 10 days and affected translation and reimbursement tools as well as databases used for salaries and timesheets. Regnier declined to confirm that report.

“We temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored," Regnier said. So far, however, Regnier said that “we have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting commission staff as a whole.”
The EU agency CERT-EU oversees the digital security of the bloc’s various institutions, which all together employ about 40,000 people just in Brussels.

title: Japan, India agree to enhance military and defense industry cooperation
summary: Japan and India have agreed to enhance their military and arms industry cooperation, including allowing Japanese troops to conduct live-fire missile training at Indian firing ranges in future joint drills
story: Japan and India have agreed to enhance their military and arms industry cooperation, including allowing Japanese troops to conduct live-fire missile training at Indian firing ranges in future joint drills

TOKYO -- TOKYO (AP) — Japan and India agreed to enhance their military and arms industry cooperation, including allowing Japanese troops to conduct live-fire missile training at Indian firing ranges in future joint drills, as their defense and foreign ministers met Thursday in Tokyo.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi joined their Indian counterparts, Rajnath Singh and S. Jaishankar, at the “two-plus-two" meeting in Tokyo.

The two Asian powers have been rapidly deepening security, defense and economic ties in recent years amid growing tension and uncertainty in the region. India and Japan also are part of the Quad grouping with the United States and Australia that aims to counter China’s influence.
“Through our cooperation, we hope to serve as the anchor for the Indo-Pacific region,” Motegi told a joint news conference after the talks.
This defense industrial cooperation will proceed under the framework of “design with Japan, make in India,” Singh said.

As an island nation with limited space to safely conduct missile tests and training, Japan needs defense partners that can provide facilities for its military to practice live-fire drills essential to improving missile capability. Japan struck a similar arrangement with Australia this year.

Japan has been fortifying defenses in its southwestern region to deter China's growing military activity and started deploying long-range missiles this year, including Type-12 surface-to-ship missiles mobilized in Kumamoto on the southern main island.
Japan has also significantly relaxed its postwar pacifist principles in recent years and lifted a ban on lethal weapons exports as part of its security, defense and economic growth strategies.

On Thursday, the four ministers agreed to promote cooperation in defense equipment and technology and to accelerate negotiations toward achieving the transfer of Japanese naval radio antenna UNICORN to India.

They reaffirmed deepening cooperation in a range of areas including air and maritime security, information sharing, search and rescue operations, naval shipbuilding and artificial intelligence, according to a ministers' joint statement after the talks.

title: El Salvador's president confirms and celebrates attack on home of key Haitian gang leader
summary: El Salvador’s president says that his troops have demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff
story: El Salvador’s president says that his troops have demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, said Wednesday that his troops demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff. It wasn’t immediately clear if he was killed.

Bukele posted a video on X that depicts an old video of Jeff posing in front of his mansion in the Caribbean country and then cuts to Salvadoran helicopters flying toward it as they fire shot after shot, with big plumes of smoke rising from Jeff’s home.
“My gift to the Haitian people on the anniversary of the Battle of Vertières,” Bukele wrote.
The 1803 battle was critical in helping secure Haiti's independence from France and transforming it into the world's first Black republic.
It wasn’t immediately known if Haiti’s police and army were involved. A U.N.-backed gang suppression force said that it wasn’t involved.

Jeff is considered one of Haiti's most powerful gang leaders. His real name is Jeff Larose, but he's known as Jeff Canaan, Jeff Gwo Lwa and Taliban. He has long controlled a community known as Canaan in northern Port-au-Prince, leading a gang of an estimated 200 members, according to the United Nations. His so-called Taliban gang based in Canaan is a very close ally of 5 Segond, which has provided it with reinforcements.
Diego Da Rin, a Haiti expert with International Crisis Group, said the attack on Jeff’s home was the obvious next step for Bukele’s operations.
Jeff built the home in mid-2024, complete with a pool emblazoned with his logo.
“It’s very easy to identify it by satellite,” Da Rin said. “It was a very defiant act by him.”
He noted that Jeff’s home is very vulnerable to an aerial attack, but it was built in a place where attacking it by land would have been very difficult.
Da Rin said Jeff was among a handful of gang leaders who have built mansions in recent years.
“In a way, they felt untouchable in their territory,” he said.
The use of explosive drones and helicopters, which Haitian police and military lack, has changed that.

Da Rin said he doubts Jeff was staying at the mansion when it was attacked early Wednesday given that on Nov. 8, Salvadoran troops attacked the home of Wilson Joseph, best known as Lanmò San Jou and leader of the 400 Mawozo gang. He wasn’t killed in the attack.
Da Rin said gang leaders have several residences and can always seek shelter in any home within the territory they control.

He noted that Jeff and Lanmò San Jou are allies and control the main roads north and east of Port-au-Prince that lead to other cities and towns, charging tolls that have become their main source of revenue.
Canaan was established as an informal community after a devastating earthquake hit Haiti in January 2010. Tens of thousands of people are estimated to now live there.
The attack comes a day after thousands of Haitians in Port-au-Prince and beyond marched in favor of Bukele, thanking him and his troops for fighting violent gangs.
On Wednesday, Haitians were again celebrating.
“Jeff is a criminal and I hope he died,” said Mario Jean-Pierre, a 45-year-old salesperson in Port-au-Prince. “We asked for help; Bukele answered us.”
Last month, Bukele deployed around 2,500 troops to Haiti after four of their own came under attack on Oct. 18 while deep in gang territory. They remain missing.
Associated Press reporter Evens Sanon in Port-au-Prince, Haiti contributed to this report.

title: A Chinese executive is convicted in a case linked to a Bangkok building collapse
summary: A Thai court has found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders guilty of illegally operating a business in Thailand
story: A Thai court has found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders guilty of illegally operating a business in Thailand

BANGKOK -- A court in Thailand on Wednesday found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders of a Thai subsidiary of a Chinese state-owned construction company guilty of illegally operating a business in Thailand in a case related to the collapse of a Bangkok office building last year.

At least 92 people died on March 28, 2025, when an earthquake struck the partially built high-rise, which was to house the State Audit Office. It was the only building in Thailand to collapse completely due to the 7.7-magnitude quake, which was centered in neighboring Myanmar.

The tower was being built by a joint venture between China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) and Italian-Thai Development. Executives from both companies are also facing separate proceedings over alleged wrongdoing related to the building’s collapse.

China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) and its director, Zhang Chuanling, were found guilty of violating Thailand’s Foreign Business Act by using Thai nominee shareholders to conceal the company’s foreign ownership and operating a construction business without the required permission. The Criminal Court in Bangkok fined the company and Zhang 1 million baht ($29,450) each and sentenced Zhang to three years in prison, while also ordering the company to cease operations.
The defendants had denied the charges and were granted bail.
China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) is a Thai-registered affiliate of China Railway No. 10 Engineering Group, part of the Chinese state-owned China Railway group, which operates internationally.

The court’s action comes after increasing public concern about Chinese influence over local business, especially through the use of Thai citizens as proxies to disguise their real ownership. In some cases, the concern extends to suspicion that such enterprises are fronts for illegal activities, including money laundering and online scams.

The involvement of Chinese companies in the building collapse and other construction-related accidents has drawn considerable attention. The most notable other accident took place in January this year on a line that is part of a Thai-Chinese high-speed railway project linking the capital to northeastern Thailand. At least 32 people were killed and dozens injured when a construction crane crashed onto a moving passenger train, derailing it.
Italian-Thai Development was also the construction contractor for the railway project, and a Chinese company handled design and construction supervision.

After the train accident, China’s ambassador to Thailand, Zhang Jianwei, said that China requires its companies to follow the rules when participating in overseas projects, and that Beijing is willing to “guide Chinese companies to actively cooperate with the Thai authorities’ investigation."

Wednesday’s court case also saw three Thai shareholders found guilty of acting as nominees for China Railway No. 10 (Thailand). Two were sentenced to six years in prison each and fined 2 million baht ($58,900), while the third received a three-year prison term and a 1-million-baht ($29,450) fine. However, the court reduced their sentences and their fines by one-fifth after they confessed to the offenses.

title: Trump, Xi and Putin hold rare 3-way talks on nuclear risks but emerge with no major breakthroughs
summary: Three leaders who view their nations as the world’s superpowers have sat around a table together for the first time to talk about reducing nuclear risks and resolving conflicts
story: Three leaders who view their nations as the world’s superpowers have sat around a table together for the first time to talk about reducing nuclear risks and resolving conflicts

SHENZHEN, China -- Three leaders who view their nations as the world's superpowers sat around a table together for the first time on Thursday to talk about reducing nuclear risks and resolving conflicts — a step they applauded as historic though they did not agree to any major breakthroughs.

U.S. President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin offered smiles and friendly handshakes, ending their talks at a villa in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen by agreeing on points including U.N. reforms and a vow to get more fuel to the market. It remains to be seen if the gathering could mark a pivot in world history — or become a quickly forgotten photo op.

The leaders made only brief remarks at the beginning and didn't take questions afterward, releasing a short statement that did not mention the wars in Ukraine or Iran, two issues that Trump said he raised with the leaders in separate one-on-ones earlier in the day.
The agreements were modest, but the rhetoric was not.

“We are really making history,” Trump said. “The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used."
Xi earlier said the meeting would focus on “promoting world peace.” Putin, for his part, said the countries “hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace.”
After the meeting, Xi called it positive, constructive and fruitful, while Putin described the trilateral talks as open and candid, calling the format “useful and substantive.”
“It is a serious collaborative work,” he said in response to a question about whether this format is something other than just an image of three leaders coming together.

The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February, and Trump has said he wants “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China. But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the U.S. and Russian stockpiles.
Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said the meeting could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals.
“We need more than diplomatic theater and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin and Trump,” Kimball said. “And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs.”
The U.S. president earlier had a separate one-on-one with Xi, their third substantial meeting this year.

Trump said they had a shared interest in having oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil shipments from the Middle East that was repeatedly shut because of attacks in the Iran war. Trump suggested he would push Xi to buy more agricultural products from America.

Xi said that relations between the U.S. and China have been “generally stable and improved” during Trump's presidency. The official Chinese news agency Xinhua reported that Xi discussed Taiwan with Trump and said the two countries needed to improve communication on economic and trade issues.

Trump also added a separate sit-down with Putin, marking the first time the leaders have met for talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal on Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“Wonderful things can come out of this — or at least start,” Trump said, calling Putin “my friend."

Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin, as relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions, while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.
The U.S. president also added that the trio would talk about ways to “protect our nations' sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court."

In their joint statement, the three countries took aim at the court, saying state officials should enjoy immunity from its prosecutions and warning that it should not abuse its jurisdiction. Putin is wanted by the court, and Trump’s administration has imposed sanctions on ICC officials and the institution itself as part of a campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel.

The U.S. president's ambitions recall an era of great power politics when wealthier countries felt entitled to decide the fate of seemingly lesser nations. Trump is negotiating with China and Russia without the involvement of Ukraine — or allies like Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Japan and South Korea that also have stakes in the outcome of any talks.

Trump has long believed his ability to create personal connections gives him a diplomatic edge. Xi made a symbolic gesture of friendship Wednesday by taking the unusual step of greeting Air Force One on the tarmac, and the two leaders turned their handshake into a one-armed hug.

But for all the compliments the U.S. president has showered on the two autocrats, the warmth has not always been mutual — and Trump does not always appear to have the same deep relationship based on common interests that Xi and Putin share.

On Wednesday at APEC, Xi greeted Putin by calling him “my old friend.” The Russian leader responded by declaring Xi to be his “dear friend.” China has helped economically support Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, providing Putin with a financial lifeline after the U.S. and its allies imposed new sanctions.

By contrast, when Xi went to the White House for a state visit in September, he was far more restrained with Trump, saying they had built a "personal rapport and stayed in touch.” Trump and Xi have one more meeting planned this year, at the G20 summit in Florida in December.
There were also signs of friction Thursday in the U.S.-China relationship despite Trump’s praise of Xi.
Chinese officials blocked a Bloomberg reporter from the trilateral meeting after she asked a question at the earlier Trump-Xi session.
Chinese television showed a video of Trump appearing drowsy, while the White House posted a clip of Trump helping Xi up an escalator.
Associated Press writers Darlene Superville, Didi Tang and Will Weissert in Washington, Huizhong Wu in Bangkok and Kanis Leung in Hong Kong contributed to this report.

title: Climate talks in overtime as nations wrestle with response to worsening global warming
summary: Negotiators at the United Nations climate talks in Turkey are working an extra day in an attempt to reach a final agreement to address global warming
story: Negotiators at the United Nations climate talks in Turkey are working an extra day in an attempt to reach a final agreement to address global warming

ANTALYA, Turkey -- Work crews were boxing up the venue of this year's United Nations climate talks in Turkey, as negotiators went into overtime on Saturday in an attempt to reach a final agreement to address global warming. But hopes are slim that additional discussions will result in concrete plans to drastically slash the use of fossil fuels.

The added day of talks came as the two-week annual summit, called COP31, which was supposed to end Friday, drew strong condemnation from activists and some countries for failing to mention fossil fuels in a draft of the final agreement. The final document is meant to address how the world will deal with climate change, which is contributing to devastating heat waves, floods and other disasters.
To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts said the world needs to urgently and drastically cut emissions from the use of coal, oil and gas.

In the lead up to these talks, the U.N. announced that the world will likely blow past the 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.
“No one knows what is happening behind closed doors, or what the outcome of COP31 will be,” said Teresa Anderson, global lead on climate justice at ActionAid International.

Inside an area of the COP31 venue known as the “pavilions,” where countries showcased their climate policies and hosted panel discussions, workers were packing up electronics and other belongings Saturday morning.
The hallways, normally bustling with participants, stood largely empty, with only a handful of security guards seen taking photos in front of the deserted pavilions.

“COP31 is in a bleak overtime, with dwindling food and water, and no sign of any progress since the alarmingly underwhelming texts we saw earlier,” said Rachel Cleetus from the Union of Concerned Scientists, who is at the venue in the Mediterranean coastal city of Antalya.

Earlier during the summit, the nonprofit Climate Action Tracker warned that progress on slowing global warming has stalled for the past five years, even as disasters — including this year’s heat waves in Europe and flooding in Nepal — become more deadly.

Countries most vulnerable to climate change, including small island nations whose lands are battered by rising seas, also say wealthy nations that caused the climate crisis must contribute more to U.N. funds to help them recover from disasters and adapt to a warmer world.
The United States, a major polluter and the world’s largest economy, did not participate directly in this year's talks.
Next year’s climate summit is scheduled to take place in Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027.

On Friday, a protester wearing a red noose around his neck and a vest emblazoned with the slogan “you are killing the future” interrupted official COP proceedings by clambering onto a table and shouting “You take out fossil fuels. You killed 1.5. There is no money. Just kill me now. The Global South cannot wait.”
The Global South is a term that isn’t geographical, but a reference to developing countries in general.
“You keep doing nothing at all. Nothing at all. Kill me now. Kill me now,” the protester shouted as he was escorted out of the room by security.
The demonstration interrupted Turkey's Minister of Environment and COP31 co-president Murat Kurum, who said “let’s try to maintain the peace in the room" before continuing with his scheduled remarks.

“Yesterday, of course, this place was buzzing and today it’s nearly empty. But all the key negotiators are here, civil society is here watching the negotiations and waiting for the next iteration of the text,” said Harjeet Singh, a strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, who has attended 18 climate summits.
“We are still stuck with many, many disagreements and nobody knows how long this will go on,” he said.

Borenstein reported from Kensington, Maryland, Delgado from Bangkok, Arasu from Bengaluru, India, and Milko from Islamabad, Pakistan. Associated Press journalist Tammy Webber contributed from Fenton, Michigan.
