We all need new sources of energy and power. But this bill, as it’s currently drafted, is not the answer.”

Oneida Nation Vice Chairman Jameson Wilson said the bill threatens the tribe's ability to protect its sacred spaces, ancestors, traditional ceremonies and culture. “Any effort to accelerate development must strengthen, not diminish and erode tribal sovereignty and meaningful consultation,” he said.

Former Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm, who led the agency in the Biden administration, said she understands those concerns, but believes recent changes by bill sponsors strengthen protections for tribal consultation and restore important state authority over water quality.
“A bigger Democratic majority can write a stronger bill,” Granholm wrote in a social media post. “But it would still need this president’s signature.”
Sen. Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, said he supports and even authored many provisions in the bill, such as streamlining transmission infrastructure.

But he voted no because the bill contains provisions he said would “irreparably harm California and the 109 federally recognized tribes who call California home.” He said he cannot sacrifice the rights of tribal governments or California’s environment.
Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, Rhode Island.

title: Reporter says Texas execution was like no other he's witnessed before
summary: There were immediate warning signs that something was amiss in the execution of Reinaldo Dennes, but no one could have predicted how the condemned killer would react to the injection of the powerful sedative pentobarbital
story: There were immediate warning signs that something was amiss in the execution of Reinaldo Dennes, but no one could have predicted how the condemned killer would react to the injection of the powerful sedative pentobarbital

HUNTSVILLE, Texas -- After covering capital punishment for The Associated Press in Texas since 1983 — and witnessing nearly 500 lethal injections — I've become accustomed to a certain routine in the procedure, although I'm reticent to describe any execution as “routine.”

It was 6 p.m. Thursday — a bell from a nearby church tolling the hour — when I and other witnesses climbed the concrete steps into the more than century-old Huntsville Unit of the Texas Department of Criminal Justice. We were led into a reception office for what normally is a very brief period to await the short trek to the death chamber to watch condemned killer Reinaldo Dennes die.
A large state of Texas clock on a wall ticked off the moments. By about 6:20 p.m., we still hadn't moved.

I knew one of two situations was likely: Dennes was resisting the execution team's attempts to insert a pair of intravenous needles into his arms, or the execution team was having difficulty finding a suitable vein for the needles.

Thirty minutes later, as we were led into the chamber by corrections officers, Dennes appeared docile. His eyes were closed and his head was pointed toward the ceiling. His white prison garb was not disheveled and no additional restraints were applied to his head, meaning no evidence of a struggle.

Now I've seen over the years any number of final statements and reactions from condemned inmates who spoke in foreign languages, prayed, recited poetry, sang, cursed, expressed love, insisted on their innocence or acknowledged their crime and one who even told a joke.
Dennes was like no other.

Asked by the warden if he had a final statement, Dennes talked about being “extremely blessed” by the love of “the father” and hoped his family and loved ones “get to know this great gift and great grace of God the father.”
He told the warden: “Go.” Almost immediately as the procedure began, his demeanor changed.
“The pain!” he exclaimed. “Go! Go!”
For nearly three minutes — and standing there furiously scribbling notes, I thought it seemed much longer — Dennes repeatedly moaned.

“Take me father! ... Take me into your arms! ... Take me father!” He occasionally interjected his cries with obscenities, a grunt and then groans. His right leg was “killing me,” he said, likening the sensation to a cramp.
“I don't think this is normal,” he said at one point.
On that, he was right. I've heard inmates say the lethal drug was hot or cold, that they could smell or taste it, or that it hurt.
At 7:08 p.m., after being examined by a physician, he was pronounced dead.

Texas prison officials said the execution team had difficulty finding suitable veins. Spokeswoman Amanda Hernandez said after repeated unsuccessful attempts — she couldn't say how many — the technicians found a vein in Dennes' left foot and another on the left side of his neck that were receptive to the IV needles.
I couldn't see. His feet were covered by a sheet and only the right side of his neck was visible to those of us who were witnesses.
The injection sites were in line with the prison system's procedures, Hernandez added. The alternate sites have been used in previous executions, although the need to do so is relatively rare.
Hernandez also suggested Dennes may have been faking, saying he had been complaining about pain from areas where no injections were attempted.
As a reporter, I'd like to find out the truth about the matter. But there's no way to know for sure.

title: Officials: Washington pulp mill violated safety standards before deadly tank rupture
summary: State investigators have revealed that a Washington pulp mill, where a chemical tank ruptured in May killing 11 people, had a history of severe safety violations
story: State investigators have revealed that a Washington pulp mill, where a chemical tank ruptured in May killing 11 people, had a history of severe safety violations

SEATTLE -- The Washington state pulp mill where a chemical tank ruptured in May, killing 11, had an extensive track record of egregious and willful safety violations, including failure to inspect or repair more than a dozen other tanks at the facility, state investigators said Friday.

Nippon Dynawave Packaging Co. faces more than $10 million in state fines, including the largest employer safety fine in state history, and investigators plan to refer their findings to prosecutors for possible criminal charges.

“Without repair or replacement, the tank walls were a ticking clock,” Dan Pitts, state Labor and Industries compliance manager, said during a press conference in Longview to announce the findings. "It was a question of time, and time ran out."
Nippon did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment about the state’s findings.

Nippon plans to restart operations in December. Officials said the company has an obligation to fix any hazards that have been identified, and the state will be closely monitoring to ensure that happens.

Besides the 11 who were killed, 12 were injured on May 26 when the tank holding more than 900,000 gallons (3.4 million liters) of “white liquor,” a highly corrosive chemical used in paper manufacturing, ruptured. The flood of caustic material was powerful enough to blow out building walls and overturn pickup trucks at the site.

“Nippon’s decision to keep G-10 operating when they knew it was not safe contributed to the death of 11 workers," said Labor and Industries Director Joel Sacks. "Because of that, we will be referring this case to prosecutors to consider criminal charges.”
The state Ecology department also announced that it has issued 34 violations that impacted air and water, and is seeking $961,000 in penalties and costs for responding to the emergency.

Most of the environmental violations were due to the impact of the white liquor that spread across the site, officials said. It reached storm drains and a wastewater treatment system, with some discharging into the Columbia River and a nearby ditch, killing fish.

State investigators said Friday the company failed to take appropriate action to address the issue in violation of state law, and similarly failed to inspect or address deficiencies in 13 other tanks at the site.

Officials also said Nippon's emergency response and planning fell short of state requirements. The company had not effectively prepared its staff to respond to an emergency, and there was no employer-led incident command for several hours after the tank failed, Pitts said.
“We believe failures in the response were a contributing factor in serious injuries to four of 12 workers who were hurt that day," Pitts said.

The state investigation mirrored an August report by the U.S. Chemical Safety Board that revealed inspectors hired by the company in 2025 found the tank that ruptured was “not fit for continued service” due to deteriorating thickness in the tank walls.

An AP review of inspections and safety complaints at the plant prior to the tank collapse found that Labor and Industries had investigated more than a dozen safety complaints at the plant since 2018 and issued almost $7,000 in fines for violations. Ecology had issued 54 environmental violation notices against the company since 2016 and fined them $41,500 for eight serious offenses.

More than $2.4 million in workers’ compensation claims have been paid for 169 employees injured on the job since 2015, the agency reported, including for injuries related to exposure to caustic substances.
After the May tank collapse, the state’s Department of Ecology filed a violation notice against the company listing 35 citations.

Nippon Dynawave said in an email Wednesday that they have remained engaged with the government agencies that are investigating the tank collapse. They said the mill has hosted hundreds of visits by regulators and investigators.

“The full deconstruction, forensic examination and technical analysis needed to determine the root cause have not yet been completed,” the company said. “The tank is currently being deconstructed, with great care being taken to log and retain portions of the tank to determine the root cause.”

Among workers killed in the rupture were brothers Tyler and Brad Covington. Their mother, Sheri Lynn King, has filed a wrongful-death lawsuit against Nippon Dynawave, saying her sons were burned and crushed by the white liquor and debris. The lawsuit claims the company failed to maintain and inspect equipment, failed to properly train and supervise employees and failed to implement safety policies and emergency response procedures.

title: NYC Mayor Mamdani is injured in soccer match against journalists
summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani says he tore his Achilles tendon while playing in a soccer match against the City Hall press corps
story: NEW YORK -- New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Friday that he tore his Achilles tendon during a pickup soccer match against the City Hall press corps and will have to wear a medical boot for the next several weeks.
Mamdani, 35, hobbled into a news conference on crutches and, when a reporter asked about his injury, explained that he got it in Thursday night's game.
As for why it happened, the millennial leader of America's biggest city identified a possible culprit in the form of a neglected pre-game warmup: “I did not stretch."
Still, the avid soccer fan appeared happy to report that he scored a goal “soon after getting on the pitch” but said he “forgot that I was 35.”
He was also quick to note that his team wound up beating the journalists' squad.
The mayor, known for a busy schedule, said he'll be wearing the medical boot for six to eight weeks and will be back on the pitch in about nine months.

title: Central Park's horse-drawn carriage drivers sue NYC over incoming ban
summary: Central Park’s horse-drawn carriage drivers have sued New York City to stop a new law that will ban the iconic tourist attraction, challenging Mayor Zohran Mamdani just minutes after he signed a bill to wind down the industry
story: Central Park’s horse-drawn carriage drivers have sued New York City to stop a new law that will ban the iconic tourist attraction, challenging Mayor Zohran Mamdani just minutes after he signed a bill to wind down the industry

NEW YORK -- Hold your horses: Central Park's horse-drawn carriage drivers sued New York City on Thursday to stop a new law that will ban the iconic tourist attraction, challenging Mayor Zohran Mamdani just minutes after he signed a bill to wind down the industry.
The law — approved after the death of a teenager last spring — is set to stop the carriage rides by June 2028.
But the union representing carriage drivers filed a federal lawsuit in Manhattan attempting to have the ban struck down, arguing the city is taking away their livelihoods.
“The City’s approach can be summarized in twelve words: immediately cripple the owners, ignore property interests and contracts, and maybe compensate,” the lawsuit reads.

The lawsuit is the latest turn in a long fight over the carriage rides, as animal welfare activists and industry supporters have tussled over whether the carriage rides amount to animal cruelty or are simply a romantic throwback to the city's past.

At a bill signing ceremony at City Hall on Thursday, Mamdani lauded the role of horses in the city’s development but said the animals should no longer be hauling tourists around a perpetually busy Central Park among joggers, cyclists and other passersby.
“Our city has changed and now it is time for our laws to change, too,” said Mamdani, a Democrat.

City lawmakers reignited their push for a ban earlier this year in response to the death of 18-year-old Indian tourist Romanch Mahajan, who died after jumping from a runaway carriage in what appeared to be the first fatality in a horse carriage accident since they were introduced in Central Park.

Over the years, horses have collapsed or gotten startled and run off into cars or other objects. In response, the city has put various safety regulations in place for the industry, including veterinary checkups, vacation time for horses and a retirement age for the animals.

City Hall has promised to release a career transition plan for those in the carriage industry next April that includes job training, educational pathways and stipends, though drivers argue their future remains uncertain.

"Despite the good intentions of the mayor, the protections he outlined recently should have been written into the legislation," said John Samuelsen, head of the Transport Workers Union, which represents carriage drivers.
The union's lawsuit argues the law is unconstitutional and that the city violated local legal procedures when it approved the law. It names the mayor and various other city officials as defendants.
A spokesperson for the city's law department said it is reviewing the case.

title: Iran war costs surpass $48B as lawmakers demand unreleased estimates on base damage
summary: The Iran war’s costs have risen to an estimated $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13
story: The Iran war’s costs have risen to an estimated $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13

WASHINGTON -- The costs of the Iran war have risen to an estimated $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13, but because that total does not include damage to U.S. bases attacked in the Middle East, lawmakers are pushing for the Pentagon to provide those figures.

Arthur Miller, a Pentagon budget official, provided the latest overall cost estimate Thursday to the Senate Armed Services Committee, which is considering his nomination to be Navy comptroller. The $48 billion figure includes the costs of military operations, as well as for replacing equipment and munitions.

Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut pressed Miller for an estimate on damage to U.S. installations, which Miller said he didn't have. Republican Sen. Roger Wicker of Mississippi, the committee’s chair, directed Miller to try to provide an answer as soon as possible.
An Associated Press analysis found that Iran attacked aircraft hangars, systems that detect incoming strikes, warehouses, troop housing and more, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage.

The war's price tag has been a flashpoint in Congress, with debates over costs intensifying as the Trump administration asks lawmakers to pass a $1.5 trillion defense budget. After the unpopular war and its economic effects contributed to severe Republican losses in the midterm elections, financial battles over the conflict will only escalate once Democrats take control of Congress in January for the remainder of President Donald Trump's term.
The Pentagon has faced growing calls from Democrats to release estimates on the damage Iran has done to American bases in the Middle East through missile and drone attacks.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, grilled acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao on the costs of the war at his confirmation hearing Tuesday for the permanent job.

Citing independent estimates and media reports, Warren said the U.S. naval blockade on Iranian shipping costs about $32.5 million a day, while an Iranian attack on the Navy’s regional headquarters in Bahrain did at least $400 million in damage.

Cao confirmed the figure for the blockade but said he could not offer a full damage assessment in Bahrain because “it’s a nonpermissive area for us to go." Cao told a reporter months ago that Iran “blew the hell out of Bahrain.”

title: Cincinnati Zoo says Fiona the hippo can't undergo surgery after swallowing a hat
summary: The Cincinnati Zoo says staff members are doing everything they can to help its beloved hippo Fiona after she swallowed a knit hat
story: The Cincinnati Zoo says staff members are doing everything they can to help its beloved hippo Fiona after she swallowed a knit hat

Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo's famed hippo, underwent a colonoscopy this week, and now veterinarians are trying a new way to help her pass a knit cap that she swallowed after it slipped into her enclosure.
The zoo's animal care team borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm, hoping the shaking will help move things along through her digestive tract, the zoo said Wednesday.
Video released by the zoo Wednesday shows Fiona snorting and moving about her indoor enclosure.
Veterinarians sedated her Tuesday for a second time to evaluate her condition, said Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health.
An ultrasound showed some bunching of her intestines, indicating she is still trying to pass the obstruction, Wenninger said. They also conducted a colonoscopy, using a 9-foot scope, he said.
Specialists have told the zoo that surgery isn’t an option for full-grown hippos, he said.

Fiona, who became a global sensation as a tiny newborn after her premature birth in 2017, has inspired books, a line of beer and a bobblehead. During her first year, the zoo recorded her progress while fans worldwide followed her growth online.
She initially couldn’t stand on her own and weighed just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms) at birth, 25 pounds (11.3 kilograms) less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species.

The beloved hippo swallowed the hat just over a week ago. A visitor tossed it into the air, and a ceiling fan caught and catapulted it through a small opening above the area’s viewing windows, said zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley.
Zoo staff are now monitoring her around the clock, trying to keep her hydrated and giving Fiona her favorite foods to help her pass the knit cap, the zoo said.
“Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she has always liked,” Curley said Wednesday. “And they were happy to see her respond.”

title: UK, EU agree deals on trade and youth movement, reshaping post-Brexit relationship
summary: UK and EU agree deals on trade and youth movement, pledging an “ambitious and dynamic” post-Brexit relationship
story: UK and EU agree deals on trade and youth movement, pledging an “ambitious and dynamic” post-Brexit relationship
BRUSSELS -- UK and EU agree deals on trade and youth movement, pledging an “ambitious and dynamic” post-Brexit relationship.
THIS IS AN APNewsAlert. Check back for updates. AP's earlier story is below.

A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials met with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences, and just perhaps, to pave the way for them to get back together.

Burnham said the two sides would agree to a “pragmatic” set of deals that will make it easier for food products and young people to move between Britain and the bloc, but leave big questions about the relationship unanswered. Months — likely years — of negotiations lie ahead on everything from student fees to manufacturing rules.
“The deal is done,” a British government spokesperson said, adding that details would be published in a joint statement later.

Burnham was scheduled to hold just under an hour of talks in Brussels with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Then they'll all meet in a plenary session with U.K. government ministers and European commissioners.

Burnham has described the rare EU-U.K. summit — only the second since Britain became the first country to leave the world’s biggest trading bloc — as a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce.
“The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained,” he said this week.

Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc. But he's stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining.

Ahead of the meeting, von der Leyen said she wanted it to be “a summit of ambition and concrete results. More opportunities for young people. Easier agrifood trade. And a stronger cooperation on economic security.”
Burnham pitched the package of agreements expected to be agreed Friday as a way of “cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people.”
He said “a closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe.”
The deals are set to include an agreement for up to 100,000 young adults from Britain to live and work in EU countries for up to three years, and the same number of Europeans to come to the U.K.

There will also be an emissions trading agreement and a deal to remove checks on food and agricultural products that will make things cheaper and easier for British exporters to Europe. Burnham said Friday the deals could add 0.5% to Britain’s economy — he'd previously set it at 0.4%.

But nothing in U.K.-EU relations is ever quick or simple. An EU official said the package is contingent on the two sides reaching agreement on university tuition fees in the next six months. EU negotiators want European students to pay domestic fees if they study in Britain rather than the higher fees for foreign students, something the U.K. has resisted. The official said negotiations had not been easy but they sensed good will to resolve the issue.
The official was designated to brief reporters about the summit but only on condition that they not be named.
Talks are also continuing on Britain's desire to have access to the bloc’s “made in Europe” rules for manufacturing.
To get the deals, the U.K. must accept some EU rules and standards that it has no role in setting. Supporters of Brexit say that undermines Britain’s independence.

“I’m afraid that the great Brexit debate has just started again,” Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told the BBC. He said “it’s perfectly clear that this very, very soon becomes a debate about: do we rejoin or do we stay out?”

The war in Ukraine, and the U.K.’s military strength, are drawing the two back together, and the summit provides the EU with an opportunity to discuss stronger cooperation on security and defense, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration.

“Our security and prosperity are closely intertwined, making a strong partnership between us essential,” Costa said ahead of the meeting. “By deepening our cooperation, we can strengthen our ability to address the challenges of our time, strengthen our resilience and promote stability in Europe and beyond.”

Nevertheless, feelings remain raw, and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the U.K. rejoining. They are weary from the shifting demands of seven British prime ministers over the last decade and want real clarity about the country’s intentions.

Ireland’s ambassador in London, Sonja Hyland, said that when Britain voted for Brexit, “there was a lack of clarity as to exactly what that meant.” If Britain wants to reopen negotiations, she said, it must “make a clear decision as to what it wants.”
Lawless reported from London.

title: Fed minutes: Higher interest rates needed in December as inflation worries mount
summary: Nearly all Federal Reserve officials expect the central bank will lift its key interest rate by a quarter point in December, minutes from a meeting last month showed, while some supported a hike in October and two floated the possibility of a half-poin...
story: Nearly all Federal Reserve officials expect the central bank will lift its key interest rate by a quarter point in December, minutes from a meeting last month showed, while some supported a hike in October and two floated the possibility of a half-poin...

WASHINGTON -- Nearly all Federal Reserve officials expect the central bank will lift its key interest rate by a quarter point in December, minutes from a meeting last month showed, while some supported a hike in October and two floated the possibility of a half-point increase next month.

The minutes, released three weeks after the Oct. 27-28 meeting of the Fed's rate-setting committee, also said a “vast majority” of the 19 members of the Fed's policymaking committee worried that inflation could persist even if gas prices kept declining and the impact of tariffs and the buildout of AI infrastructure faded.

The minutes will solidify expectations for a rate hike not only in December but likely early next year as well. Wall Street investors already see the odds of a December rate hike at nearly 95%, according to CME Fedwatch. When the Fed lifts its key rate, over time it can also raise borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans and credit cards. Home sales have withered as mortgage rates have topped 7% in recent months.

The Fed kept its key rate unchanged at 3.9% in October after raising it for the first time in three years in September. Chairman Kevin Warsh at a news conference Oct. 28 gave little guidance on the central bank's next moves, but the statement issued after the Fed's meeting acknowledged that “inflation remains elevated.”

The minutes said “some" policymakers supported lifting rates in October. Two of them, Fed governor Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, formally dissented in favor of higher rates. President Donald Trump has sought to fire Cook, but the Supreme Court ruled in June she could keep her position while the case is litigated.

Inflation has accelerated this fall and is showing signs of broadening beyond industries directly affected by higher oil and gas prices or tariffs, a trend that has raised alarm among many policymakers. Several have spoken out in favor of more rate hikes in the past week.

Fed governor Christopher Waller said in an interview on CNBC early Wednesday that inflation is “headed in the wrong direction and it’s spreading out ″ into more goods and services. Waller is one of the Fed's seven governors and a member of its rate-setting committee.

“If you really want to get it down, you’ve got to start taking more aggressive actions,” Waller said. He reiterated his support for a half-point rate increase at the Fed’s December meeting, double the usual hike. He also said that several more hikes — not just the two that many economists forecast — might be needed to tame inflation.

The minutes suggested that one other official also agreed that a half-point increase should be considered in December, though it’s not clear that the official is a voting member. Twelve of the 19 members of the committee vote on rate decisions, though all participate in the debates. The minutes don’t identify which officials took which positions.

Waller noted that in the past three months, core inflation, which excludes the volatile food and energy categories, has run at about a 3.5% annual rate, far above the Fed’s target of 2%. Businesses increasingly appear willing to pass on their own rising costs and also believe their customers can handle price increases of about 3%, he added.
“That’s the kind of psychology I think we need to start breaking,” Waller said.

Waller also took a shot at Warsh by arguing that one reason he supported a half-point hike is that without greater communication, financial markets won’t know whether a quarter-point increase in December will be followed by a similar move in January. If investors do have a sense of further hikes in the pipeline, they’ll push up market rates in anticipation and help the Fed cool inflation, Waller said.
Yet Warsh has steadily refrained from providing such guidance, which he has said locks the Fed to a predetermined path.

Separately, John Williams, president of the New York Fed and vice chair of the Fed's rate-setting committee, has pushed back against the potential for a half-point increase. He told Axios Tuesday, “I don’t think the situation calls for dramatic action.”

Other Fed officials have suggested many more hikes are likely necessary. Alberto Musalem, president of the St. Louis Fed, said Tuesday in a speech in Buenos Aires that “the economy will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027” to bring inflation down.

The economy is expanding at a healthy pace, he added, and interest rates aren’t high enough to restrain borrowing and spending sufficiently to cool inflation. Musalem does not have a vote on rates this year.

Mary Daly, president of the San Francisco Fed, said last week that she is leaning toward supporting further rate hikes, and added that she also worries that companies are increasingly willing to pass on higher costs to consumers.
“That’s the inflationary impulse that we want to avoid,” Daly said.

title: Helicopter that crashed, killing 1 and injuring 2, was flying 'extremely' low: NTSB
summary: Investigators say a helicopter that crashed earlier this month in Biscayne Bay had been flying so low that it hit the water on a turn
story: Investigators say a helicopter that crashed earlier this month in Biscayne Bay had been flying so low that it hit the water on a turn

MIAMI -- A helicopter that crashed earlier this month in Biscayne Bay, killing one person and critically injuring two others, had been flying so low that it hit the water on a turn, the National Transportation Safety Board said Wednesday.

The Robinson R44 II helicopter went down Nov. 4 near Bill Baggs State Park off Key Biscayne while on a trip to film a powerboating event offshore, the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said. The pilot died, and a photographer and videographer on board were injured.

The helicopter was making low-altitude turns “extremely” close to the surface of the water, according to the safety board's preliminary report. Some of the helicopter's doors had been removed to facilitate photography and videography. On one turn, the rotor blades hit the water and brought down the aircraft.

The photographer told investigators the helicopter flew low and parallel to a boat's right side, then turned and got ahead of it for a “good shot” as the boat passed underneath, according to the report. Then the videographer observed the rotor blades strike the water.

Television news video of the crash showed the helicopter upside down underwater with two yellow floats attached to the bottom of its landing skids. Those emergency floats are designed to help keep a helicopter afloat in a water landing.

Witnesses in nearby boats made distress calls, and a good Samaritan tried to help one of the victims, Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said. Rescue workers from several local agencies, as well as the U.S. Coast Guard and U.S. Customs and Border Protection, responded to the crash.

title: Book excerpt: "We Thought They'd Never Leave" by Tony Shalhoub with Josie Adams
summary: The Emmy- and Tony Award-winning actor and his daughter collaborate on a book featuring reflections on food and extended family, including their yearly ritual of a week-long summer reunion.
story: We may receive an affiliate commission from anything you buy from this article.

Emmy- and Tony Award-winning actor Tony Shalhoub's new book, "We Thought They'd Never Leave: Musings on Food and Family" (written with daughter Josie Adams, and published by Gallery Books), offers reflections on food and his extended family, including their yearly ritual of a week-long summer reunion.
Read an excerpt below, and don't miss Tracy Smith's interview with Tony Shalhoub and Josie Adams on "CBS Sunday Morning" November 22!
Prefer to listen? Audible has a 30-day free trial available right now.
Origin Story
What kind of lunatic family willingly gathers fifty-plus people in one place for seven days straight with no catered food, no outside help, and no exit strategy? Mine.

Every July, we converge in Wisconsin like salmon returning to spawn. Only with more card games, more garlic, and slightly less grace. Outsiders never believe it when I explain it to them. Nearly all my relatives, across four generations, cooking every meal from scratch, cleaning up the fallout, negotiating sleeping arrangements, and arguing over who's on the hook for Tuesday breakfast. No, we don't get paid. Yes, we do it every year. And the most bewildered question I'm always asked is ... Why?!

I used to respond with logistics. I'd explain how each family takes a night to cook, how we rotate the duties—head chef, sous chef, cleanup crew—as if we were on a ship, alone at sea with no port in sight. I'd describe how the menu is posted months in advance, how someone inevitably forgets the garlic, how someone else then inevitably overbuys the garlic, how someone else altogether inevitably burns the garlic, and how, miraculously, it all gets eaten anyway.

I'd outline the sleeping arrangements: the cousins packed in bunk beds like sardines, the uncles snoring in recliners, the blow-up mattresses that never survive the week. But logistics only explain how it works, not why it works. And that's the real question, isn't it? Because if you drill down, this reunion is objectively insane. Most sane people spend their summers escaping family obligations—jetting off to beaches, renting cabins far away from their in-laws, finding any excuse to avoid the awkward conversations and mismatched expectations that come with extended kin. We, on the other hand, run toward them—voluntarily spending seven days each summer marinating in each other's quirks, grievances, and toum sauce.

Truth is, a reunion should not be confused with a vacation. It's work. It's heavy lifting—sometimes literally, when you're carrying cases of tomatoes up the steps or hauling coolers of ice across the lawn. It's emotional labor, too: smoothing over past grudges, refereeing card games, and determining which conversations are "on the table" and which are simply "tabled."

Which is why, to explain why we do this, to understand this ritual of ours—the chopping and bickering and feeding of too many people until the table groans—I need to go back a hundred years, to another table on another continent, where the question wasn't how to make food for fifty, but whether there would be bread enough for one.

title: Here are the GTA 6 songs you'll hear cruising around Vice City
summary: Grand Theft Auto 6 players carry out missions to songs by artists such as Cardi B, Lana Del Rey and Travis Scott.
story: Grand Theft Auto 6 relies on a murderer's row of musical hitmakers to provide the backbeat for cruising around Vice City.

The latest installment in the video game franchise, which officially launched on Thursday, features 34 original songs from a range of artists, including Cardi B, Lana Del Rey, Travis Scott and Morgan Wallen. The game's official album was created in partnership with Atlantic Records, and will be available on music platforms such as Spotify and Apple Music beginning on Nov. 20.
Rockstar Games, the company behind the GTA series, is also offering fans limited-edition vinyl and CDs featuring the original tracks.
Music is an essential part of the GTA experience for players like 34-year-old Kansas City resident Cameron Logan Cox, who credits the game's music over the years with helping springboard his career.
"I went on to become a filmmaker and director for a hip-hop label," he told CBS News. "I really don't think I would have had that musical affinity if not for GTA."

In addition to the official GTA 6 soundtrack, gamers will be exposed to countless other tracks through "in-game radio," a feature in GTA 6 that allows players to listen to songs from fictional radio stations while they carry out their missions. They can turn on a station while they drive through Vice City, or via their phone.
"My favorite thing in GTA has never been a mission," Cox told CBS News. "It's the car, the radio and nowhere I have to be."

GTA 6 offers 22 stations, according to industry media outlet GameStop. Some have DJ personas, such as the Cocoteo FM station, which is hosted by characters voiced by Puerto Rican singers Bad Bunny and RaiNao, according to Rolling Stone.

GameStop has a list of some of the songs in Vice City. Among the hundreds of tracks are old hits like "Let Your Love Flow" by the Bellamy Brothers and "Pour Some Sugar on Me" by Def Leppard, as well as more recent hits like Chappell Roan's "HOT TO GO!".

title: Gamers, start your engines. Grand Theft Auto 6 is ready to roll.
summary: The latest, long-awaited version of the hit video game franchise launches at midnight local time on Nov. 19 in countries worldwide. Here's what to know about GTA 6.
story: In the immortal words of Carl "CJ" Johnson from an earlier edition of Grand Theft Auto, "Ah s***, here we go again." After 13 years and two delayed launches, video game fans are finally getting their hands on Grand Theft Auto 6.

GTA, as it's widely known, has evolved since its launch in 1997 into one of the biggest franchises in entertainment and one of the few sure hits in the ferociously competitive video game world. Tens of millions of people globally are expected to pick up their joysticks as Rockstar Games, the company behind the series, rolls out GTA 6 on Nov. 19 in countries around the world.

As fans eagerly await the latest GTA installment, Rockstar has whipped up interest with a series of trailers and even an extended look on Netflix. In typical fashion, however, the company has kept the hype simmering by withholding key information about the game ahead of its official launch this week.

"Having been over a decade since the last full release of a Grand Theft Auto game, all that energy just keeps getting bottled up and bottled up, and people are reading into every tweet and every little piece of news that's coming out of Rockstar to try and glean all the details of this game," Andrew Marok, director of equity research for digital media at financial firm Raymond James, told CBS News.
Here's what to know about the long-awaited release of GTA 6.
What is GTA 6 about?

The latest GTA installment centers on the stories of Lucia Caminos, the game's first-ever female protagonist, and Jason Duval. Jason, who has been working for drug runners, craves a quieter life but keeps getting dragged back into crime, according to Rockstar's synopsis of GTA 6. Lucia, meanwhile, has recently left Leonida Penitentiary, where she landed after "fighting for her family."

When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair becomes entangled in a wider conspiracy. The series is based in Vice City, inspired by Miami, in the fictional state of Leonida. Rockstar has touted the location as the most detailed version of the game yet, with architecture, beaches, roads and bars all inspired by South Florida.
There's "this concept of GTA 6 being just bigger than the game," Marok said.  "It's also about the immersion in the world of Vice City."
What equipment do I need to play the game?

Players will need a PlayStation 5 or an Xbox Series X/S console to play GTA 6. Rockstar told players who are preloading the game to plan ahead, as they may need up to 212 GB of storage space, depending on their device.
When can people start playing?

The game officially debuts worldwide on Thursday, Nov. 19. Rather than a single launch time, GTA 6 is rolling out at midnight local time in countries around the world, giving some users access before others. This website shows the countdown time by country.

Pre-orders for the game began back in June. But users weren't allowed to start pre-downloading on their PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles until Nov. 10, according to Rockstar. Gamers were also able to purchase a "code-in-box" version, a physical case that contains a code users can input to download the game from the PlayStation Store or Xbox.
How much does it cost?
Grand Theft Auto 6 costs $79.99 for the "standard edition" and $99.99 for the "ultimate edition." The latter contains an exclusive collection of cars, weapons and apparel.
What are players saying?

New Zealand was among the first countries where players could access the game. One 25-year-old told CBS News he set up his PlayStation account to appear as if he were in New Zealand — where the game is already live — rather than his home in the United Kingdom, to access it as soon as possible.
"It's definitely more immersive than previous entries," he told CBS News, requesting anonymity because he is taking a day off from work to play GTA 6. "Visually, it's incredible."
Other gamers were also quick to praise GTA 6's visual quality and action-packed plot.

"The gameplay dynamics are just amazing, and the graphics are great, and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep, which is impressive," Adam Simmons, a 50-year-old in Wellington, New Zealand, where the game has already rolled out, told The Associated Press.

On Metacritic, a review aggregator website, players gave GTA 6 a score of 99 out of 100. "Grand Theft Auto VI, against all odds, has somehow managed to not only meet but surpass all my expectations," one user wrote.
How long does it take to play?
Insider Gaming, a website focused on the video game industry, said it takes an average of roughly 50 hours to complete all of the missions in GTA 6.
When will online play launch?

The online, multiplayer version of the game introduces new missions and allows players to stay immersed in the world of GTA after completing the more linear single-player version. It's free with the option of in-game purchases, according to Marok of Raymond James.
Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar's parent company, hasn't confirmed GTA Online's availability, though it seems likely given its enormous revenue potential.
"That's where GTA 5 made so much of its money," Marok said.
Will there be a PC version?

Rockstar Games did not respond to a request for comment about whether it will release a desktop version of the game. Historically, a PC version has been released about 12 to 18 months after the console version, according to Marok. However, the company could decide to launch it sooner.

"I think that there are reasons why Rockstar and Take-Two would want the PC version of the game out sooner than usual, and a lot of that has to do with the Grand Theft Auto Online component of the game, which is the multiplayer, ongoing monetization piece of it," he told CBS News.
Who plays GTA?
Male millennials and Gen Zers represent the key demographic playing GTA 6, according to a recent report from Sensor Tower. The company estimates 72% of players are male, while 57% are under 35.
What music is featured in the game?

GTA 6 features an original adaptive score from Justice, the Grammy-winning French electronic duo featuring Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay. The music is "dynamically tuned to the different ways players engage with the world of Vice City and Leonida throughout Jason and Lucia's story," Rockstar Games said on its website.
The 30-track "Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score" is scheduled for release Dec. 11 and includes collaborations with Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.
Who are the voice actors?

Rockstar has not disclosed the full voice cast. However, actress Manni Perez was nominated for her voice acting in the "Best Performance" category at The Game Awards, an annual ceremony that celebrates the video game industry. Actor Stephen Root has also confirmed to the AP that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly disclosed his participation.
How many GTA 6 units have already been sold?

The company had sold 19 million units, including pre-order copies, and generated $1.84 billion in revenue by Thursday, according to Sensor Tower. The market intelligence and digital analytics platform said earlier this month that GTA 6 is the "most pre-ordered game in history."
Raymond James projects that Rockstar will sell 50 million units of the game from launch through the end of Take-Two's fiscal year 2027, which runs until March 31.
"That would be by some distance the biggest launch in video gaming history," Marok said.

GTA 5, released in 2013, has sold nearly 235 million copies, according to Take-Two. The game has generated more than $10 billion in revenue over the last 13 years, according to Victor Matheson, an economist at the College of the Holy Cross who studies sports and major events.
How much did GTA 6 cost to make?
Rockstar hasn't disclosed the exact figure, but analysts estimate GTA 6 cost upward of $1 billion to produce, which would make it the most expensive video game in history.
"I would be shocked if it was under a billion dollars because they've been working on this for the better part of a decade," Marok said.
Asked about the price tag during a recent Wall Street Journal event, Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick didn't offer an exact figure, saying only, "It was expensive, and it took a long time."

title: CBS to air Kennedy Center Honors in December
summary: CBS has reached a one-year deal to air the awards ceremony next month, sources said.
story: The Kennedy Center Honors may have left the Kennedy Center itself, but the annual awards gala isn't leaving its longtime broadcast home. CBS has reached a one-year deal to air the awards ceremony next month, according to sources familiar with the arrangement.

This year's event, scheduled to be taped on Sunday, Dec. 7, and aired on Dec. 27, will be held at Capital One Arena in downtown Washington. Honorees include musicians Paul Anka and Barbara Mandrell, composer David Foster, actor Andy Garcia and playwright David Mamet.

In September, the Kennedy Center board voted to close the performing arts center amid a legal dispute over building upgrades and attempts to add President Trump's name to the facade. Mr. Trump said he would only help fundraise for renovations if his name was added to the facade. A federal judge in Washington, D.C., however, ruled that only Congress had the authority to change the building's name.

While modest maintenance projects continue, planning for the major renovations are underway and a construction schedule cannot be set until an ongoing federal court case halting construction is resolved. A court hearing is set for Thursday.

CBS has broadcast the Kennedy Center Honors each year since 1978. The multiyear contract lapsed after the 2025 show, but the arts center and the network reached a short-term deal for this year's show last week. The program will also stream on Paramount+.

President Trump co-hosted the show in 2025, punctuating artistic performances with several speeches throughout the evening. The White House did not respond to a CBS News inquiry on whether the president would attend this year.

title: Bezos says he was "heavily involved" in casting Pattinson as 007
summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos says "it was obvious" to him and others that Robert Pattinson should be the next James Bond.
story: Amazon founder and executive chairman Jeff Bezos said Tuesday that he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.

Speaking at Semafor's Silicon Valley and The World forum in California, the head of the retail and entertainment giant that now owns the rights to the 007 franchise spoke about what he called the "real old-fashioned screen tests" for five Bond finalists, complete with "full costume, real sets."

On Friday, the team of selectors spent several hours going over the screen tests of each actor, Bezos said in remarks reported by Semafor, adding that while they were all "extraordinarily talented … there was something special about Rob."
Bezos said the group was initially biased against Pattinson, "because he's already so famous," and they had been inclined to choose someone "a little more unknown."
The role of the iconic British spy has historically gone to lesser-known actors, who have then made their name doing the Bond movies.
"But in the screening tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond," Bezos said of Pattinson, who shot to fame with his starring role in the "Twilight" vampire movies.

Amazon bought MGM, which co-owns the rights to the Bond franchise, in 2022. Pattinson will be the first Bond not forged under the creative stewardship of the Broccoli family, who had run the franchise since 1962, when the first movie featuring 007, "Dr. No," was released.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement after he was unveiled as the seventh actor to take on the role. "To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

He will step into the shoes of Hollywood leading men Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig to star in the 26th Bond movie, which will be directed by Denis Villeneuve. It is expected to hit screens in 2028.

title: New James Bond is announced after rampant speculation
summary: After rampant online speculation about who would take over the iconic spy character from Daniel Craig, the franchise announced who the new 007 will be.
story: Robert Pattinson is the new 007. After rampant online speculation about who would take over the iconic spy character from Daniel Craig, the franchise announced Monday that Pattinson will be the next James Bond.
He will be the seventh actor to play the role since the first Bond film, "Dr. No," was released in 1962.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement. "... To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

The naming of Pattinson comes five years after the beloved franchise's last film, 2021's "No Time to Die," which marked the first time in Bond's 64-year history on the silver screen to end with the character's death.
But 007 will be reborn in the 26th Bond film, directed by Denis Villeneuve. It will be the first since Amazon MGM took over the franchise.
For months, fans had been debating the merits of other potential 007s, including names like Callum Turner, Josh O'Connor, Jack Lowden and Nicholas Hoult.
Pattinson only entered the rumor mill recently after the revelation that he screen-tested for the role, the Associated Press reported, along with a few other finalists.

"Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey," Villeneuve said in a statement. "We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."
Pattinson is already associated with three mega-franchises: "The Batman," "Twilight" and "Harry Potter."

Since his breakthrough in "Twilight," Pattinson has also worked in more independent films such as "Good Time," "The Lighthouse" and "Mickey 17." Earlier this year, he drew rave reviews for his villainous performance in Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey."
The British royal family responded to the news on social media, saying: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."
Now in the Bond role, Pattinson follows in the footsteps of Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Craig.

title: Raye leads the 2027 Grammy nominations. See the list.
summary: English singer-songwriter Raye is up for 11 awards at the 2027 Grammys, followed by Spanish singer Rosalía​ with nine nominations.
story: English singer-songwriter Raye leads the 2027 Grammy Award nominations, the Recording Academy announced Monday.

Raye is up for 11 awards at February's ceremony: record, song and album of the year — the first time she's been nominated in those big categories — as well as songwriter of the year non-classical, a variety of pop categories and music video.
Her 11 nods also mean she has tied Beyoncé's record at the 2025 Grammys for the most nominations in a single year by a female artist.
Speaking of Bey: She continues her reign as the most-nominated artist in Grammy history, scoring her 100th nod for "Morning Dew (Donk)" in the R&B solo performance category.

Raye, who is riding the success of her critically acclaimed album "This Music May Contain Hope," has 15 Grammy nominations across her career. She's never won one, though she was previously recognized by the Recording Academy with the noncompetitive Harry Belafonte best song for social change award.

Spanish singer Rosalía, fresh off her album of the year win at the 27th annual Latin Grammy Awards on Thursday for her avant-garde "Lux," follows Raye with nine nominations. She's a first-time nominee in all the categories she's up for: record, song and album of the year as well as pop solo performance, alternative music performance, alternative music album, Latin song, global music performance and music video.

Following her are Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo, Phoebe Bridgers and first-time nominee Ella Langley, who are tied with seven nods each. Bruno Mars, Leon Thomas and 2026's best new artist winner Olivia Dean have six nominations each.
Taylor Swift's nomination is her fifth consecutive studio album to be nominated for album of the year, something only one other artist has ever done: Kendrick Lamar.

Only recordings commercially released in the U.S. between Aug. 31, 2025, and Aug. 28, 2026, were eligible for nominations. The final round of Grammy voting, which determines the winners, will take place between Dec. 10 and Jan. 7.
The 2027 Grammy Awards will air Feb. 7 at 7 p.m. Eastern, live on ABC for the first time since 1972, from the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. It will also stream on Disney+ and Hulu.

title: 4 NFL officials work 2 games each due to ground stop, a rarity
summary: Four NFL officials worked two games Sunday — a rarity stemming from Friday's nationwide ground stop ordered by the FAA that threw airlines' schedules into complete disarray.
story: Cincinnati — Don Willard did something on Sunday that the NFL hopes doesn't ever have to be duplicated — refereeing two games in one day.

Willard was the referee Sunday afternoon for the Miami Dolphins' game against the Indianapolis Colts in Indianapolis before he and three other members of the crew made the 114-mile trip to work the prime-time contest between the Pittsburgh Steelers and Cincinnati Bengals.

The reshuffling happened after the Federal Aviation Administration called for a nationwide ground stop Friday. The stop caused consternation and chaos for professional and college teams throughout the country and even resulted in moving at least one college football game from Saturday to Sunday.

NFL officials audibled by reassigning game officials for this week's matchups to stadiums closer to cities where they reside so they could drive, and Willard was asked to take over as the lead ref for the two games.

Willard usually works NFL games as a side judge. About an hour before kickoff in Indianapolis, he did the traditional microphone check and then he handled the coin toss duties typically reserved for referees.
Willard wasn't the only one doing double duty Sunday.

Umpire Terry Killens, field judge Jabir Walker and side judge Justin Larrew also jumped in a minibus and made the two-hour drive down I-74 to work the game in Cincinnati. It's the first time this officiating crew has worked together.
The four officials arrived in Cincinnati at 6:39 p.m., giving them some time to prepare before the 8:20 p.m. kickoff.

There were two instant replay reversals during the first half. A 23-yard completion to Pittsburgh's Germie Bernard was overturned when replay saw Bernard's toe was just out of bounds. An interception by Cincinnati's Jordan Battle was also reversed when a second look showed the ball hit the ground.
However, the crew called only 12 penalties in a game that usually sees a lot of flags because of the intensity of the Steelers-Bengals rivalry.

"I thought they did a great job managing a very difficult game, very testy game, obviously by both sides. So hats off to those guys for what they pulled off today. I know it was a long day for them," Bengals coach Zac Taylor said.
League officials didn't make any of the four officials who did double duty available to the media for either of Sunday's games.
NBC Sports rules analyst Terry McAulay, who worked three Super Bowls, said during Sunday night's "Football Night in America" pregame show that what the crew did was extraordinarily challenging.

"At a high level, it's a brand-new crew working together to work this game tonight that did not have at all the normal preparation - studying tendencies, studying formation style of play, and especially for this game, studying matchups on both sides of the ball. AFC North divisional games are brutal to officiate," he said. "Just working one NFL football game for three hours is incredibly mentally exhausting. When it's done, you're mentally drained. These guys have to do it now twice in one day. They don't have the normal recovery time. I know when I did it, my recovery time was never less than four hours."
The Dolphins didn't have any travel issues, a team spokesman said.

title: Billy Evans tells his side of "You Can See Everything," Elizabeth Holmes' portrayal
summary: In his first TV interview, Billy Evans, partner of disgraced Theranos co-founder Elizabeth Holmes, talks about his characterization in the documentary "You Can See Everything," as well as threats he says have been made against his family's safety.
story: Billy Evans may be the most-talked-about person in the most-talked-about film of the year, the documentary "You Can See Everything." He sat down with "CBS Sunday Morning" for his first-ever TV interview.

Why now? "You gotta learn really painful lessons sometimes in life," he said. "And with Elizabeth going through everything she did in the press, the lesson that was ingrained in us is, 'You can't lose your voice.'"

"You Can See Everything" is a film by Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder, who shot to fame as an absurdist comedian, and who (along with cameras) moved in with Evans and his partner Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks before the disgraced Theranos founder reported to prison in 2023.

Evans, a 34-year-old MIT grad who'd also worked in high-tech, emerges as a shape-shifting central character. Asked if he is the person we saw in the film, or something else, Evans said, "I'm deeply passionate about my family and about the work that I do. But no, I am not some controlling monster who's leveraging his wife for insert-whatever-anybody-is-saying. No, I am not those things."
It's easy to understand why the genre-bending film has become a cultural phenomenon … harder to understand why Evans agreed to do it.

"I think sometimes I take too big of risks," he said. Such as? "Inviting Nathan Fielder into your home for 34 days and trusting somebody to have the right to portray you in any way, shape or form that they so choose."

In the film, Evans is portrayed as a villain – controlling and manipulative. Yet, Evans doesn't seem angry about that: "It's super-painful, but me being angry about it doesn't help change it. Look, I'm going to live my life with integrity and with who I am, and I hope people can see that over time. But if they don't, what I care about is the people that I know, people that love me."

In fact, of the documentary that has gotten rave reviews, Evans says, "I love the film," despite the fact that he is made out to be a villain. "I would have preferred for that not to be the case, but it's entertainment, you know, and I didn't get to control that edit."
His goal, he said, was "to have people see Elizabeth. And when I watch that movie, I see the person that I love in exactly who she is."

In 2014 Forbes Magazine crowned Holmes the youngest self-made female billionaire. By 2017, the year she and Evans met, she was under investigation for defrauding investors for a diagnostic machine that she falsely claimed could test for hundreds of diseases with a single drop of blood.

Evans says when they first met, he did not know who she was. "I had been at her office earlier that week," he said. "I had, like, seen her the same week. But no, really, like, the first time I met her, I did not know."

"You Can See Everything" leaves us questioning what the truth is. There are also moments that are cringe-worthy, as when Evans is filmed in the shower completely naked. [You really can see everything.]

"I did not give consent to do that," said Evans. "Now, did I know they were filming me in the shower? Yes. But we would film 16 hours a day. Like, all sorts of things were filmed with assurances made. I was just as surprised as the rest of the country to have my whole body on camera for the world to see, and it's been an awkward experience in having, like, your kids' teachers see that. It's really uncomfortable."

Evans said there were "inappropriate" and "awkward" things that happened every single day, as well as requests to film things that, he said, "are not appropriate for television. All sorts of things that the details I'd rather spare the audience."
The film's production company, A24, said, "Everything that was filmed was filmed with their consent."

Some who see the film leave convinced the co-director, Nathan Fielder, had feelings for Holmes. "I think that there are bits that are played up to criticize his own bias," said Evans. "This is a film about, what can you trust? And at the end nothing is clear."

Evans says he has not spoken to Fielder since he's seen the film. "I think they're probably worried I'm gonna sue 'em," he said, adding he has no intention to do so. "Because maybe I'm a different person than most people think I am."

Evans lives with their two young children in Texas close to Holmes' prison, and carries a gun 24/7, he says, to keep his family safe. "We have threats of violence against us daily," he said. "I've got two kids. Threats of violence daily. And I would never forgive myself for having the tools, the skills, and the ability to protect my family and not doing it.

"I will give you an example: The other day, I was driving my kids to school. And a car came up behind us really, really quickly. And we stopped at the light. And the guy starts screaming next to me. And this isn't just road rage, okay? And his window is down. And he is screaming the most vile things you have ever heard about: 'I know where you live. I know who you are. I know where your kids sleep, and the things that I will do to you.' And it was terrifying."

Even given the fallout from the movie, he says he would do it all again: "With the same people, making the same film again, with everything that I know right now? 100%. Because I would also have a better understanding of what I was walking into."
Elizabeth Holmes could transfer to a halfway house next summer. Until then, Evans and their children visit her every week behind bars.

Having his children see their mother in prison, Evens said, has become "strangely normal. Like, I hate it. I absolutely hate that my daughter's first steps were in federal prison. I hate that. … But it doesn't mean that we can't find joy as we experience this. And our job, to them, is not to talk about how much it hurts and how painful it is, but to find the joy in seeing how many acorns we can collect in the prison yard and fit in a water bottle. It's finding, you know, the small, little games that we can play to make each time we go to the same place, every weekend, feel like you're going to Disneyland."

Evans said he used to count the days she was in prison, but that became too painful. "It's been since May 30th of 2023," he said. "I miss her so much. You know, I talked to her right before I came in here. And I told her, I said, 'I'm kinda nervous.' And she said, 'Just be zen. Enjoy it. Embody love. And I'll talk to you, when you're done.'"

title: The Reader: A new review source for book lovers
summary: With most newspapers and wire services closing the book on sections devoted to book reviews, Washington Monthly introduces its new online resource, offering reviews, essays, and recommendations by some of the world's top writers.
story: It's become an all-too-familiar story: Earlier this year, the Washington Post put an end to Book World, its weekly book review supplement.
"Books are expensive," said bestselling author Jonathan Alter. "Readers need help to know what's good out there."

Alter says Book World's closure created a void: "Thirty years ago, there were 30 American newspapers that, as part of their Sunday newspaper, had a book review section," he said. Today, only The New York Times still maintains a separate book review section.
"So, we stepped into the breach, and we're doing something about it," said Alter, who is co-founder of The Reader, a new, general interest, online book review, to be published every weekday.

Executive editor Haley Sweetland Edwards said, "We will have mostly book reviews, but also essays about books, columns about the literary book world, and top authors like Robert Caro and Margaret Atwood and Ann Patchett will be providing recommendations of books that have slipped below the cultural radar."

The Reader is part of Washington Monthly, a non-profit magazine. Edwards says authors lined up to be part of it: "We have 31 Pulitzer Prize-winners who have agreed to be contributors over the next year. These are the crème de la crème, and they will be reviewing for us."

Alter said, "We will review books that are going to become big bestsellers, but we're also going to review those books that sometimes fly under the radar, that are really good and that just aren't getting the recognition that they deserve."
And that's where "Sunday Morning" comes in. Each weekend, we'll offer two books for your consideration – one fiction, one non-fiction – courtesy of The Reader.

title: Can Anthropic win hearts and minds by curing hearts and minds?
summary: Anthropic says Claude Science can drive breakthroughs in drug discovery. It could also open lucrative commercial opportunities, experts say.
story: Fresh off its record-setting initial public offering, Anthropic now must show investors that it can sustain growth and generate profits. The company has a plan for that: curing some of the world's gnarliest diseases.

In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic states that AI holds the potential to "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine, potentially curing diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases, and the major infectious diseases."

Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei said in a post on X in August that he believes "it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!)."
Speeding in the right direction

Developing breakthrough drugs is among the most promising avenues of research for AI, potentially bringing treatments for a range of conditions to market much faster than is currently possible, according to scientists and industry analysts.

"AI can accelerate research. It will help you get there faster, but it's not just speed — it's directional speed," Neerav Kaushal, an AI and molecular biology expert at Michigan Technological University, told CBS News. "Let's say you're at the top of the mountain and your aim is to find a drug for cancer that lies in the valley. AI will not just help you get down there faster — it will help you get down to the right valley where the drug is."

For Anthropic, meanwhile, developing drugs could open up potentially enormous commercial opportunities. The company has partnered with biotech and pharmaceutical companies that use its Claude Science model for various purposes. Anthropic also operates its own AI-powered biology wet lab in San Francisco that has already made scientific discoveries.
"If you can use a large language model to condense any part of the timeline, it is very economically valuable," Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan told CBS News.
The challenge for Anthropic will be how it turns its life sciences research into profits. That could take time, Khan told CBS News.

"How this becomes lucrative for Anthropic is a very important question, and I think it's a question Anthropic hasn't figured out yet," Khan said. "Coding is its best-proven use case, followed by cybersecurity applications, then financial and legal research."
But the potential to move the needle for both Anthropic and its pharma partners is significant.

"If you improve your drug's efficiency by a couple of percentage points, that can make a world of difference," Khan added. "You'll get asymmetric payouts in the sense that if a model can help with any part of the process, it's very economically valuable."

For example, he expects a drug developer like Eli Lilly and Co., which partners with Anthropic to give its employees access to Claude, would be willing to pay "hundreds of millions or billions of dollars to make its arthritis drug 2% better than it is."
A way to win hearts and minds by curing them?

Developing potentially lifesaving drugs could have other benefits for Anthropic. By applying tools to the life sciences and using them to improve human life, the company could help shift the narrative around AI to a more positive one, according to experts.

"If you are the AI company that helps advance some kind of cure or solution to a sickness or illness that's prevailed for quite some time, I think that gets you a ton more trust with consumers and end users," Khan said. "Because you end up becoming the company that is actually improving the quality of life for humans at large."
