title: Marine Corps hero under federal investigation
summary: Retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal, whose bloodied visage was depicted in an iconic Iraq War photo, is under investigation stemming from his tenure as a high school JROTC instructor.
story: Henderson, Nevada — One of the most celebrated Marine Corps veterans, whose heroism during the Iraq War earned him the nation's second-highest award for combat valor and a place in military history, is the subject of a criminal investigation over allegations stemming from his tenure as a high school instructor for a Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps, CBS News has learned.

Retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal, who served in the Marine Corps for 34 years, is under investigation by the Naval Criminal Investigative Service, the primary federal law enforcement agency for matters involving the Navy and Marine Corps.

The allegations against the highly decorated Marine veteran have not been disclosed by the law enforcement agency. However, federal agencies told CBS News that the investigation concerns the period of time when he worked as a JROTC instructor at the Basic Academy of International Studies. The academy is a public high school in Henderson, Nevada, operated by the Clark County School District.

The federal investigation marks a dramatic turn for a Marine whose actions on the battlefield made him a symbol of military courage. Kasal's heroism was captured in a 2004 photograph showing him in the Second Battle of Fallujah. His uniform was soaked in blood, and he was being helped out of a building by two Marines. His right leg was shattered, and his body riddled with gunshot wounds and grenade fragments, but he still gripped a pistol and combat knife. The scene was later immortalized in statues installed at two Marine bases. He retired after 34 years of service and was the recipient of two Purple Hearts and the Navy Cross, the second-highest decoration for combat valor, behind the Medal of Honor.

On Wednesday, the Marine Corps told CBS News that the service is "aware of the allegations against a retired Marine Sergeant Major which occurred while he was employed as a civilian JROTC instructor by the Basic Academy of International Studies."
The Marine Corps also said that the Naval Criminal Investigative Service "is actively investigating the allegations, as the Department of the Navy's lead for felony-level criminal investigations."
Separately, Denise Caskey of NCIS confirmed that its field office at Camp Pendleton in California is conducting the investigation.

NCIS does not typically confirm active investigations, making this an unusual case. The agency commonly investigates matters of homicide, sexual assault, fraud and even terrorism and espionage cases. The agency also conducts counterintelligence investigations, working with other federal agencies to identify threats to national security.
Kasal did not reply to CBS News' multiple attempts to contact him.

CBS News traveled to Henderson, Nevada, and over the course of the last two weeks spoke to nearly 40 people, including former students, school district employees, city officials, parents, U.S. military service members and Marine veterans who served with Kasal. Some asked for anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly or feared reprisal.

The cadets CBS News spoke to alleged Kasal often gave rides home to a select group of female cadets. He would take them to Starbucks and spend time with certain students outside of school-sponsored functions. Some also described instances when he was alone with a cadet in a room.

A former school district employee told CBS News that Kasal was advised on several occasions about the perceptions surrounding his relationships with students and was warned against putting himself in potentially compromising situations, including being alone in a room with a cadet.

One former female cadet described developing an unusually close relationship with Kasal after meeting him in 2020, when she was 14. She said she confided in him about difficulties at home and personal matters, including her relationships with boys. After knowing her for barely a year, Kasal offered to adopt her, saying in a text message, "I'm not asking as charity. I'm asking because your [sic] wanted."

When her family members learned of Kasal's offer, she said, they made it clear that adoption was not an option. She said that her relationship with Kasal continued, and she remained comfortable confiding in him about deeply personal matters. The cadet alleged some of their conversations involved sexual rumors that had been spread about her and why Kasal believed some of the problems she was experiencing stemmed from her relationship with her father. In retrospect, she said she realizes that those conversations were inappropriate for an instructor to have with a teenage student.

She now says she thinks Kasal crossed other boundaries, alleging that Kasal invited certain cadets to spend time at his home and at his cabin, she said, including for at least one birthday celebration. He did not extend invitations to everyone in the program. She also claimed that Kasal drove one student home nearly every day.

The Clark County School District told CBS News Kasal was hired by the school district three months after he retired from the Marine Corps, in August 2018. He resigned in August 2025, the school district said.
Enrollment in Basic Academy's JROTC program fluctuates from year to year, averaging roughly 135 students. The program is overseen by a senior Marine instructor and a senior enlisted leader.
When Kasal transitioned from the Marine Corps to the high school JROTC program, he sought to restructure it to more closely resemble the military service.

Some former cadets described him as professional and organized, crediting him with establishing strict standards and bringing a sense of discipline to the program. They also praised the time, energy and personal resources he devoted to his students.

Samantha Francisco, 22, who was in the program from 2018 to 2022, said, "I can't say enough about how amazing he was," and that "he genuinely cared about everybody and taught us incredible lessons." She added that she and her husband, who was also in the JROTC program, still talk weekly about Kasal or something he taught them.

Ashley Vazquez Romo, 22, another cadet from that period, said Kasal "poured his heart and soul into the program." She recalled that he sometimes helped pay for program outings and purchased equipment, including a CPR training mannequin, so students could practice.

Damien Greenwell, 22, who participated in the JROTC program from 2018 to 2022, told CBS News that he deeply respects Kasal for his military service and mentorship, especially to cadets with a troubled home life. But Greenwell also said that over the years he questioned Kasal's conduct on several occasions, adding that even if the decorated Marine's intentions were innocent, his actions could appear inappropriate to an outside observer.

"He would mentor us on how to be a proper leader — which is his job — but he would go a bit beyond this. Sergeant Major [Kasal] helps people in a time of need and that's very honorable," Greenwell said.

"If someone couldn't eat, he would pay for their food. If someone didn't have a ride home, he would help them out. It's awesome, it's great and very commendable," Greenwell said. "But if you're regularly getting Starbucks for a girl … it looks kind of weird … and with driving people home on a consistent basis, it looks bad. You need to have a certain kind of boundary between you and students."
Greenwell told CBS News he remembers a night that still "shocks him a little." It happened in 2024, two years after Greenwell graduated.

Greenwell claimed he went to Lowe's home improvement store around 9 p.m. and saw Kasal's truck in the parking lot. In the store, he observed Kasal walking with a student who he believes was a senior at the high school or a newly minted graduate.

"It was just really weird to me," Greenwell said, recalling that he briefly exchanged greetings with Kasal and the student before the two continued down the aisle. CBS News is withholding the student's name for privacy reasons.

Greenwell said over the years of observing Kasal, he developed doubts about him. He believed the optics could be interpreted as inappropriate, but at the same time wonders if Kasal could just be trying to help students navigate the difficulties of life. But even if he found a relationship between Kasal and a student odd, he was "not gonna say anything. Like, who am I to tell [a] sergeant major?"
Daniel Gillan, who participated in the program from 2018 to 2022 and later enlisted in the Marine Corps, said JROTC was good for him and that Kasal was part of the reason he ended up joining.

The program "gave me a lot of structure and discipline," Gillan said, adding that Kasal helped him "become a better person overall, and once you become a better person, things will fall into place for you."

Gillan said he never witnessed Kasal engage in inappropriate behavior. He sees Kasal as having made an effort to create memorable experiences for students by organizing group hikes, camping trips and other activities outside the classroom. He said Kasal recognized that some students did not have a good home life, and he wanted to make the JROTC program enjoyable and inclusive, emphasizing that all cadets were invited to participate.

Still, he acknowledged that Kasal appeared to favor certain cadets, sometimes buying them coffee, for instance. Gillan said Kasal had also bought coffee for him, but he didn't think it was inappropriate, describing him as a "nice guy."

Gillan also alleged Kasal would take cadets on hikes without seeking permission from the school, but he said this was more a matter of convenience. The hiking trail was only a few minutes away from Basic Academy.
"It was about a 10-minute drive from Basic, and [about] 20 cadets would go. Whoever wanted to go, they would go. We would all carpool," Gillan said, and the hikes were just about an hour.

"Legally, you gotta get [trips] ran through the school, and they gotta approve of it, … but [Kasal is] not gonna wait for [the school] to take two weeks to [approve] an event that takes one day to get back."
One former male cadet, who joined the program in 2019 and now serves in the U.S. military, alleged that Kasal invited him to visit his cabin in Iowa over the summer.

The trip was not school-sponsored, he said, and "it was just going to be the two of us." He says he declined the invitation because he was playing a sport that summer. At the time, he said, he did not consider the invitation to be inappropriate, believing Kasal had extended it because they shared an interest in the sport.

Greenwell said that at one point, he heard a rumor that Kasal was trying to adopt a fellow cadet but that he didn't believe it was true. When CBS News told him that Kasal had offered to adopt a former female cadet, Greenwell said he was "very surprised, shocked and disappointed."
"Even if you have the best intentions in the world, it still looks bad, no matter how you put it, because she's a minor," said Greenwell.

The Defense Department and local school districts share responsibility for overseeing JROTC programs because they are federally sponsored and operate in high schools nationwide. Although instructors are employed by school districts, they must also be certified by their respective military branches, which are responsible for monitoring their professional conduct and ensuring compliance with military standards.
The military services certify and oversee instructors, while school districts handle employment decisions, classroom supervision and compliance with local education policies.

JROTC instructors must acknowledge in writing that they will not engage in prohibited activities between JROTC instructors and students. The rules ban instructors from developing personal, intimate or sexual relationships with cadets, engaging in inappropriate communications and attending social gatherings with students on a personal basis. The restrictions apply from an instructor's first contact with a cadet until six months after the student leaves the JROTC program.

Under the rules, instructors are generally not allowed to give students rides in their personal vehicles, including rides home from school. Exceptions may be made when a student's safety or welfare is at risk or for official school functions involving multiple students. The rules specifically prohibit an instructor from transporting a single student in their personal vehicles.

Instructors are also not allowed to have cadets or other students in their homes. Other interactions, such as purchasing coffee or refreshments for students, are not explicitly prohibited. But such interactions could raise questions about compliance with the rules.
Instructors must sign the acknowledgment before beginning their duties as JROTC instructors and recertify it annually.
When CBS News received the initial news tip regarding Kasal, the Marine Corps said it was aware of allegations and of an investigation, but made no mention of NCIS' involvement.

The Henderson Police Department initially said it had no record of a complaint about Kasal. The Clark County Detention Center and the Clark County District Attorney's Office also did not have any complaints about Kasal on file when contacted some two weeks ago.

Later, during that same period, a spokesperson for the Henderson Police Department said the Clark County School District Police Department was handling the matter. Multiple calls and emails to the Clark County School District and the school district's police department went unanswered. Lt. Bryan Zink of the Clark County School District police department referred inquiries to the school district.
Last week, when CBS News emailed to check in on its inquiry, an email sent in error to CBS News asked a human resources manager to "disregard the request."
When CBS News asked why the request for information was being disregarded, Bryan Callahan, the district's public information officer, emailed for the first time: "We are looking into your request."

When questioned by a CBS News reporter in Henderson earlier this week, Callahan said he was not aware of an investigation of Kasal by the Clark County School District or the school district's police department.

Before he retired from active duty, Kasal reflected on his time in Iraq. The Second Battle of Fallujah in November 2004 was the bloodiest battle involving U.S. Marines since the Vietnam War, marked by brutal house-to-house fighting against Iraqi insurgents.

In 2018, Kasal told CBS News' David Martin that he had entered the building to rescue fellow Marines trapped by insurgent gunfire during one of the war's bloodiest battles. By the time he emerged, Kasal had been shot seven times, shielded a wounded Marine from an exploding grenade and refused medical treatment until others received care.
His actions earned him his second Purple Heart and the Navy Cross.
The photograph of Kasal became an iconic symbol of Marine resilience and sacrifice. The Marine Corps Heritage Foundation named a photojournalism award for Kasal.

The photograph inspired a bronze statue called the "No Man Left Behind" monument, which is installed at both Camp Pendleton in California and Camp Lejeune in North Carolina, according to the Marine Times. The sculpture was the work of John Phelps, a Navy Vietnam veteran whose son Chance was killed in Iraq in 2004, the newspaper reported.

When CBS News first learned about the criminal investigation into Kasal earlier this month, the retired sergeant major was in New York as the guest of honor at an event hosted by the NYPD Marine Corps Association to commemorate 251 years since the founding of the U.S. Marine Corps and honor Marines who also serve as New York City police officers. The New York Post reported that Kasal was presented a framed retirement shadowbox by NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch at police headquarters in Manhattan.
James LaPorta reported from Henderson, Nevada. Julia Kimani Burnham and Eleanor Watson reported from Washington, D.C.

Editor's note: For the past three years, James LaPorta has served as a judge for the Marine Corps Heritage Foundation annual awards program. He has never judged the award category named for retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal.
Editor's note: An earlier version of this article misspelled former JROTC cadet Daniel Gillan's name. The article has been updated.

title: 3.9-magnitude earthquake rattles Los Angeles area
summary: According to the U.S. Geological Survey, the earthquake struck about a half mile north-northwest of Commerce, California, which is about 7 miles from downtown Los Angeles.
story: An early-morning 3.9-magnitude earthquake rattled the Los Angeles area on Friday.
According to the U.S. Geological Survey, the earthquake struck around 3:25 a.m. about a half-mile north-northwest of Commerce, California, which is about 7 miles from downtown Los Angeles.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass posted about the quake on social media, saying it likely woke up many Angelenos.
"While unsettling, there are no immediate reports of damage or operational impacts, including at LAX," Bass wrote. "The LAFD and City teams will continue to monitor and update as needed."
People reported feeling the quake as far away as Lancaster, California, about 80 miles north of downtown L.A., and Poway, California, about 115 miles to the south, the USGS said.

Shortly after 5:30 a.m., the LA Fire Department provided an update that no significant infra/structure damage or injuries were noted. The spokesperson added that the LAFD Earthquake Mode is complete and normal operations will resume.
"Use this event as a reminder to prepare for inevitable earthquake activity in our region," the LAFD said.

title: Americans need help affording homes. Can Congress deliver?
summary: Lawmakers may face more pressure in 2027 to focus on bipartisan housing proposals that would lower the cost of buying a home.
story: With voters pressing for relief from high costs in the midterm elections, lawmakers may face more pressure in 2027 to focus on bipartisan housing proposals that would lower the cost of buying a home.

In recent years, rising home prices, tight inventory and high mortgage rates have locked out many would-be first-time homebuyers. Three-quarters of prospective property buyers said that financial hurdles, such as rising borrowing costs, have prevented them from buying a home this year, according to a July survey from financial services firm FICO.

Some lawmakers from both parties have already introduced bills aimed at helping Americans achieve homeownership, with the proposals focused on reducing upfront costs. The midterm elections, which flipped control of both the Senate and House to the Democrats, could give those proposals fresh momentum in 2027.
"This is kind of one of those rare pockets where everyone can agree housing is expensive — 'We got to do something,'" Kate Wood, a lending expert at NerdWallet, told CBS News.

One Democratic-led proposal would provide up to $20,000 to first-generation homebuyers and up to $25,000 to low-income households to cover down payments. Another bipartisan bill, introduced in February, would permit first-time homebuyers to funnel unused education savings toward a down payment.

Experts outside of Congress are also pitching possible solutions. Lael Brainard, who served as the director of the National Economic Council during the Biden administration, has advocated for lowering the down payment on a federal loan to $1,000, while Ted Tozer, president of Ginnie Mae under former President Obama, has argued for zero-down mortgages for certain borrowers.
Inspiration from the ROAD Act
Lawmakers are likely to want to build on the success of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a landmark bipartisan housing bill passed last year to boost housing supply and bring down costs.

Given that much of the regulatory and zoning action occurs at the state and local levels, Wood expects Congress to focus, in part, on offering incentives to local governments to encourage more construction and affordable housing, as it did with the ROAD Act.

One proposal that housing analysts are watching is the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, a bill introduced in September that focuses on permitting reform, including making it easier to receive permits for some housing developments.
"At its core, the bill is about permitting energy and infrastructure projects and getting them approved faster," said Jake Krimmel, a senior economist for Realtor.com.
The Senate voted to approve BAAJA, as it is known, earlier this week.
Political obstacles

Democrats have historically been more focused on providing direct support for first-time homebuyers and on increasing federal spending on housing programs, Dennis Shea, a housing policy expert at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said in an email to CBS News.
"Expect more substantial appropriations for housing than a Republican-controlled Congress would deliver, and more 'demand-side' initiatives like down payment assistance," Shea added.

Aside from the bill that would provide down payment assistance for first-generation and low-income homebuyers, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, a Democrat from Illinois, has proposed a new refundable tax credit of up to $25,000 for qualified first-time homebuyers, delivered in up to $5,000 chunks over five years.
Even with Democrats vowing to tackle housing affordability, however, they may be limited in what they can achieve, experts said.

Despite having a Democratic majority in the Senate and House as newly elected lawmakers are sworn in next year, President Trump could veto anything they pass. Lawmakers would need a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override a veto, which would require them to muster bipartisan support.

"Despite their significant electoral gains during the recent election, Democrats still need buy-in from the White House and at least four Republican senators to move legislation over the legislative finish line," Shea said.

title: Can Anthropic win hearts and minds by curing hearts and minds?
summary: Anthropic says Claude Science can drive breakthroughs in drug discovery. It could also open lucrative commercial opportunities, experts say.
story: Fresh off its record-setting initial public offering, Anthropic now must show investors that it can sustain growth and generate profits. The company has a plan for that: curing some of the world's gnarliest diseases.

In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic states that AI holds the potential to "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine, potentially curing diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases, and the major infectious diseases."

Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei said in a post on X in August that he believes "it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!)."
Speeding in the right direction

Developing breakthrough drugs is among the most promising avenues of research for AI, potentially bringing treatments for a range of conditions to market much faster than is currently possible, according to scientists and industry analysts.

"AI can accelerate research. It will help you get there faster, but it's not just speed — it's directional speed," Neerav Kaushal, an AI and molecular biology expert at Michigan Technological University, told CBS News. "Let's say you're at the top of the mountain and your aim is to find a drug for cancer that lies in the valley. AI will not just help you get down there faster — it will help you get down to the right valley where the drug is."

For Anthropic, meanwhile, developing drugs could open up potentially enormous commercial opportunities. The company has partnered with biotech and pharmaceutical companies that use its Claude Science model for various purposes. Anthropic also operates its own AI-powered biology wet lab in San Francisco that has already made scientific discoveries.
"If you can use a large language model to condense any part of the timeline, it is very economically valuable," Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan told CBS News.
The challenge for Anthropic will be how it turns its life sciences research into profits. That could take time, Khan told CBS News.

"How this becomes lucrative for Anthropic is a very important question, and I think it's a question Anthropic hasn't figured out yet," Khan said. "Coding is its best-proven use case, followed by cybersecurity applications, then financial and legal research."
But the potential to move the needle for both Anthropic and its pharma partners is significant.

"If you improve your drug's efficiency by a couple of percentage points, that can make a world of difference," Khan added. "You'll get asymmetric payouts in the sense that if a model can help with any part of the process, it's very economically valuable."

For example, he expects a drug developer like Eli Lilly and Co., which partners with Anthropic to give its employees access to Claude, would be willing to pay "hundreds of millions or billions of dollars to make its arthritis drug 2% better than it is."
A way to win hearts and minds by curing them?

Developing potentially lifesaving drugs could have other benefits for Anthropic. By applying tools to the life sciences and using them to improve human life, the company could help shift the narrative around AI to a more positive one, according to experts.

"If you are the AI company that helps advance some kind of cure or solution to a sickness or illness that's prevailed for quite some time, I think that gets you a ton more trust with consumers and end users," Khan said. "Because you end up becoming the company that is actually improving the quality of life for humans at large."

title: Too many House Republicans are missing work, Mike Johnson says
summary: Dozens of House members didn't show up to vote this week. They're still getting paid.
story: Washington — Too many House Republicans skipped work this week, and House Speaker Mike Johnson isn't happy about it. Their absences are holding up legislation in the last few days the GOP controls Congress.

In a "Dear Colleague" letter he posted on X Friday, Johnson said "we need every House Republican to remain fully engaged," and lamented that the House was forced to postpone a vote scheduled earlier this week "because we didn't have enough members in town."
"To state the obvious, barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our two-year term," Johnson wrote.
Johnson's letter comes after GOP leaders had to pull a scheduled procedural vote from the floor due to attendance issues, with 14 Republicans missing.

Members of Congress will be paid until early January. The base salary for a rank-and-file House Republican is $174,000, while those in leadership positions earn more. "The Twentieth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution specifies that our clock doesn't run out until noon on January 3rd," Johnson concluded. "LET'S SCORE EVERY POINT WE CAN AND LEAVE IT ALL ON THE FIELD!"

Both Republicans and Democrats missed votes this week, although more Republicans were absent. According to the House clerk's office, in the last six floor votes since Nov. 11, between 23 and 35 members failed to vote. On Thursday, the final day in the House session this week, 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats and one independent missed votes.

Republicans have a packed to-do list before the end of the year, which includes passing a funding bill that would avert a government shutdown on Dec. 11, as well as the annual defense policy bill. Republicans also hope to get the farm bill and permitting reform bill across the finish line during this lame-duck period.
Speaking to reporters Thursday at the Capitol, Johnson said, "Attendance is a great frustration for me right now. We'll be addressing that with members."

"I am going to be here working," he said. "The leadership team are going to be here working. We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can't do that unless people are present at work."
Votes were canceled on Friday to allow lawmakers to return to their districts and states for the Thanksgiving break. The House won't return until Monday, Nov. 30.
Several of those who did not show up were among the more than 30 incumbent House Republicans who lost their seats this month.

Among the 14 Republicans who missed votes on Wednesday, those who were defeated in November included Reps. Lauren Boebert of Colorado, Monica De La Cruz of Texas, Scott DesJarlais of Tennessee, Max Miller of Ohio, and Jeff Van Drew of New Jersey. Other GOP lawmakers who missed votes are not returning to Congress or lost their elections for higher office.

title: Beloved hippo Fiona dies days after swallowing hat
summary: Fiona the hippo, who survived being born prematurely and rose to global fame, has died, the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden announced Thursday.
story: Fiona the hippo, who survived being born prematurely almost a decade ago, and whose story captured hearts around the world, has died, the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden announced Thursday.

Fiona, a Nile hippopotamus, had ingested a knit hat that ended up in her enclosure by accident almost two weeks ago, the zoo said, and despite the team's efforts to get it out of her system, "it was ultimately too much to overcome."
"We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo Director Dave Jenike said in a news release. "We did not expect this outcome.  She fought until she couldn't anymore."
A Cincinnati Zoo spokesperson confirmed to CBS News that the hat Fiona swallowed had been tossed in the air by a zoo visitor, then catapulted into the enclosure by a ceiling fan.

A necropsy showed the hat was in the middle of her small intestine, about 25 feet beyond the final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines, the zoo said in a news release shared Friday. Endoscopies were unable to reach the object, and surgical removal was not an option, according to director of animal health Dr. Mike Wenninger.
"No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked," Wenninger said.

Before Fiona's death, veterinarians closely monitored her health, turning to an unconventional method to try to help her pass the blockage by borrowing a vibration plate from a horse farm. They had Fiona stand on the device several times a day, hoping the vibrations would help move the material through her digestive system.

"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Jenike said. "She was dearly loved by her Zoo family and countless others around the world. Her loss will be felt deeply by so many."

Fiona would have been 10 years old this January. Her birth in 2017 drew the attention of millions on social media after she was born prematurely, weighing just 29 pounds, far below the typical 55-120 pounds for a newborn Nile hippo. Fiona was the first Nile hippo born at the zoo in 75 years.
To support baby Fiona, zoo staffers worked around the clock to care for her, including bottle-feeding her and helping her learn to swim.

In August 2022, Fiona's little brother, Fritz, was born at the Cincinnati Zoo. Christina Gorsuch, the zoo's director of animal care, said Fritz and the zoo's other hippos, Bibi and Tucker, have been eating and behaving normally since Fiona's death. The area around the Hippo Cove will be closed through the weekend to give space to the animal care team, who are "shaken and trying to navigate this loss," the zoo said.
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine called Fiona "a true icon" of the zoo, saying in a social media post that she "captured the hearts of Ohioans and those around the world, bringing joy to millions."

"Fiona was a symbol of perseverance and joy in Cincinnati," Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval wrote on X. "She brought smiles to so many faces, from kids to parents to visitors from around the world.   Our city is heartbroken, but we couldn't be more grateful that she was part of our lives and our community as a whole."
The Cincinnati Bengals even paid tribute to Fiona, saying: "Rest in peace, Fiona. The queen of the Queen City."
In response to inquiries about donations, flowers or other ways to pay tribute to the beloved hippo, the zoo said it asks "that people honor Fiona by spreading love and cheer to those around you."

title: Maps and charts show record number of measles cases in U.S. this year
summary: CBS News has been tracking a record number of measles cases and outbreaks around the country in 2026. The majority of cases are among those who haven't been vaccinated.
story: So far in 2026, the U.S. has recorded the most measles cases in more than three decades as outbreaks spread in multiple states, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

By mid-July, the number had already surpassed all of 2025, which had been the worst year in recent history with more than 2,200 confirmed cases. By November, the number of cases topped 5,000, more than double the previous year's total.
The ongoing outbreaks resulted in the U.S. losing its official measles elimination status, which it had held since 2000.

"It's profoundly sad and disappointing," Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of preventive medicine and infectious diseases at the Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told CBS News. "What a tragedy. We have had children die of measles this past year. That should never have happened. Those deaths and all those cases, 5,000-plus, were completely preventable."

In August, health officials in Pennsylvania reported the state's first two deaths connected to measles in 35 years. Several more deaths associated with measles were later reported as the state's outbreak surged, and deaths were also reported in New York and Wisconsin.

Measles is one of the most contagious of all infectious diseases. In some cases, it can cause severe infections in the lungs and brain that can lead to cognitive issues, deafness or death. But it can be prevented by vaccination, which medical research has proven to be safe and highly effective.
The CBS News data team has tracked confirmed measles cases nationwide as new data is released by state health departments and the CDC.
Out of the 2,289 confirmed cases in 2025, more than 750 were connected to an outbreak in West Texas that led to the deaths of two children.

Prior to 2025, the highest number of confirmed cases in the U.S. in recent years was 1,274 in 2019, driven by outbreaks in New York, California and Washington state. Most years, the total was much lower.

Health experts point to lower vaccination rates as the main reason for increases in preventable infectious diseases like measles. The vast majority of cases have been in people who were unvaccinated, and outbreaks have spread in communities with lower vaccination rates.

CDC data shows about 92.4% of kindergartners in the U.S. got their measles-mumps-rubella shots in the 2025-2026 school year, down slightly from 92.5% the previous year. The figure has declined from 95.2% during the 2019-2020 school year — a critical threshold to keep people safe. Only 10 states hit the 95% threshold last year.
"When more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated, most people are protected through community immunity (herd immunity)," the CDC states.

"I think that parents, for most kids, especially for the measles vaccines, the DTP, all the standard childhood vaccines, it's very important that parents vaccinate their kids," Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, the director of the National Institutes of Health, said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
Research has found no evidence of increased rates of autism among those who are vaccinated compared to those who are not. Vaccines also undergo intensive safety testing.

title: NWSL Championship to bring fans "the best soccer in the world"
summary: The next frontier in growing women's soccer in the U.S. is where the players train and play their games.
story: Women's professional sports have been on a winning streak for years — from triumphs on the world's biggest stages to securing equal pay and salaries off the field.
The next frontier in growing women's soccer in the U.S. is where the players train and play their games.
Only the Kansas City Current — who are playing in the NWSL Championship against the Washington Spirit on Saturday — have their own home stadium, CPKC Stadium, in Kansas City, Missouri.
"To see how far it has come, I'm grateful," Current captain Lo'eau LaBonta told "CBS Mornings." "But now at Kansas City we are pushing the limits, setting the standard. We want people to catch up."

The other 15 teams in the league lease or share existing stadiums, which means the "home" team generally uses the "away" locker room, its championship banners aren't on display, and other events may take priority over their matches.
"When you come in, it doesn't feel like a Spirit home game," Kim Stone, CEO of the Washington Spirit, told "CBS Mornings." "You're renting and it looks like it."
She added: "When you give women the best environments, when you give them the best training, when you give them the best coaches, you get the best product on the field."

The Washington Spirit are the "home team" in Saturday's NWSL Championship match. The game will be played at Audi Field, the home of MLS team D.C. United, with more than 20,000 fans expected to pack the stadium.
Kickoff is set for 8 p.m. ET Saturday, Nov. 21, on CBS and streaming on Paramount+.
"They are the best in the world"
NWSL Commissioner Jessica Berman says the fans have been one of the biggest drivers for the league's growth over the past five years.

"If you look at women's sports over the past few years, the thing that has changed is that people are buying tickets. People are watching on TV and that is actually creating a business for us to grow," she told "CBS Mornings." "It is also the players, and they are the best in the world."

"When people are excited about soccer, like they were after the men's World Cup this summer, they now realize that they can watch the best soccer in the world — it happens to be women, but the best soccer in the world — in the NWSL," she added.
When asked if the league should focus on building the current fan bases or expanding the league itself, Berman said: "Both matter."

"One of the things that we're so excited about from this past season is that our growth and our average attendance, which is now over 11,000 across all of our markets, is actually coming from the base of the league," she said. "So, it is not just the records we are breaking, like we did in Denver with 63,000 fans, but consistently, week over week, we are actually raising the bar."
She said it is also important to expand the league to new markets across the country, to make sure "more people get an opportunity to experience our game in their local community."
Men in Blazers Media Network CEO Roger Bennett told "CBS Mornings" on Friday that the NWSL Championship and the buzz around it exemplify the league's growth over the last 14 seasons.

"We are living in an incredible time," he said. "I have come to the NWSL Championship for the past seven years and … the thing is growing. This NWSL Championship used to be a day; now it is five days, an extravaganza. Brands are coming in. There's a commercial investment."
He continued: "You've got these incredible teams with incredible owners who are investing deeply — just superheroes, really. ... We are on the cusp of a new era."
NWSL to crown new champs
The NWSL Championship title match on Saturday features two teams who are salivating at the chance to raise the trophy.

The Current, who were the runners-up in 2022, are in pursuit of their first championship, while the Spirit are chasing their second franchise title. They last won in 2021 when they beat the Chicago Red Stars, 2-1.
This will be the third year in a row for the Spirit in the championship match. They lost to Orlando Pride in 2024 and Gotham FC in 2025.
"I think it is going to be tight; hopefully there's a bunch of goals," U.S. Soccer legend Megan Rapinoe told "CBS Mornings" on Friday.
The 2026 NWSL Championship between the Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current at Audi Field in Washington, D.C., airs Saturday, Nov. 21, at 8 p.m. ET on CBS and streams on Paramount+.

title: Audacious California train thieves film multimillion-dollar robberies
summary: The FBI estimated cargo theft losses in the U.S. and Canada reached nearly $725 million in 2025.
story: A ring of thieves allegedly targeted dozens of freight trains in Southern California, stealing more than $22 million in merchandise — and brazenly filming the robberies themselves — before their arrests following a 14-month investigation.

It's just one example of the growing problem of train heists in the U.S. The FBI estimated cargo theft losses in the U.S. and Canada reached nearly $725 million last year — up 60% from the year before. The Department of Homeland Security estimates cargo theft costs the U.S. between $15 billion and $35 billion a year.
Police say these thefts disrupt supply chains, potentially leaving customers with delivery delays and higher prices.

The alleged thieves in California targeted at least three dozen freight trains over more than two years and stole millions of dollars' worth of goods including Nike sneakers, electronics and power tools, federal prosecutors say.

The crew coordinated their robberies through Instagram, the prosecutors said. Then they would board a moving train, cut air hoses or brake hoses to force emergency stops, and haul stolen goods to nearby stash houses.

Almost every step of the thefts was filmed. One video shows a suspect sawing into a cargo container above a moving train, then multiple men moving merchandise. One man even poses for the camera as the theft is carried out.
The stolen items would then be sold on the black market.

Fourteen men were arrested for their involvement in the theft ring. They face charges including conspiracy, theft of interstate railroad cargo, possession or receipt of stolen interstate railroad cargo, and violence against railroad carriers, according to a news release from the Department of Justice. Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman referred to the case as "the granddaddy of all train cargo theft prosecutions in L.A. County."
During a news conference, LAPD Deputy Chief Alan Hamilton remarked that criminal investigations are "always easier when they post their own stuff on social media."

Law enforcement agencies nationwide are stepping up efforts to curb these kinds of theft rings. In October, CBS News took an exclusive look behind the scenes of a first-of-its-kind national blitz where federal agents, railroad police and law enforcement in more than two dozen states worked together to track thieves targeting cargo trains.

During the operation, officials used infrared drone technology to track heat signatures along train tracks and in rail yards. Cmdr. Michael Ware, who leads the Cook County Sheriff's Police Organized Retail Crime and Cargo Theft Task Force, told CBS News the technology is "like a third eye in the sky" that gives law enforcement "an advantage" and collects evidence. He showed CBS News video of one example of two men breaking the seals on a cargo container holding $35,000 worth of electronics.

"A lot of times we apprehend the guys and they come out like there's no way we have no proof. I wasn't in a container and they see the drone footage like 'you got me.' So it's a game-changer," Ware said.

title: New UFO files show contractor planned vault for "exotic material"
summary: The Pentagon's latest batch of UFO files includes a report from a government contractor detailing plans for an underground vault to store "exotic material or tissue" it was seeking.
story: Washington — The Pentagon released a new batch of UFO files on Friday, including one report from a government contractor detailing plans for an underground vault to store "exotic material or tissue" and recovered "hardware" it hoped to obtain.

The report was among 43 files included in the eighth release of UFO, or UAP, documents. The records mostly consisted of historical documents from the Air Force and CIA dating from the 1950s, with others describing more recent events.
What's in the new UFO files?

The July 2009 report was produced by Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies as part of a Defense Intelligence Agency program, funded by Congress at the urging of then-Sen. Harry Reid, to study potential future aerospace threats.

The 538-page document said the company identified the need for "a highly secure underground vault" to store "hardware and biological samples from the corporate world and/or from private individuals and groups located elsewhere, including Brazil." It would be located in Nevada.

"It was recognized by the BAASS administrator that there was no highly secure facility at BAASS to store exotic material or tissue that the organization could obtain," the report said. "Accordingly, the BAASS administrator designed an underground facility to be located in North Las Vegas at the Bigelow Aerospace facility."
The facility would be buried under 15 to 20 feet of dirt and feature a 5,000-square-foot vault with "3 foot thick walls" and a thick steel door.
"Any surface structures protruding from the ground will be extensively camouflaged," the report said.

There's no public record that the vault was ever built. Subsequent BAASS reports the Pentagon has released make no mention of it. A Defense Intelligence Agency official found the company's reports had "limited value" several months later, and the Pentagon's research project ended in 2012. Bigelow Aerospace, BAASS's parent company, laid off its entire workforce in 2020.
A copy of the BAASS report appeared online last year, but Friday's release is the first time the Pentagon has made it public.

Friday's documents also include files and videos of more recent UAP encounters. Three clips captured by the military and submitted to the Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office show white dots moving across the screen.
Another file details strange detections captured by a civil air-surveillance radar in 2023. Eight detections were picked up over 84 seconds between 55,000 and 70,000 feet in the sky.

"If the detections were associated with a single continuous track, their cumulative point-to-point displacement would be approximately 38.5 miles, yielding a minimum mean horizontal ground-speed estimate of 1,650 mph," the Pentagon said.
The slide notes that the available data was "not sufficient" to establish that all eight detections were caused by the same object.

The older files in Friday's release include one account from 1953 by Clarence "Kelly" Johnson, the chief engineer for Lockheed who later designed the U-2 and SR-71 spy planes. Johnson told the Air Force that he spotted a dark, elliptical object hanging motionless against a "gold and red" sky while watching the sunset at his California ranch.

"I wondered why this one object was so dark, considering that the sun was behind it. I immediately thought that some aircraft had made an intense smoke trail; so I studied the object closely. It was apparent, after my first few seconds of consideration, that the outline of this object did not change," Johnson wrote.

He said he watched the object through binoculars before it sped off "in a long shallow climb." At about the same time, a Lockheed test crew flying offshore reported chasing what looked like "a very large flying wing" that shrank to "a mere speck."
An Air Force record included in the file categorized the sighting as a lenticular cloud.

title: Can Democrats force an end to the Iran war when they take Congress?
summary: With Democrats set to take decisive House and Senate majorities, some members want to pressure the Trump administration to end the Iran war. The exact plan is not clear.
story: Washington — For months, Democrats have made ending the Iran war a core part of their pitch to midterm voters, promising that if they win control of Congress, they'll push President Trump to end an unpopular conflict that they blame for price increases.

Now, with Democrats set to take decisive majorities in the House and Senate next year, some members want to use the power of the purse to pressure the Trump administration to wind down the war, using must-pass bills as leverage. Exactly when — and how — they plan to act are less clear.

Democratic Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut told CBS News before the election that she would support "cutting off the funds for the Iran war." DeLauro is set to chair the powerful House Appropriations Committee, which has the ability to block funding.
"If they want money, they have to get congressional approval," DeLauro said.

The first pressure point could arrive in a matter of weeks, before Democrats take control of Congress. Lawmakers face a Dec. 11 deadline to extend funding for most federal agencies and prevent a government shutdown. Several Democrats have argued the party should block any stopgap bill that doesn't restrict funding for the Iran war.
But some top House Democrats who will control key committees next year are backing away from that approach, warning it could lead to a shutdown.

DeLauro is part of government funding negotiations and favors a short-term extension until February if full-year appropriations measures are not passed by the deadline. She indicated that she is against using a continuing resolution as leverage.

"I think that the American people would like to see us end the war," she told reporters Wednesday. "I also believe that the American people may not believe that shutting the government down ends the war."
In a statement to CBS News on Thursday, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York said he would oppose a continuing resolution "if I believed shutting down government helped us actually achieve that."
"But I believe it would only shut down parts of government that Americans rely on," said Meeks, who is the incoming chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

The party's House and Senate leaders — Rep. Hakeem Jeffries and Sen. Chuck Schumer — support ending the Iran war but have not specified what their approach will be, including whether they're open to attaching language to a stopgap funding bill.
Jeffries said Tuesday the House and Senate appropriations committees are in "active conversation" about how to fund the government.
"I don't want to get out ahead of that process," he told reporters at a news conference. "What is clear is that the reckless and costly war of choice in Iran needs to end. It should end today."
Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who is challenging Schumer for majority leader, has argued the party should use the Dec. 11 deadline to force restrictions on the Iran war.

Van Hollen said in a statement last week that any funding deal "must include language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran." It was cosigned by Sen. Tammy Duckworth of Illinois, progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and more moderate Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado.

Some Democrats also plan to offer amendments to any government funding deal to block war funding until the conflict is authorized by Congress, including Bennet, Duckworth, Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Schumer-allied Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York.
Senate Democrats discussed how to proceed during a closed-door lunch meeting on Tuesday. Van Hollen told reporters they "had a very good discussion," but there was "no final decision."

Reps. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona and Ro Khanna of California said they would also vote against any funding package that "does not explicitly prohibit funds from being used for offensive operations in Iran."
What could Democrats do next year?

After Democrats formally take control of the House and Senate in January, they could have several opportunities to attach Iran war-related language to must-pass legislation, in addition to voting on standalone bills and resolutions to restrict the war.

Lawmakers will likely need to extend government funding again, and they will need to raise the debt limit at some point next year. The appropriations process for the 2028 fiscal year and the annual National Defense Authorization Act are two other possible points of leverage.

Schumer told reporters earlier this month that "we are going to end the war," and said, "the Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people."
Still, blocking the president from taking military action in Iran could be a challenging task.

"It is a complicated thing to force the president to stop using military force, and does require an alignment of political opportunity, savvy legislating, coordination that just is going to take time and political capital to implement," said Scott R. Anderson, a former State Department attorney and Brookings Institution senior fellow.
Mr. Trump has vowed to use his veto power liberally. Democrats would need support from several Senate Republicans and dozens of House Republicans to override his veto.

Beyond that, Mr. Trump and other presidents have claimed sweeping authority to direct the military. The president did not seek congressional authorization for the Iran war. Instead, he told lawmakers shortly after the war began that he "acted pursuant to my constitutional authority as Commander in Chief," in a notice issued under the War Powers Resolution, which requires the president to notify Congress of military hostilities within 48 hours.

That 1973 law also limits hostilities to 60 days — with an extra 30-day grace period to withdraw troops — unless lawmakers pass an authorization for use of military force, and it allows Congress to pass resolutions directing the president to terminate hostilities before then.

House and Senate Democrats have used that law to vote to terminate hostilities several times this year, drawing support from some moderate or anti-interventionist Republicans. One war powers resolution cleared both chambers in June. But the Trump administration has brushed off those votes, arguing the War Powers Resolution is unconstitutional. On Thursday, the Senate blocked another House-passed resolution, losing Republican support for reining in Mr. Trump on Iran.
Jeffries said Tuesday that House Democrats are discussing whether to force more votes on war powers resolutions this year.

"It's something that's under discussion right now, and we'll take a look at vehicles that we have available to us," he said. "But it certainly is the case that early on in the new Congress, we're going to aggressively move to end the reckless Republican war of choice in Iran."
Later in the day, during an interview at the Atlantic Summit in Washington, Jeffries indicated that Democrats would vote next year on a resolution "that has the force of the law."
The resolution that cleared the House and Senate in June was passed under a procedure that did not require the president's signature.
Jeffries said the goal is to send a war powers resolution to Mr. Trump's desk, essentially daring him to veto it. The war remains deeply unpopular with Americans.
"There's nothing more powerful than putting that bill on the president's desk," Jeffries said.

Meeks told CBS News that starting in January, "I will introduce a War Powers Resolution, support legislation that cuts off funding for this war, and require the administration to take diplomacy seriously by sending real diplomats, not the president's golf buddy and son in law."

Other Democrats have backed using funding bills as leverage. Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia said in one recent interview that if the Trump administration doesn't follow already-passed war powers resolutions, "our only choice is to use the appropriations process to forbid funding for war operations, unless the president gets the legally required authorization by Congress."

Asked about Democrats' plans, a White House official told CBS News: "As President Trump and Secretary Rubio stated, our economic pressure campaign is devastating Iran to such an extent that the President does not have any need to conduct major combat operations."
"The Democrats continue to prove that have no agenda to improve the lives of the American people, just plans to baselessly obstruct the President's agenda," the official said.
What could restrictions on the Iran war look like?

There is some history of Congress constraining the president's ability to make war. In 1973, the House and Senate overwhelmingly passed legislation blocking the government from using funds for hostilities in Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos. Then-President Richard Nixon signed it into law.

Anderson told CBS News that if lawmakers want to force an end to the Iran war, they could pass legislation that either prohibits hostilities with Iran outright or bars the president from using federal funds to pay for the war, or both.
"You need some sort of affirmative bar to block the president from acting," he said. "Even then, there's kind of a question of, 'Does the president listen? How enforceable is it?'"
Another open question: What specific military actions Democrats might try to ban.

The U.S. has not conducted large-scale offensive operations against Iran in recent months, but the conflict has remained at a simmer. The two countries have exchanged occasional strikes — typically after the U.S. military alleges imminent threats from Iran — and the U.S. has enforced a blockade on Iranian ports and escorted oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

Anderson says Congress could try to bar the Trump administration from resuming offensive bombings, and the blockade on Iran could also be restricted. Defensive operations are likely to be exempted, though the bill would need to be worded carefully.

In the past, Anderson notes, presidents have argued the Constitution inherently gives them the power to carry out operations to defend U.S. nationals, regardless of any legislative complications — an argument President Gerald Ford used to evacuate Saigon and order some other operations around the tail end of the Vietnam War.
"If you do an absolute funding cutoff, what do you do when you have U.S. vessels traversing the Strait of Hormuz and they do get shot at by Iranians, or American sailors get captured?" he said.

Democrats have yet to publicly lay out a plan for how they plan to counter the administration if it defies Congress on ending the war. If Democrats believe the administration isn't complying with its obligations, the House or Senate could sue, but the outcome could be hard to predict.
Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, the incoming chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, has argued that impeaching Mr. Trump over the war should be an option.
"How are we going to stop him? What law are we going to pass when he chooses not to obey the law?" Smith said in an interview with CNN last month, prior to the election.

Smith told The New Republic earlier this month that even if Democrats forbid any funding for the war, "the legal language and the loopholes — the ways that Trump can sort of jump out of it — those will all continue to be challenges."
"We are headed into uncharted territory here," Smith said.
Anderson said he believes Democrats are serious about passing restrictions on the Iran war, but it could take multiple attempts and plenty of "political fighting and legal maneuvering."
"People do need to be patient," Anderson said. "There is this expectation that Democrats won and the Iran war will end tomorrow. That is not what is going to happen."

title: 2-year-old who went missing in desert found by volunteer
summary: Jay Stewart was overcome with emotion during a news conference as he recalled the moment he found a missing 2-year-old curled up under a bush just after midnight on Wednesday.
story: A 2-year-old who went missing was found safe, if not a little cold, by a volunteer after spending seven hours alone in the Arizona desert.
Jay Stewart was overcome with emotion during a news conference as he recalled the moment he found her curled up under a bush just after midnight on Wednesday.
"To find that little scared child, the way she popped out of that bush, it was, I'll never forget it as long as I live," he said.

Stewart responded to a post from the Pinal County sheriff pleading for help after Vella Campillo, wearing only a diaper, wandered out of her yard outside Eloy, Arizona, just before sunset Tuesday. The sheriff's office said in a statement the search involved more than 100 people on foot.

"We used drones, helicopters, everything that we could throw at it," Pinal County Sheriff Ross Teeple said. "We forget in the wintertime that very remote areas like this can get extremely cold very fast. And she's a small body producing very little heat. So the drones with the heat signatures could not pick up anything."

Stewart had been searching on foot for three hours when he spotted her about a mile and a half from her house. He said in a video posted to the sheriff's office's Facebook page that he was calling the little girl's name when he heard her yell, so he shined his flashlight on a bush, "and she popped up. It was a life-changing moment."
"I grabbed her and picked her up and then she was, like, clinging to me so tight, so tight," he said at the news conference.
He tucked the toddler inside his jacket. Thankfully, she was uninjured.

"I know you've been asked this 1,000 times, whether you feel you're a hero, and you say you're not, but I'm here to tell you that, when you watch the body camera footage, it's obvious that you're that little girl's hero," Teeple said in the social media video.

Stewart said at the news conference, "The scariest thing for parents is to lose a child. I can't imagine what they were going through. They thanked me profusely, of course, but they didn't need to thank me. It's what we do."

title: Trump pardons deceased MLB slugger Pete Rose
summary: President Trump said Thursday he has granted a "Complete and Total Pardon" to Pete Rose, MLB's late all-time hits leader who was banned from the league for gambling.
story: President Trump said Thursday he has granted a "Complete and Total Pardon" to Pete Rose, Major League Baseball's late all-time hits leader who was banned from the league and, until recently, the Baseball Hall of Fame for gambling.

The president announced the move in a post on Truth Social, writing that Rose — who died in 2024 — "was treated terribly by Major League Baseball in not allowing him to go into the Baseball Hall of Fame. Politics, I guess!"

Mr. Trump did not specify what the pardon of Rose will cover. Rose wasn't charged with gambling, though he did plead guilty in 1990 to filing false income tax returns, serving five months in prison. Asked for more details on the pardon, a White House official pointed to Rose's tax charges.
During his more than 20 years as a player, most of them with the Cincinnati Reds, Rose racked up a record 4,256 hits and won three World Series. He later managed the Reds.

But his career was marred by the revelation that he had placed bets on games, including some Reds games. Rose agreed to a lifetime ban from Major League Baseball in 1989 — a move that prevented him from being inducted into the Hall of Fame.

He asked to be reinstated on four occasions. Twice, in 1997 and 2020, then-MLB Commissioner Bud Selig and current Commissioner Rob Manfred, respectively, did not respond to the petitions. His petitions in 2015 and 2022 were rejected.

He was then posthumously reinstated last year. Manfred met with Mr. Trump less than a month before Rose was reinstated. Manfred said at the time that Rose came up during their conversation, "but I'm not going beyond that." Under Hall of Fame rules, Rose could be inducted as early as 2028.

Mr. Trump has long argued that Rose was mistreated by the league, a view that stretches back to before his first term as president. In late 2015, Mr. Trump wrote on social media: "He's paid the price. So ridiculous - let him in!"

The president has repeatedly floated issuing Rose a pardon. In a White House event earlier this month, Mr. Trump acknowledged that Rose shouldn't have gambled but noted that sports betting is now widely legal, and pointed out that "he was gambling on his own team."
It is unclear what effect the pardon will have. Rose was released from prison in 1991, and pardons do not apply to the Baseball Hall of Fame.

title: Russian missiles pummel Ukraine and hit NATO soil in Poland
summary: Missiles flew into Poland overnight as Russia hit Ukraine with "one of the largest attacks" since the war began, killing at least 8 people.
story: Poland's government said Russian missiles landed in the country overnight as Vladimir Putin's forces hammered Ukraine with what President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called "one of the largest attacks" since the war began. The strikes on Ukraine killed at least eight people, according to Zelenskyy.
The prime minister of Poland, a NATO member, decried the Russian weapons landing in his country as "an intentional provocation" of the U.S.-led military alliance.

"We know that what landed on Polish soil came from Russia. Therefore — ⁠and this is not just my own assessment, but ‌also that of our foreign partners, including those within NATO — it does not look like an ‌accident," Prime Minister ⁠Donald Tusk said. "It ‌appears that we ⁠are dealing with an intentional ⁠provocation."

NATO and Allied planes responded to the incident, including Polish F-16s, Swedish JAS 39 Gripens, a Dutch A330 Multi Role Tanker Transport (MRTT) aerial refueling aircraft and others. NATO and Allied ground-based air defenses were also alerted.

"Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic impotence with precisely this kind of terror," Zelenskyy wrote, adding that Putin's attempt to "redraw the world" with his Chinese and U.S. counterparts during their summit Thursday in China had been a "failure."
"Hard to regard it as a coincidence"

Russia fired more than 400 drones and 110 missiles at Ukraine overnight and early Friday, including cluster munitions, Zelenskyy said in a fiery social media post. Some of the Russian weapons hit the Austrian embassy and landed near the Netherlands embassy in Kyiv, prompting France to call for a meeting of the United Nations Security Council.
"Russia will have to answer for this," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot wrote in a social media post.

Poland's defense minister said three Russian weapons, believed to have been two missiles and a drone, entered southeast Poland's airspace on Friday. Poland scrambled fighter jets and Patriot anti-missile systems in the country's southeast were activated, but no injuries were reported.
Drones have repeatedly entered the airspace of Poland and other NATO countries, mostly near Ukraine but not all, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022.
The Article 5 collective defense clause in NATO's founding charter states that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all 32.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said in a Friday social media post that he had spoken with Tusk "about the grave violations of Polish airspace overnight" and stressed that the alliance stands "in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend."

"This incident is clearly dangerous — a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," Rutte said. "I condemn Russia's attacks as well as its ongoing war. We continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine."

NATO's Supreme Allied Commander for Europe, U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, was in "close contact with Poland's chief of defense and minister of defense as Poland's investigation into the overnight airspace violations continues," his spokesperson Martin O'Donnell told CBS News on Friday.

Thousands of troops from 11 European countries that support Kyiv, members of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, are currently in Poland taking part in a major military exercise framed as training for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine.
According to Polish defense officials, two missiles thought to be Russian Kh-101s and one jet-powered drone landed between 30 and 60 miles inside Polish territory from the border with Ukraine.

"It is hard to regard it as a coincidence that the time and place of the violation of Polish airspace coincide with the Coalition of the Willing's exercises," Deputy Polish Prime Minister and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote in a social media post.

The escalation comes a day after President Trump sat with Xi and Putin —   whom he greeted warmly and called his friend — in Shenzhen, China, for a rare face-to-face meeting that seemed to achieve little.

The presidents discussed the Ukraine war, which Mr. Trump has long pushed to end through negotiations, but soon after the 90-minute meeting, Putin ruled out direct talks with Kyiv, citing a strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces that severely damaged a highly symbolic bridge linking Russia and Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.

"We will respond to these strikes," Putin warned Thursday. "I want everyone to know this. I believe that our retaliatory actions … will be far more painful than what the Kiev regime did to the bridge."
At least 8 killed, dozens wounded in Ukraine

Ukrainian forces managed to intercept 79 of the 110 missiles Russia launched overnight, Zelenskyy said, but none of the 27 ballistic missiles, which he attributed to Kyiv's lack of interceptors. He has been pleading with the Trump administration to help Ukraine replenish its missile interceptor stocks for months, saying the shortage is being paid for in civilian lives.

Russia's attack targeted Kyiv and nine other regions, leaving more than two dozen people wounded in addition to the eight confirmed to have been killed, according to Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi.
"Missiles hit critical infrastructure in the capital, including bridges," he said. "A water supply facility, office and commercial buildings were damaged."

A hospital in Kharkiv was damaged, as well as businesses in the Mykolaiv, Odesa and Chernihiv regions, and residential buildings in the regions of Dnipropetrovsk, Vinnytsia, Sumy, Chernihiv and Lviv, which is in the far west, close to Poland, Koretskyi said, adding that energy infrastructure was also hit.
Some nuclear plants were forced to reduce power generation after the attacks, according to an energy ministry official.

"The tactics of the strike this time were particularly vile," Zelenskyy said in his post on social media, noting that there had been "several groups of missiles with pauses of 20-30 minutes to complicate extinguishing the fires, clearing the rubble and recovery."

"A clear response from the world to all this is also needed," he said. "It is important that there are not only statements from partners about supporting Ukraine and Ukrainians, but also the implementation of specific agreements on air defense … We very much hope that the Pentagon will release the supply that we expect."
