title: Iran takes pointed jab at Trump Cabinet secretary for moving onto military base
summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent moved to a military base amid reported Iranian assassination threats a senior official says reached an advanced stage.
story: Denying reports of tension over a statement about Republican midterm losses, President Donald Trump confirmed support for Vice President JD Vance's comments regarding the war. While highlighting Navy operations and oil prices, Trump labeled Iran's leadership as evil and detailed historical conflict. Ultimately, he emphasized that U.S. cannot allow Iran to obtain a nuclear weapon under any circumstances.

Iran mocked Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, calling the official "sweetie" on social media after reports emerged that he had moved from his Washington, D.C., home onto a military installation amid security threats attributed to Tehran.
Bessent made a public appearance Friday, sitting nearby as President Donald Trump addressed reporters in the White House briefing room.
"Are you interviewing from a military base sewer right now, sweetie?" Iran's South African embassy posted on X alongside a screenshot of Bessent from an earlier television interview.
An Iranian official confirmed to Fox News Digital that the X account belongs to the embassy.
TRUMP'S TOP OFFICIALS RETREAT BEHIND MILITARY GATES AS EX-FBI DEPUTY POINTS TO WHAT'S FUELING THREATS

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent listens as President Donald Trump speaks during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House Nov. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

Bessent is the latest senior Trump administration official to relocate to a military base, joining a growing number of top officials living behind military gates as federal authorities confront security threats extending beyond the White House.
"Obviously, it's a high threat level for us to move," Bessent said while addressing the move during a Nov. 15 appearance on Fox Business' "Sunday Futures with Larry Kudlow."

A source familiar with the situation previously told Fox News Digital, "After The Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary’s Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase, which have now forced the secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety.
"The news media has an obligation to act responsibly amid growing threats against public officials."
BESSENT BLASTS NEWSPAPER EDITOR OVER 'RECKLESS JOURNALISM' AFTER IRAN THREATS FORCE MOVE TO MILITARY BASE

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House Nov. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

Threats against Bessent had reached "more than an advanced stage" amid reported Iranian assassination threats, a senior administration official told Fox News Digital when news broke of the decision to move the Treasury secretary on base. The official did not elaborate on the nature of the threats.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and other administration officials have moved to military installations or protected government housing.
Under Bessent, Treasury launched Operation Economic Outcast in August to disrupt Iran’s oil-smuggling, financial and cryptocurrency networks.
BESSENT WARNS IRAN'S OUTSIDE BACKERS TO 'STAY AWAY' AS TRUMP SEEKS TO 'ASPHYXIATE' TEHRAN'S ECONOMY

President Donald Trump takes questions from reporters during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House Nov. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
He said Treasury would "sever every economic lifeline" sustaining the Iranian regime and warned that entities facilitating money laundering for Tehran could be cut off from the U.S. dollar system.

Since then, Treasury has targeted Iran’s oil-smuggling shadow fleet, sanctioned eight Canada-based money services businesses it says helped Iranian entities move funds and moved to cut crypto exchange MEXC Global off from the U.S. financial system over alleged illicit transactions.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

On Nov. 18, Treasury announced action against a gold-and-cash smuggling network it said was run by Hezbollah and Iran’s IRGC-Quds Force. Bessent said the U.S. would continue to "disrupt Iran’s attempts to exert influence in the region and fund its proxies."
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Trump wags finger at 'really rude' reporter, tells her she belongs in the 'back row' during press exchange
summary: Donald Trump wagged his finger at a reporter, calling her "really a rude person" and telling her she belonged in the "back row" at the White House.
story: President Donald Trump dismissed a female journalist as "really a rude person" and waved his finger at her while wrapping up Friday’s event.

President Donald Trump rebuked a female reporter at the end of a White House news conference Friday, wagging his finger at her, calling her "really a rude person" and telling her she belonged in the "back row."

The exchange unfolded as Trump wrapped up a lengthy news conference following his return from an Asia trip, just after inviting White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller to the podium and praising Miller's work on immigration and deregulation.
Before addressing the press corps, Trump defended Miller's temperament, noting that critics often view him as overly strict on immigration.
CHINA BLOCKS BLOOMBERG REPORTER FROM TRUMP-PUTIN-XI MEETING OVER QUESTION TO TRUMP

President Donald Trump addresses reporters in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Nov. 20, 2026, after returning from trilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

"He’s really a talent, and he’s got a big heart. A lot of people think he doesn’t. They think he’s hard on immigration, harder on this. He’s got a tremendous heart. In many ways. They think he’s got too big a heart. But we’ll talk about that," Trump said before breaking off to address the journalist.
"Who are you with. Who are you with?" Trump asked while waving his finger in her direction.
After the reporter replied, "Who are you?" Trump sharply criticized both her demeanor and her seating placement in the room.
JOE ROGAN SAYS PODCASTERS HAVE NO BUSINESS AT TRUMP PRESS CONFERENCES ALONGSIDE REAL JOURNALISTS
President Donald Trump takes questions from the press corps during a White House news briefing in Washington on Nov. 20, 2026, following his Asia trip. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
"And you’re really a rude person," Trump said.
When the reporter tried to speak again, beginning, "So if you’re talking about it," Trump cut her off and told her she should not be seated near the front of the press area.
"I’m not talking to you. I’m not telling you. You shouldn’t be in the front row. You should be in the back row," Trump said.
TRUMP AND DANA WHITE HONOR MARINE CORPS BAND WITH SIX-FIGURE CHECKS IN FIRST EVENT ON NEW HELIPAD

President Donald Trump listens as Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks during a White House news briefing in Washington on Nov. 20, 2026, following Trump's return from a diplomatic trip to Asia. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

Trump then pivoted back to his closing remarks, inviting attendees to an afternoon ceremony and concert on the White House helipad with UFC CEO Dana White to honor and award money to U.S. military musicians.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"They’re unbelievably talented people, and we’re going to honor them in just a little while. And thank you for your fairness. Thank you for your questions. And Steve, thank you, J. D. Thank you. And Marco, thank you very much. Thank you everybody," Trump said as he concluded the appearance alongside Miller, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Somali community leaders bristle at broad blame even as youth gang violence surges from Minnesota to Maine
summary: Ramsey County Sheriff Bob Fletcher says about 100 of 300 young alleged Somali gang members in the Twin Cities were arrested, but many cycle back into gang life.
story: Minneapolis talk radio host Jon Justice discusses Somali gang violence in Minnesota and the impact on local communities on 'The Ingraham Angle.'
Somali community members in Minnesota pushed back Thursday against blaming the broader Somali American population as law enforcement officials warned of a surge in youth gang violence.
Members of the Somali community and law enforcement leaders met to discuss gang-related crimes in the Twin Cities, KSTP 5 Eyewitness News reported Thursday.

Ramsey County Sheriff Bob Fletcher estimates there are about a dozen Somali gangs involving roughly 300 young people in the metro area out of an estimated 1,000 to 2,000 total gang members across the region.
Fletcher said many gang members who do get arrested ultimately continue participating in "the gang life."
CULTURE CLASH LAID BARE AS VIOLENT SOMALI GANGS GRIP SUBURBAN COMMUNITIES: ‘THESE KIDS ARE DIFFERENT’
The Minneapolis skyline in and around where Somali gangs are cropping up (Arthur Maiorella/Getty Images)

"Well, many of them are [arrested]. I mean, we’ve arrested probably 100 of those 300," Fletcher told KSTP 5 Eyewitness News. "Many of them cycle out. Just because you arrest them doesn’t mean they’re not going to continue to participate in the gang life."
The Ramsey County Sheriff's Office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment Friday.
However, some people at the community meeting said the Somali community in the Twin Cities metro area is being singled out unfairly.
Abdirizak Bihi, a Somali American social activist, said Thursday that "we cannot arrest our way" into fixing youth crime, KSTP 5 Eyewitness News reported.
"I’m concerned. I’m a father," Bihi said. "We cannot arrest our way into solving this problem for any youth.
"Of course, anyone who commits a crime, we have laws."
MINNESOTA HOMECOMING SHOOTING SUSPECT OUT ON BOND AFTER GUNFIRE SENDS FOOTBALL FANS FLEEING; 3 OTHERS ARRESTED
Downtown Minneapolis Dec. 4, 2025  (Stephen Maturen/Getty Images)
Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension Superintendent Drew Evans suggested that preventing gang violence can be "difficult to measure," CBS News reported Thursday.

"What a meeting like this does is it brings (the) community together in a way to really understand what the drivers of violence are to begin with," Evans said. "Prevention is always going to be difficult to measure. You're not going to be able to prove the negative if something didn't occur."

The tensions in the Twin Cities mirror similar struggles in other U.S. cities with large Somali American populations, where local officials and community leaders are also grappling with spikes in youth gun violence and debates over how to confront it.

In Lewiston, Maine, police reported 35 gun-related incidents this year, including 22 that involved juveniles, Fox News previously reported in October. The city houses a large population of Somali refugees and refugees from other African nations.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"I don’t feel safe. I fear for my life," Mohamed Muhumed, a Lewiston teenager, previously told Fox News Digital. "I saw someone get punched in the middle of the sidewalk over there. It’s crazy."

Maine Immigrant and Refugee Services Executive Director Rilwan Osman and his team unveiled a Voices Against Gun Violence program in June, which included daily workshops and community discussions throughout the month as part of a broader effort to address youth gun violence in the city, WGME reported June 1.
"We are asking people to pledge that they can talk about gun violence at home in their communities, at school, outside their school," Osman said, according to WGME.

The Minnesota BCA announced in an Oct. 19 news release that more than 40 law enforcement agencies agreed to "use an existing investigative model to coordinate efforts and strengthen collaboration in addressing gang and group violence." The plan also "employs county-based quick reaction teams for specialized and rapid uniformed patrol and investigative response when criminal activity occurs," according to the agency.
When reached for comment about its efforts to address gang-related crime in Minnesota, the BCA referred Fox News Digital to its Oct. 19 news release.
SOMALIS IN MINNESOTA UNLEASH FURY ON TRUMP AFTER FEDS RAID ILHAN OMAR'S DC HOME

Somali residents walk through Minneapolis’ Cedar-Riverside neighborhood, often called "Little Mogadishu," home to one of the largest Somali communities in the United States. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital)

Former state Trooper John Nagel told Fox News Digital in October that some Minnesota Democrats have their "heads in the sand" and hindered law enforcement from stopping Somali American gang-linked violence in the state before it escalated.

"They're being restrained by politicians, people that are trying soft on crime, people that are trying to send somebody other than a police officer to take care of issues, and it's not working," Nagel said at the time.
Police in Eden Prairie, Minnesota, previously said an Oct. 2 shooting outside Aerie Stadium at Eden Prairie High School's homecoming was connected to Somali gang activity.
About 84,000 Somali individuals live in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area, PBS News reported in December 2025.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., sent a letter to U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen July 23 flagging concerns about the "alarming rise" of Somali gang violence in the North Star State.

"I’ve said it before, and I’ll say it again. If you won’t assimilate, then get the hell out of here. First it was an estimated $9 billion in fraud. Now it’s out-of-control violence," Emmer said in a statement. "These Somali gangs have shot up high school graduations and assaulted players on opposing basketball teams with tire irons. It’s absolute madness, and something must be done."
In Columbus, Ohio, police announced the arrests, indictments or convictions of 21 BL-800 gang members in February 2024, WOSU 89.7 NPR News reported.
Det. Eric Clouse said that the "BL" in the gang's name initially stood for "Bantu Life" or "Bantu Love" in reference to Somalia's Bantu ethnic community, according to the outlet.
Fox News' Paul Steinhauser contributed to this report.

title: Trump responds after Vance blames Iran war for midterm losses, VP says his job is to support president
summary: President Donald Trump says he would launch the war against Iran again, as JD Vance blames midterm losses on voter anger over the conflict and oil prices.
story: Denying reports of tension over a statement about Republican midterm losses, President Donald Trump confirmed support for Vice President JD Vance's comments regarding the war. While highlighting Navy operations and oil prices, Trump labeled Iran's leadership as evil and detailed historical conflict. Ultimately, he emphasized that the U.S. cannot allow Iran to obtain a nuclear weapon under any circumstances.

President Donald Trump said Friday that he would still have launched the military operation against Iran, pushing back against reports of friction with Vice President JD Vance after Vance attributed Republican midterm election losses to the ongoing conflict.

Speaking to reporters following his trip to Asia, Trump addressed questions about whether he was displeased with Vance’s post-election assessment that the conflict drove Democratic gains in the next Congress.

"I didn't say I was unhappy with it," Trump said alongside Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. "I thought the statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing that if we're asked, I would have said that: ‘Would you do it again?’ Absolutely. The answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon."
VANCE'S SCATHING IRAN WAR POSTMORTEM PUTS POTENTIAL 2028 GOP SHOWDOWN IN FOCUS: 'EVERYONE KNOWS WHY'

President Donald Trump on Friday defended Vice President JD Vance's assessment of the GOP setbacks in the midterm elections that he blamed on the Iran war. Trump said he would have launched the war despite the political costs, citing Tehran's nuclear ambitions and the threat it poses in the Middle East. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

The remarks followed a series of posts on X by Vance a day after the midterm elections, in which Democrats won majorities in both the House and the Senate — along with the Texas governorship — blaming voter frustration over the conflict and elevated oil prices.

"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote. "If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
VANCE COURTING DISGRUNTLED TRUMP VOTERS TO FORM ‘NEW RIGHT’ ALLIANCE AFTER REPUBLICAN BLOODBATH, SOURCES SAY
On Friday, Trump called Vance's assessment "accurate" and acknowledged that fuel costs rose amid the fighting, though he said the spike was milder than anticipated.
"The war drove up prices, fuel prices far less than I thought," Trump said. "I thought it would go up to $300 a barrel. You know, it's almost down to $80 a barrel right now."
FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS
Despite the political fallout, Trump maintained that the military action was necessary to counter Tehran’s nuclear ambitions and to protect Israel and other Middle Eastern nations.
Vance affirmed that preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon justified the political cost, while emphasizing his alignment with Trump.
RUBIO DEFENDS TRUMP'S IRAN WAR AS NOT 'NECESSARILY POPULAR, BUT NECESSARY'

Vice President JD Vance speaks during a news conference following a military briefing at the Civilian Military Coordination Center on Oct. 21, 2025 in Kiryat Gat, Israel. (Nathan Howard - Pool/Getty Images)

"What I've said is the goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we need to be doing," Vance said. "It's the biggest state sponsor of terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage or, God forbid, they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands, potentially, of innocent people."

"I think the president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again," Vance added. "My view is that my goal, and my job, is to support the president of the United States."
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Tech outage cascade exposes US vulnerabilities to foreign cyber threats
summary: Six days of outages hit Microsoft 365, banks and NSA Net, and experts like Tommy Waller warn the disruptions may be more than just a coincidence.
story: Center for Security Policy President Tommy Waller warns that a string of outages affecting the NSA, banks and major technology systems raises national security concerns, even as officials rule out a coordinated cyberattack.

U.S. adversaries have spent years developing ways to disrupt the country's critical infrastructure in a conflict, and the wave of technology disruptions affecting everything from banks to the National Security Agency has offered a reminder of how detrimental those failures could be even without a cyberattack.
The string of outages has fueled speculation about whether the incidents are connected, though Trump administration officials have ruled out a coordinated cyberattack.

National security experts caution that while the outages do not establish malicious activity, they underscore the stakes of protecting systems that underpin everything from financial transactions to military operations.
TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS
"We know that our adversaries use that domain to attack our critical infrastructure," Tommy Waller, a national security expert with the Center for Security Policy, told Fox News Digital.
"Modern warfare, our people and our critical infrastructures are a prime target for all of our adversaries."
China accused the NSA of launching a cyberattack against its national time service. (Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images)

In a span of six days, technical disruptions affected Microsoft 365, commercial air travel, payroll and human resources software, banking transactions and the National Security Administration's highly classified internal communications network.
Some led to massive impacts on everyday life, including only the second-ever nationwide ground stop on all commercial flights since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.
"This is not a cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation-state," Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Tuesday on Fox Business' "The Claman Countdown."

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin similarly insisted the disruptions had "nothing to do with cyberattacks," suggesting that technical failures could become more common as new technology is introduced.

"I believe we're going to see more of this as new technology rolls out," Mullin said Tuesday. A day earlier, he sought to reassure Americans during an appearance on Fox News' "Hannity," saying, "Well, breathe. The homeland is secure. Our banking system is secure."
PRESIDENT TRUMP DOWNPLAYS PANIC OVER TECH OUTAGES: ‘NOBODY’S GOING TO PLAY GAMES WITH US’
But the disruption at the NSA, one of the nation's most sophisticated intelligence agencies, has drawn particular scrutiny.
United Airlines planes parked at Newark Liberty International Airport in Newark, N.J., Nov. 3, 2025. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The agency's highly classified internal communications network, known as NSA Net, went down Tuesday, disrupting employees' ability to communicate classified information internally. Employee attendance at the agency's Fort Meade, Maryland, campus was "staggered" throughout the week to ease systems' use, and the network did not resume operations until Friday.

"This latest thing at the NSA is more problematic because their systems are generally not tied to anybody else, particularly their classified ones," national security and cybersecurity expert Steve Bucci told Fox News Digital.
"And, so, that being coincidentally, you know, in this sequence makes it a little harder to just write off."

A U.S. official attributed the disruption to routine maintenance, saying the NSA experienced temporary interruptions to some internal systems but that its critical operations and national security capabilities remained fully functional.
Waller said the NSA outage could have been "self-induced" by efforts to patch vulnerabilities but questioned whether the broader string of disruptions was coincidental.
"The widespread and persistent nature of it and the types of infrastructures that are being targeted — appear to be targeted — that, to me, says that it's more than just a coincidence," he said.
Daniel Hoffman, a former CIA station chief and Fox News contributor, warned the institutions experiencing outages are already prime targets for foreign adversaries and cybercriminals.

"Every single one of these entities is a target, and so are you and I," Hoffman told Fox News Digital. "Every single day, 24 hours a day, China, Russia, North Korea, Iran, criminals, hackers are trying to target the banks. They're trying to target Microsoft, obviously."
Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House for comment.

The threat has already reached American infrastructure. In July, hackers targeted more than 30 municipal water systems in Minnesota, part of a broader wave of cyber intrusions across multiple states that forced some utilities to switch to manual operations and disrupted water service. Federal investigators examined possible Iranian involvement, though the attacks were not definitively attributed.

The Pentagon is also preparing for the possibility of widespread infrastructure failures during a major conflict. Under its FORTRESS initiative, military bases across the continental United States are being directed to prepare to sustain essential operations for at least 90 days without outside support, according to documents previously reviewed by Fox News Digital.

"We don't want to rely on standard civilian municipal infrastructure to run our national defense. We just simply can't. It's an intolerable risk," Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell previously told Fox News Digital.

Waller pointed to longstanding Chinese military writings that contemplate attacks on civilian communications and infrastructure during a conflict, arguing that the United States must consider the broader threat even when individual outages appear unrelated.
"Again, I am not saying that China did this. But if China wanted to, this is in their doctrine, right?" Waller said.
GROCERY STORE CYBERATTACKS ARE ‘PSYCHOLOGICAL WARFARE’ THAT COULD STRIKE US, FORMER FBI AGENT WARNS

In 2024, U.S. intelligence and law enforcement agencies warned that Chinese state-sponsored hackers known as Volt Typhoon had infiltrated American communications, energy, transportation and water systems, positioning themselves to potentially disrupt critical services during a conflict with the United States.

New research published last month found that the group had continued targeting government, defense and critical infrastructure networks through a separate hacking operation, even after U.S. authorities moved to dismantle parts of its infrastructure.
Bucci, however, noted that an adversary seeking to compromise American infrastructure might have little incentive to cause widespread, visible failures that could expose its activities.
Banking problems and widespread flight disruptions marked a stretch of technology troubles that also hit Microsoft and Workday. (Reuters)
"They might want to go in and do things to implant stuff for later use," Bucci said when asked whether foreign adversaries could be testing vulnerabilities in critical U.S. infrastructure.
"But you usually don't do a weight test where you make stuff fail or get glitchy because that can then warn the target," he added.
The disruptions have also prompted calls for greater transparency from federal officials and private companies responsible for critical systems.
"For our economy to function, people need to have some confidence in banks, among other things," Hoffman said. "So, kind of need to tell us what's going on."
Waller also urged greater transparency about infrastructure vulnerabilities and the steps being taken to address them.

"Number one, just tell the truth and be transparent," Waller said.

title: Speaker Mike Johnson calls upon House Republicans to show up for work
summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson issued a letter pressing his Republican colleagues to show up for work during the final stretch of the 119th Congress.
story: Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram breaks down the progressive pushback House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries faces after winning the Democratic nomination. Pergram also discusses how Democratic demands for Medicare-for-all and aggressive congressional investigations could test party unity.
House Speaker Mike Johnson issued a message Friday calling on his colleagues to show up for work so Republicans can advance their priorities before Democrats take over the chamber next year.

"This week we had to postpone the rule scheduled for the Floor because we didn't have enough Members in town. To state the obvious, barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our full two-year term," Johnson wrote.
"Over the next 44 days, we need every House Republican to remain fully engaged so we can get even more of our important priorities signed into law."
MIKE JOHNSON NOT RUNNING TO LEAD HOUSE GOP AFTER HISTORIC MIDTERM LOSSES

U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson speaks before presenting Gamal El Sadat with the Congressional Gold Medal, posthumously honoring his father, former Egyptian President Anwar Sadat, at Statuary Hall in the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., Nov. 18, 2026. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)
While Democrats routed Republicans during the 2026 midterms and will consequently have majorities in both chambers of Congress next year, Republicans still control the House and Senate majorities.

"The Twentieth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution specifies that our clock doesn't run out until noon on January 3rd. LET'S SCORE EVERY POINT WE CAN AND LEAVE IT ALL ON THE FIELD!" Johnson urged in the letter.
REPUBLICAN SENATOR OPENS DOOR ON POSSIBILITY OF A PRESIDENTIAL BID IN SHIFT FROM PAST POSITION
The U.S. Capitol Building Nov. 16, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Outgoing Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C. — who lost the South Carolina special Republican U.S. Senate primary runoff to Sen. Darline Graham, after running unsuccessfully in the Palmetto State's GOP gubernatorial primary — shared Johnson's post on X.
"You don’t deserve a paycheck when you don’t show up for work. And the American people aren’t happy to hear their elected officials want to stay home. Our work is far from over," Norman asserted.
SPEAKER MIKE JOHNSON PROJECTED TO CRUISE TO RE-ELECTION FOR FIFTH HOUSE TERM

Speaker of the House Mike Johnson hits the gavel ahead of the arrival of U.S. President Donald Trump for the State of the Union address in the House Chamber of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., Feb. 24, 2026. (Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images)

"Well said, @SpeakerJohnson," Rep. Mark Harris, R-N.C., wrote in a post when sharing the speaker's letter.

"We have a duty to our constituents to fulfill the job we were elected to do and ensure their voices are heard on the House Floor. Since being sworn into the 119th Congress, I have not missed a single vote. Every member should be committed to doing the same until the very end."
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Dozens of FBI and DOJ personnel are investigating Peltola's Alaska victory
summary: At least 50 FBI agents and over a dozen DOJ lawyers are probing Sen.-elect Mary Peltola over the alleged "Decoy Dan" scheme, with 200 subpoenas sent.
story: ‘Fox News @ Night’ anchor Trace Gallagher reports on Democrat Mary Peltola defeating GOP nominee Dan Sullivan in the Alaska U.S. Senate race, flipping the ninth GOP-held seat.

At least 50 FBI agents and more than a dozen lawyers from the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) are working on an investigation into Sen.-elect Mary Peltola, D-Alaska, and her alleged involvement in recruiting a candidate with the same name as her opponent, Fox News has learned.
The Associated Press projected Peltola's victory on Tuesday, forecasting that she'd defeat incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, with 50.1% of the electorate's votes.

However, senior DOJ officials have opened an investigation into Peltola's campaign and Democratic operatives to determine if any laws were broken in an effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan, a third candidate with almost the exact same name as the incumbent senator, to run.
Attorney General Todd Blanche "sees the Peltola fraud as so egregious, he is putting a lot of resources into the criminal investigation," an ally close to Blanche told Fox News Digital.
ALASKA DEM PELTOLA DEFEATS SULLIVAN, FLIPPING 9TH GOP SENATE SEAT AFTER 'DECOY DAN' UPROAR
The DOJ has sent over 200 subpoenas as part of the probe, which sources told Fox News is focused on the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC).
Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola speaks at an election night event Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Anchorage, Alaska.  (AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson)
At least five field offices are involved in the effort and nearly 100 letters have been sent out informing involved parties to preserve their records.
TIM SCOTT DECLARES ALLEGED 'DECOY DAN' PLOT A 'CRIMINAL OFFENSE' AS DOJ INVESTIGATION ROCKS ALASKA
High-profile elections attorney Marc Elias, whose law firm represents the Peltola campaign, was one of the recipients of a preservation letter.
A federal grand jury is meeting in Alaska once a month to review evidence, Fox News has learned. The Justice Department declined to comment.
DOJ FACES ‘HEAVY LIFT’ IN ALASKA ELECTION APPEAL AS SEPARATE CRIMINAL PROBE CONTINUES
Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and former Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska.  (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images; Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Sen. Sullivan has previously slammed Peltola for allegedly scheming to get the alternate Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
"This was a secret project that they had. And then they worked on it for over a year. And then she consistently lied about it," Sen. Sullivan said.
SEN DAN SULLIVAN BRANDS PELTOLA’S ALLEGED BALLOT SCHEME A ‘SCANDAL AT THE HIGHEST ORDER’
Peltola, for her part, denies ever knowing anything about recruiting efforts to get Daniel J. Sullivan, aka "Decoy Dan," on the ballot.
"I just want to clear the air," Peltola told supporters during an October speech in Juneau.
PELTOLA INSISTS 'I KNEW NOTHING' ABOUT ALLEGED 'DECOY DAN' SCHEME AS SULLIVAN ALLEGES SHE IS 'STILL LYING'

"I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters. I know I can beat Dan Sullivan," she said.
Mary Peltola launches her campaign as a Democratic candidate for Senate in Anchorage, Alaska, on Jan. 17, 2026. (Reuters)

A New York Times bombshell report released in October claimed that Peltola campaign staffers and senior aides at the DSCC jointly plotted to get the "Decoy Dan" on the ballot in an effort to confuse voters.
MARY PELTOLA'S CAMPAIGN, DEMS BACKED COVERT SCHEME TO FIELD SPOILER CANDIDATES IN ALASKA SENATE RACE: REPORT
The DSCC has also denied involvement in the alleged scheme.

Peltola, according to the AP, garnered 144,486 votes to Sen. Sullivan's 131,965 votes. A third candidate, Republican Gerald Heikes, received 6,105 votes. All other candidates, including Daniel J. Sullivan, received 5,561 combined votes.
Alaskan officials have yet to certify the state's election totals, having previously targeted Nov. 25 as the date to certify.
The DOJ had initially filed a civil lawsuit to try and delay certification, but the department now views that lawsuit as moot, as all votes have been counted.

title: Cruz turns tables on Democrats crying foul over GOP's 11th-hour judicial confirmation blitz
summary: Ted Cruz accused Senate Democrats of hypocrisy for ramming through 22 federal judges after the 2024 election while blasting Republican hearings as rushed.
story: Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, responds to Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., during a Senate Judiciary Committee nominations hearing on Capitol Hill on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026.

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, criticized the "hypocrisy" of his Democratic counterparts over their selective outrage stemming from Republican senators' push to confirm President Donald Trump's judicial appointees before Democrats take control of the Senate in January.

"And what did the same Senate Democrats who just gave sanctimonious speeches do? They rammed through 22 federal judges in November and December before leaving," Cruz said of Democrats, referring to their actions following the 2024 elections.

Cruz's remarks came during a Senate Judiciary Committee nomination hearing on Wednesday, where seven judicial nominees were introduced to committee. The Texas senator was responding to accusations from Sen. Cory Booker, D-N. J., who said Republicans were "rushing" the judicial hearings and in his 13 years in office, he has never seen the committee hold "back-to-back" hearings without the minority's consent.
MAJORITY LEADER THUNE SAYS SENATE GOP WON'T 'STAND IDLY BY' AS DEMOCRATS TAKE CONTROL OF CONGRESS

A split image of two major political events: On the left, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, speaks at a "Get Out the Vote" rally on behalf of GOP Senate candidate Michael Whatley in Indian Trail, North Carolina, on October 29, 2026. On the right, former Special Counsel Jack Smith testifies during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing as Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., looks on, in Washington, D.C., on September 29, 2026. (Peter Zay and Win McNamee / Anadolu and Getty Images)

"You know, you don't need a particularly long memory to recognize the hypocrisy in what Senator Booker said," Cruz said, comparing Booker's "lecture" of Republicans to the theatrics of Captain Renault in the movie "Casablanca."
"He is shocked, shocked to find gambling in this institution," Cruz said.

Cruz pointed out that after President Joe Biden lost the White House and Democrats lost control of the Senate in the 2024 election, Senate Democrats "rammed through" 22 federal judges before Republicans took control in January 2025.
"You know, there's an old adage that hypocrisy is the tribute that vice plays to virtue," Cruz said.
Booker argued that Republicans were disregarding the election results and suggested that the committee wait until the next term to continue with the nomination process.

"This is not a left or right thing because I've watched both parties do this in the 13 years that I've been here," Booker said. "I'm just simply saying that this is yet another step at a time where we could have paused and done this a right way."
DEMS SEIZE THE SENATE AS BLUE TIDAL WAVE CRASHES DEEP INTO TRUMP COUNTRY, TOPPLES GOP STRONGHOLDS

Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL) during a hearing to examine the abduction of Ukrainian children by the Russian Federation on Capitol Hill on Wednesday December 3, 2025 (Demetrius Freeman/The Washington Post via Getty Images)
But Cruz noted that Booker and every other Democrat on the committee voted in favor of approving all 22 judges before the new congressional term started in 2025.

In November 2024, then-Senate Judiciary Chair Dick Durbin, D-Ill., issued a statement after the election pushing for Biden's judicial appointees to be confirmed before the end of the congressional term.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) speaks during a news conference at the U.S. Capitol on September 30, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Kent Nishimura/Getty Images)
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"The Senate must confirm every one of these highly qualified, diverse nominees before the sun sets on the 118th Congress. The American people deserve nothing less," Durbin said in a press release at the time.

There are currently 27 federal judicial vacancies with 13 nominees still waiting for approval, as Republicans work to fill the seats. Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N. Y., who is poised to become Senate majority leader when the new Congress convenes in January, vowed to block any of Trump's "crappy nominations" from being approved once Democrats take the gavel.
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Biden memoir draws fire for ‘denial’ as critics flag Gaza, racial-equity omissions
summary: Joe Biden's memoir "Promise Me, America" draws sharp reviews; critics say he stays "stubbornly in denial" about his age, Gaza, and his 2024 reelection bid.
story: Fox News' Lara Trump discusses former President Joe Biden's new memoir as he defends his 2024 debate performance with President Donald Trump. Trump details how Democrats behind-the-scenes allowed for Biden's decline to go on.
Former President Joe Biden’s new memoir has drawn sharp criticism and opened a debate about how Biden’s choices — and his account of them — will shape his legacy.

Released Nov. 17, "Promise Me, America" defends Biden’s presidency and his decision to seek re-election in 2024. The memoir drew a sharp verdict from The New Yorker writer Amy Davidson Sorkin, who said Biden remains "stubbornly in denial," while other critics scrutinized the book's account of Gaza and what it left out about racial equity. Sorkin’s criticism centers on Biden’s response to questions about his age and his continued insistence that he could have won.

"The true test of a book like this is whether its author will own his losses, too. Biden, for his part, does not," added New York Times nonfiction critic Jennifer Szalai. "He is so preoccupied with burnishing his legacy that he gets awkward and defensive when addressing the two issues many readers will be most curious about: his handling of the war in Gaza, and his decision to run for a second term."
"The news of the memoir, in short, is that there is no real news: Biden is as stubbornly in denial as ever, " Sorkin wrote.
BIDEN ADDRESSES INFAMOUS 'WE BEAT MEDICARE' DEBATE MOMENT IN NEW MEMOIR

A copy of former President Joe Biden's memoir, "Promise Me, America," is on display at Politics and Prose bookstore in Washington, DC, on Nov. 17, 2026. The book, which defends Biden's record and his 2024 re-election bid, has drawn sharp criticism from reviewers over its handling of his age and the Gaza war. (AFP via Getty Images)
The dispute around Biden's recollection of his tenure centers on two consequential decisions — his choice to seek another term and his administration’s policy toward Israel during the Gaza war.

In its review of the memoir, the Associated Press reported that Biden says he believed he was the best person to defeat President Donald Trump and that the Democratic primaries gave him no warning he was in trouble. Meanwhile, Sorkin and Szalai argued in their reviews that Biden gives too little weight to concerns about his age and fitness when recounting that period, despite acknowledging that his debate performance was poor.
"Biden’s voice gets passive; he portrays himself as the helpless victim of events," Szalai wrote. "He gets similarly defensive when recounting the war in Gaza," she added.
BIDEN ACCUSES PELOSI OF WORKING 'FURIOUSLY' BEHIND SCENES TO DERAIL HIS 2024 CAMPAIGN

Israeli soldiers monitor the northern Gaza Strip from southern Israel on July 30, 2025. Critics have faulted former President Joe Biden's new memoir for how it characterizes his relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the war in Gaza. (AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg)

Self-described socialist website Jacobin and other reviewers, including Sorkin and Szalai, criticized Biden's accounting of his relationship with Israel and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, arguing he described it in the book as if it were much more adversarial than in actuality.

Szalai wrote that Biden gets "awkward and defensive" when addressing both Gaza and his decision to seek another term, and faulted him for how he described Israeli victims and suffering versus Palestinian victims and suffering. She specifically noted that Biden used names to identify Israeli victims but "no names" for Palestinian victims, while calling his language about Palestinian suffering "passive."
"The only consistent position is inconsistency," Israeli journalist and political commentator Amit Segal said of Biden’s account of Israel policy, calling it "devoid of doctrine or strategy. "

Demonstrators gather outside a rally held by President Donald Trump at Macomb County Community College in Warren, Mich., on April 29, 2025. In his new memoir, former President Joe Biden writes that he believed he was the best candidate to defeat Trump in 2024. (Getty Images/Dominic Gwinn)

Separately, Semafor politics reporter David Weigel noted that Biden recounts signing 17 executive orders on his first day but does not mention his order establishing a government-wide approach to racial equity that mandated every executive agency to develop a DEI action plan. Weigel wrote that the word "equity" does not appear in the memoir once.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
"Biden argues instead that 'every one of my legislative accomplishments had justice baked in,' including 'equal access to vaccines,'" Weigel wrote.

"Gender gets the same treatment," he continued. "Biden, who had called anti-transgender discrimination 'the civil rights issue of our time,' never uses the word 'transgender' in his memoir. He doesn’t mention his Day 1 executive order that banned discrimination on the basis of gender identity."
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: Deadlocked Florida election decided by coin toss
summary: Jennifer Lagner won the Atlantic Beach commissioner seat after a coin flip broke a 3,162-vote tie, with Duval County election officials running recounts.
story: Fox News' Griff Jenkins and Charlie Hurt report live from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on Election Day to speak directly with local voters at a diner. Voters share their thoughts on the state's gubernatorial race, economic concerns and key midterm issues.
Jennifer Lagner won the election for Atlantic Beach city commissioner in Florida via a coin toss after successive recounts left her tied with her opponent, according to the New York Post.
Lagner and Lisa Herrold each sat at 3,162 votes after Duval County's Supervisor of Elections Jerry Holland initiated both a manual and a machine recount.
The deadlock initiated the unique tiebreaker last week in which each candidate would have the chance to win two of three coin flips.
THREE HIGH SCHOOL FOOTBALL TEAMS HAVE THEIR PLAYOFF FATES DECIDED BY A MIDNIGHT PARKING LOT COIN TOSS
Under the city's election rules, each candidate had a chance to call the coin's landing. Herrold went first, calling heads, but the coin landed tails, giving Lagner a 1-0 lead.
Lagner went next, accurately predicting heads to win the contest, securing her election victory to become city commissioner.

Supervisor of Elections Jerry Holland holds up his challenge coin to the tail's side, to be used to determine the winner of the best two-out-of-three coin-flip tiebreaker conducted by the Duval County Supervisor of Elections on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, in Jacksonville, Fla., to decide Atlantic Beach Commission Seat 4. Candidates Lisa Herrold and Jennifer Lagner were tied with 3,162 votes each. Herrold went first and guessed heads and the coin landed tails. Lagner guessed heads with the coin landing heads, winning the seat. (USA Today Network via Reuters Connect)
"This shows how great and free our country is," Lagner told a local news outlet.

"I am honored to have the opportunity to serve as your next City Commissioner for Seat 4," she wrote on Facebook. "A coin toss was certainly an unexpected and unforgettable way to bring an election to a close! Thank you to Jerry Holland and his entire team for their work throughout this election process."

Candidate Jennifer Lagner hugs fellow candidate Lisa Herrold during the best-two-out-of-three coin-flip tiebreaker conducted by the Duval County Supervisor of Elections on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, in Jacksonville, Fla., to decide Atlantic Beach Commission Seat 4. (USA Today Network via Reuters Connect)
"Jen and I have been a part of this community for years ... It was meant to be ... We’re going to look back at this and realize how unbelievable this was," Herrold told the local outlet.
SOUTH DAKOTA MAYORAL CANDIDATES SEPARATED BY JUST TWO VOTES IN SHOCKINGLY CLOSE RACE, RECOUNT EXPECTED
Supervisor Holland added, "It’s remarkable, really ... the meaning of that is every vote matters, you know, and one vote can make a difference."

Candidate Jennifer Lagner, center, shakes hands with fellow candidate Lisa Herrold during the best two-out-of-three coin-flip tiebreaker conducted by the Duval County Supervisor of Elections on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, in Jacksonville, Fla. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
Last Friday's coin flip wasn't the first time in Duval County history that an election tie was broken in an unconventional manner.

In the 2014 Neptune Beach City Council race, Rory Diamond and Richard Arthur broke their tie by choosing from a series of numbered ping pong balls. Arthur, who selected the ping pong ball with a higher number, won.

title: Trump and Dana White honor Marine Corps band with six-figure checks in first event on new helipad
summary: President Donald Trump and Dana White will each donate $100,000 to the Marine Band, America's oldest continuously active professional musical organization.
story: The U.S. Marine Band performed at a ceremony welcoming China’s President Xi Jinping at the White House in September 2026.
FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump and UFC President and CEO Dana White will announce six-figure personal contributions to one of America's oldest musical institutions.

The President’s Own United States Marine Band played a key role in America's 250th birthday celebrations and official state business this year — and a White House official tells Fox News Digital that the pair want to "express their appreciation for the band’s exceptional talent, professionalism and commitment to excellence."

Trump and White announced Friday afternoon on the new White House helipad on the South Lawn that they increased their combined gift from $200,000 to $500,000 of their own money after realizing the size of the ensemble. No taxpayer dollars will be used for the $500,000 gift.

"Now, it started off with 200,000, and I said, how many people are there? I thought there were 70, but it’s about 107. And a lot of people joined. So we decided to increase it," Trump said during the event, which was the first-ever held on the new South Lawn helipad.
The U.S. Marine Corps band performs ahead of the Freedom 250 Grand Prix in Washington, D.C., on Sunday, Aug. 23, 2026. (Elizabeth Frantz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"We’re now making it at 500,000. Now everyone’s going to get a lot of money," Trump added.

All 135 members of the band will attend alongside senior military leaders, including Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao and Commandant of the Marine Corps General Eric Smith.
TRUMP TAPS ‘TRUE WARRIOR’ HUNG CAO AS NAVY SECRETARY AFTER 4 MONTHS AS ACTING LEADER

"‘The President’s Own’ United States Marine Band proudly embodies American excellence and tradition – and their melodies have accompanied defining moments in our nation’s history," White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told Fox News Digital.
"President Trump will partner with Dana White to generously celebrate their elite musical talent and unwavering dedication, conveying his gratitude to some of our Nation’s finest musicians."
The band performed at UFC 250 on the South Lawn of the White House in June, learning each fighter's song in a first-of-its-kind event featuring seven fights.
It also performed at the White House in September when Chinese President Xi Jinping came to Washington for bilateral talks with Trump.

President Donald J. Trump and UFC President and CEO Dana White enter the Octagon following the UFC lightweight championship fight during the UFC Freedom 250 event on the South Lawn at the White House on June 14, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Jeff Bottari/Zuffa LLC via Getty Images)
DANA WHITE SAYS 'I DON'T GIVE A S---' IF TRUMP FRIENDSHIP COSTS HIM BUSINESS, 250TH EVENT WAS TRUMP'S IDEA
Band members serve as musical ambassadors for the Marine Corps at national and international venues.

The Marine Band is the oldest continuously active professional musical organization in the United States. It was founded by an act of Congress in 1798 and has served every U.S. president except for George Washington.
Thomas Jefferson gave the band its nickname, "The President's Own." It traveled with Abraham Lincoln to his 1863 Gettysburg address.

The United States Marine Band performs prior to an arrival ceremony for King Charles III on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, April 28, 2026. (Yuri Gripas/Abaca/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
For the first time ever, the Marine Band has been nominated for a 2027 Grammy Award. Specifically, the nomination is for Best Orchestral Performance.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

There are 10 active Marine Corps Fleet Bands. Members of those bands attend Marine Corps Recruit Training and earn the title United States Marine, and are held to the same standards of discipline, physical fitness and professionalism.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Republican senator opens door on possibility of a presidential bid, in shift from past position
summary: Republican Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri, who previously said he did not intend to pursue a presidential bid, is now opening the door to the possibility.
story: Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., warns that the House’s failed attempt to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth is just the beginning on ‘Jesse Watters Primetime.’

Following the GOP’s widespread midterm losses, Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo. — who in September indicated to the Washington Examiner that he had "no intention" of running for president in 2028 — is now leaving the door open to a White House bid.

"After this most recent election, I think everybody that cares about the future of the party, the future of the country, has a lot of thinking to do," the senator said to The Associated Press when asked about his presidential aspirations. "So I’ll just say I have a lot of thinking to do."
Democrats delivered a midterm election drubbing and will control the House and Senate majorities next year.
JOSH HAWLEY SHOOTS DOWN PROSPECT OF 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID, SAYS HE HAS 'NO INTENTION' OF RUNNING: REPORT

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., arrives for a Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee confirmation hearing in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"I was alarmed by the results of the election, and I’m concerned about the direction of both my party and the country," Hawley told NBC News when asked whether he is thinking about running for president. "And I want to do my part there. I’m trying to think through what my part is. But I certainly want to do my part for the future."

"Listen, I don’t want to give you a misconception that, for sure, I have plans or intentions," he noted, according to the outlet. "What I said to you is the honest to goodness truth, which is just that I’ve got four years here to serve in the Senate, and I’m just trying to think about where I am and what’s in front of me, what can I do to help the country go forward."
"I'm concerned about what comes next for the party. So I don’t know what my role is in that yet, but I’m trying to give it some serious thought, and I’m no further along than that," he said.
HAWLEY ZEROES IN ON LIA THOMAS LOCKER ROOM CONTROVERSY: 'DID THEY CONSENT?'

U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., speaks during a hearing on "Arctic Frost Accountability: Oversight of Telecommunications Carriers' Responses to Jack Smith's Witch Hunt" in the Hart Senate Office Building on Feb. 10, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

Hawley's comments mark a notable reversal, as he previously shot down the idea of pursuing the presidency in 2028, telling the Washington Examiner in September, "No, I have no intention of doing so, period."
Hawley, who has served in the Senate since early 2019, won reelection in 2024, meaning his current term will not end until early 2031.

title: America's largest IPO ever carries potentially seismic implications for political spending ahead of 2028
summary: Anthropic makes its stock market debut Thursday at a $1.5 trillion valuation as its seven co-founders each pledge to give away 80% of their equity.
story: FOX Business breaks down Anthropic's historic $81.34 billion IPO, the largest public offering on record, surpassing SpaceX and valuing the Claude AI maker at roughly $1.5 trillion. The blockbuster Wall Street debut could deliver massive payouts to Anthropic's founders, employees and early investors, including Ashton Kutcher.

Anthropic’s Thursday stock market debut, valued at around $1.5 trillion, is the largest in American history and, given promises made by its founders, is likely the preface to a similarly historic flood of cash into the political system.

Bloomberg projects that each of Anthropic’s seven co-founders will be worth approximately $24.5 billion now that their artificial intelligence firm has gone public. Each of the seven has also pledged to give away 80% of their equity in the firm to philanthropic causes — a promise that has raised eyebrows given Anthropic’s links to a controversial moral philosophy and its history of spending big to influence elections.

Effective altruism, which some of Anthropic’s early funders and employees have voiced support for, generally treats massive political and philanthropic giving as a moral obligation to prevent AI "doomsday" scenarios, such as a rogue agent working to exterminate the human race. Though the company's founders have distanced themselves from the movement, some early employees and other figures associated with Anthropic have maintained connections to its ideas, particularly its emphasis on preventing potentially catastrophic risks from artificial intelligence.

Politically, this has manifested as Anthropic's leaders throwing large sums of money behind efforts to regulate AI development. This approach has often put Anthropic at odds with the White House and its Republican allies, who are pursuing unchained innovation to spur economic growth, a dynamic that could become even more tense now that the firm’s leaders have billions of dollars at their disposal.
ANTHROPIC CEO CALLS ON AI INDUSTRY TO SLOW DOWN TECH RACE, DRAWING SUPPORT FROM ELON MUSK, SAM ALTMAN
Dario Amodei, CEO and co-founder of Anthropic, attends the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, Jan. 23, 2025. (AP Photo/Markus Schreiber)

A Fox News Digital analysis of campaign finance filings found that Anthropic employees donated about $7.1 million to Democrats and Democratic-aligned committees, compared to just around $3.7 million to Republicans and Republican-aligned committees during the 2026 electoral cycle.

Such a split is noteworthy given that Anthropic offers to match shares donated by its employees by contributing additional shares to the organizations they opt to support. If the firm’s employees decide to give large chunks of equity to left-of-center organizations, for instance, it would result in a significant Anthropic-funded financial windfall for the left.

"I think there’s a lot of overlap between certain left-of-center causes," Nathan Leamer, a consultant who works on tech policy, told Fox News Digital when asked about the political orientation of Anthropic’s employees and effective altruists more broadly. "They've benefited from capitalism, but their worldviews do not always reflect free market values."
TECH POWERHOUSE’S REGULATORY PUSH BEARS SIMILARITIES TO A NOTORIOUS WASHINGTON STRATEGY

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, accompanied by U.S. President Donald Trump, Oracle co-founder, CTO and Executive Chairman Larry Ellison, right, and SoftBank CEO Masayoshi Son, speaks during a news conference in the Roosevelt Room of the White House on January 21, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

While Anthropic's rank-and-file employees appear to favor Democrats in their political donations, some of the company's most prominent financial contributions have gone toward a political network seeking to influence both parties around AI regulation, rather than exclusively supporting one partisan side.

Anthropic’s founders and longtime employees have comparatively little in the way of direct partisan donations, with much of their money being directed toward Public First, a super PAC network that supports candidates in both parties who favor stronger AI safeguards.

Defending Our Values PAC, on the right, and the Jobs and Democracy PAC, on the left, spent millions of dollars influencing Republican and Democratic primary elections during the 2026 cycle to boost candidates seeking to advance safety-related AI regulations. The Democratic PAC spent far more, around $20 million, than its GOP-focused counterpart, which paid out just under $8 million.

As 2028 approaches, the seven co-founders' newly acquired fortunes could give them substantially greater financial capacity to support causes and organizations they believe in — and presidential primaries will be a natural target for their newly acquired war chests.

In the general election, whichever candidate takes a position more aligned with Anthropic’s preferred regulatory stance may be able to count on large sums to back their bid for the White House. The new funds also enable Anthropic and its allies to focus on a much broader range of down-ballot races to win more allies in Congress and state legislatures.
HOUSE COMMITTEE PASSES FOREIGN FUNDING TRANSPARENCY ACT TO EXPOSE FOREIGN DONATIONS TO NONPROFITS

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and President Donald Trump are at the center of a growing clash after the Trump administration designated the AI firm a national security supply chain risk and severed its Pentagon contracts. (Samyukta Lakshmi/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Explicitly political organizations aren’t the only ones likely to see their coffers swell from the deluge of cash.

A cottage industry of think tanks and advocacy organizations has sprung up in D.C. and San Francisco to conduct research and make arguments aimed at convincing those with power of the merits of robust AI safety regulation. Many nonprofit advocacy organizations, including 501(c)(4) groups such as Public First Action, are not required to publicly disclose their donors, making it difficult to identify the full network of individuals and organizations financing the push for AI regulation. Anthropic, however, made its initial $40 million donation to Public First Action to support such education and policy work.

"I can tell you among civil society — think tanks and foundations and other organizations in the nonprofit world — this is absolutely making an impact," Leamer told Fox News Digital when asked about this dynamic. "I was in a conversation last night with a conservative organization who was telling me they're being offered hundreds of thousands of dollars to engage in a more [effective altruist]-aligned worldview, even though it's not necessarily where they are philosophically … If that’s happening among people I’m talking to, I can’t imagine how many more they’re talking to."
AI 'DOOMERS' RISK KNEECAPPING US VS CHINA, BUT EX-PENTAGON VET SAYS BOTH EXTREMES MISS THE MARK

Dario Amodei, co-founder of Anthropic, looks toward Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta Platforms, and President Donald Trump during a press briefing with AI executives outside the West Wing of the White House on Sept. 29, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Getty Images)

An individual close to the think tank world, requesting to remain anonymous, told Fox News Digital that donors aligned with Anthropic and effective altruism are already attempting to throw money around with the aim of influencing conservative thought leaders. In their telling, prospective funders will approach right-of-center organizations and offer them funding to research topics they are already interested in, such as child safety, then use that grant funding as leverage to influence their messaging.

Much of this messaging has been oriented toward pushing regulation to slow AI development so that engineers can devise mechanisms to stop the technology from being used for evil, or from inadvertently hurting people.

Anthropic’s leaders maintain that such regulations are necessary to prevent AI from harming humanity, whereas its detractors argue that such guardrails will kneecap America’s ability to compete with China. Some critics have argued that Anthropic is pushing for safety laws as a way to create rules that it can then exploit to give itself a leg up over rivals.
WHO IS DARIO AMODEI, THE ANTHROPIC CEO PUSHING INDEPENDENT AI OVERSIGHT?
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei speaks on the day Anthropic holds its initial public offering at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City, on Nov. 19, 2026. (Brendan McDermid/Reuters)

Some have traced Anthropic’s caution toward AI development to the effective altruist movement, which itself has segments who predict that unregulated advancement in the field may bring about the end of humanity.

Critics of effective altruism, which holds that individuals should seek out the avenue through which they can do the most good for each dollar spent, argue that its emphasis on speculative threats, including catastrophic artificial intelligence, can divert resources from immediate problems such as poverty.

In its extreme manifestation, some effective altruists have argued that one of the most efficient ways to engage in charitable giving is by improving the welfare of shrimp, as hundreds of billions of shrimp are farmed annually, so even modest improvements in how they are treated could reduce enormous amounts of suffering at relatively little cost. Mainstream effective altruists, however, generally argue that funds should be directed toward researching AI safety given the near-infinite negative downside of the technology destroying humanity.

That Anthropic’s leaders will actually open their pocketbooks to the extent promised, or even to these causes in particular, is not guaranteed. The IPO’s prospectus calls the commitments "voluntary, revocable expressions" of philanthropic intent that "do not constitute legally binding obligations."
Their ability to spend will also be dependent on Anthropic’s stock holding value amid a turbulent political and economic environment.

Anthropic and Public First Action did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Thursday.

title: Van Hollen scores support from another Dem amid Senate majority leader bid
summary: Sen. Elissa Slotkin said she will back Sen. Chris Van Hollen for the Senate Democratic leadership role as he challenges Sen. Chuck Schumer.
story: Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., looks to become the next Senate majority leader in his bid against Sen. Chuck Schumer. Van Hollen says there are 15 people to back him in this election. He also weighs in on the DSA agenda and more during 'Fox News Sunday.'
Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., said Thursday she will back Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., as he challenges current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for the majority leader slot.

"I've been clear as well that I don't think that Senator Schumer is best positioned to be our next leader. I'm encouraged that people like Chris Van Hollen got in the race, and because I've been clear that I wasn't supporting Schumer, I will be supporting Chris Van Hollen," Slotkin stated in a video posted to social media.
BERNIE SANDERS SAYS HE WON'T BACK SCHUMER AS PUSH FOR NEW LEADERSHIP GAINS STEAM

U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., speaks during a forum on President Trump's crypto dealings co-hosted by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., in the Dirksen Senate Office on July 27, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

"But I think no matter the outcome, it's going to be imperative for our leaders to demonstrate how they're going to incorporate that next generation, and what big and bold ideas, specifically, they're going to put forward in the first 100 days," she said.

Van Hollen shared Slotkin's post on X and wrote, "@SenatorSlotkin & I agree: the American people spoke, and we need new leadership in the United States Senate. Now is the time to act boldly, and we’re going to work together to deliver results."
TOP DEM CRIES 'WEAPONIZATION' AS COMMENTS WARNING YOUNG PEOPLE NOT TO JOIN TRUMP ADMIN LAND HER IN HOT WATER

Then-Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed listens as U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., speaks during a town hall campaign event in Warren, Mich., on Oct. 3, 2026. (JEFF KOWALSKY/AFP via Getty Images)

title: Elon Musk's space giant cozies up to Dem power brokers as party vows to put his empire under siege
summary: Elon Musk's SpaceX hired five Democratic lobbyists as Democrats promise probes into Ukraine satellite claims, Pentagon reliance and Chinese investors.
story: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman discusses SpaceX's role in America's race to return to the moon, potential congressional scrutiny of Elon Musk and the agency's search for new astronauts on 'Fox & Friends.'
Elon Musk’s SpaceX has hired a team of veteran Washington lobbyists with Democratic connections as the party prepares to take control of Congress and intensify scrutiny of his business empire.

Democratic lawmakers have signaled plans to investigate several aspects of Musk’s business dealings and government relationships, including allegations that SpaceX improperly restricted Ukraine’s satellite communications, whether the Pentagon has become overly dependent on the company and potential conflicts of interest stemming from Musk’s relationship with the Trump administration.

Against that backdrop, newly released public records show SpaceX has retained five veteran lobbyists from Mehlman Consulting, a bipartisan D.C.-based government affairs firm, several of whom have deep ties to Democratic lawmakers and former administrations.

SpaceX, with a market capitalization of nearly $2 trillion, is home to Musk's holdings in aerospace engineering, artificial intelligence, telecommunications and space transportation. If Democrats successfully knock it down a peg, the resulting loss in value could send shock waves throughout the economy.
DEMOCRATS SET SIGHTS ON ELON MUSK PROBE AFTER MIDTERM WINS, BUT PRITZKER DRAWS A SURPRISING LINE

Elon Musk on Saturday continued to defend Starlink after Ukraine faced more than a week of speed restrictions that disrupted its war effort against Russia, saying SpaceX has done more to defend the country than any other private company "by far." (Getty Images)
Musk has worked to publicly distance himself from the right wing since the GOP's poor midterm performance, recently stating that he’s "not MAGA" at a New York Times summit.

"I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much. Or maybe it would have been much worse without that," he said at the event. "I’m not sure what MAGA means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that."
HOW ELON MUSK GOT BACK IN TRUMP'S ORBIT AFTER NUCLEAR FALLOUT, INSIDERS REVEAL: 'WATER UNDER THE BRIDGE'
Elon Musk listens during a Cabinet meeting with President Donald Trump in the White House on Monday, March 24, 2025, in Washington. (AP/Pool)

Musk isn’t the first tech leader to throw money to Democratic operatives, seemingly to prepare for the incoming congressional majority. Palantir, another frequent target of Democratic criticism, has also retained lobbyists with ties to the party.

"I think at the end of the day, these companies have an inordinate amount of money, and they will try and put it wherever they can in order to stave off any real accountability," Aya Ibrahim, a senior fellow at the AI Now Institute and a former Biden administration official, told NPR of Palantir’s hirings.
WHY CORPORATE AMERICA NEEDS ONE PLAYBOOK FOR A DIVIDED WASHINGTON AFTER NOVEMBER

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is open to an investigation into Elon Musk for his time serving in the Trump administration as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images; Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

Technology stocks took a sharp hit in the days after Democrats won their stunning midterm victory, with AI infrastructure and data-center companies among the hardest hit as investors weighed the prospect of tighter regulation.
The throng of lobbyists adds to Musk’s already large arsenal of paid influencers, which includes Republicans and Democrats at the state and federal levels.

Musk’s new agents include the former deputy chief of staff to Sen. Maria Cantwell, who is slated to take over the powerful Commerce Committee in January, a former aide to Vice President Al Gore and a host of other one-time high-ranking Democratic staffers. The effective date of registration listed on the lobbying records was Oct. 1, around the time many were predicting Democrats would win control of Congress.
