title: Trump will face reporters after historic Xi-Putin talks as war questions linger
summary: President Donald Trump faces reporters Friday after Shenzhen summit with Xi Jinping and Putin yielded a nuclear risk pledge but no Ukraine breakthrough.
story: President Donald Trump meets with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a summit in China to discuss reducing nuclear weapons and global cooperation. Lucas Tomlinson reports live on the historic talks, while guest Dennis Wilder, former NSC director for China, joins Bill Hemmer and Dana Perino to analyze the potential impact on international relations and tensions in Ukraine and Iran.

President Donald Trump is set to face reporters Friday after wrapping up a historic visit to China that brought him together with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for unprecedented three-way talks.

The leaders struck a warm diplomatic tone despite lingering questions over the war in Ukraine, nuclear arms negotiations and tensions in the Middle East — as well as stalled trade negotiations between the U.S. and China.

The summit in Shenzhen marked the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia, bringing Trump face-to-face with two of America's chief geopolitical adversaries. Washington has spent years arming Ukraine in its war against Russia, while the Pentagon has long identified China as its primary "pacing challenge" in the Indo-Pacific.
Trump's scheduled press conference at noon on Friday will offer an opportunity to elaborate on what the meetings accomplished and whether the diplomatic discussions will lead to concrete agreements.
The three leaders are meeting on the sidelines of the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting hosted by China from November 18–19. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
CHINA BLOCKS BLOOMBERG REPORTER FROM TRUMP-PUTIN-XI MEETING OVER QUESTION TO TRUMP

The gathering between the three world powers produced a joint declaration pledging dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, maintaining stable energy supplies and reforming the United Nations, but stopped short of announcing major breakthroughs on Ukraine or Iran.
President Trump described his trip as "Great and Highly Consequential" in a Truth Social post announcing that he will hold a press conference at the White House midday on Friday.

Trump last appeared in the briefing room on Nov. 9, 2026, with UFC CEO Dana White after the president joked about offering him the press secretary job. On Nov. 13, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy held a White House briefing regarding the FAA nationwide ground stop.

The president has not had a press secretary since Katie Zacharia's few-day stint last month in the role succeeding Karoline Leavitt. Zacharia held one briefing on Oct. 13, 2026, but was removed from the job after widespread backlash regarding her ability to serve in the role and her claims to be an attorney.

Throughout the China visit, Trump emphasized his personal relationships with Xi and Putin, praising the Chinese leader for an elaborate welcome that included a military flyover and referring to both presidents as friends.
"President Xi and I have formed an outstanding personal relationship," Trump said during their bilateral meeting Thursday. "Some people are unhappy when they hear that, but I'm very happy about it."
Trump also told Xi that their friendship had grown closer over the years and predicted the two countries would avoid major problems as long as they remained in power.

During a separate meeting with Putin, Trump greeted the Russian leader by calling him "my friend," despite the lack of a breakthrough in his longstanding efforts to negotiate an end to Russia's war in Ukraine.
The president later expressed optimism about those efforts, saying he had spent much of his bilateral meeting with Putin discussing the conflict.
"I think things are happening," Trump said during the trilateral meeting. "I think that he and I hope the other side would like to see an end to that war."

President Donald Trump is greeted by China's President Xi Jinping as he arrives at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on November 18, 2026. (Mandel NGAN/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Putin also acknowledged that Ukraine had been a focus of his separate discussions with Xi and Trump, but the three leaders' joint declaration made no mention of the conflict or any new peace initiative.
The summit also put nuclear arms control back in the spotlight months after the expiration of New START, the last remaining treaty limiting U.S. and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.
Trump argued that the three countries were uniquely positioned to reduce the world's nuclear stockpiles, while acknowledging the difficulty of persuading nuclear powers to give up their weapons.
"Once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them," Trump said.
TRUMP HOLDS THE NUCLEAR CARDS TO PLAY AGAINST CHINA AND RUSSIA ON ARMS CONTROL
The leaders ultimately agreed to pursue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation, but announced no binding arms reductions or timetable for negotiations.

Trump also pointed to potential cooperation with China on Iran, asserting that Washington and Beijing shared an interest in preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon and keeping energy flowing through the Strait of Hormuz.
"Both the United States and China have an interest in ensuring that energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, and that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon," Trump said during his meeting with Xi.
"We both feel that very strongly on both points," he added.

The remarks were notable given China's economic ties to Tehran, including its purchases of Iranian oil, which have provided an important source of revenue for the Iranian government despite Western sanctions.

Beijing's commercial relationship with Iran has complicated U.S. efforts to isolate Tehran, although Trump's remarks did not establish whether China had agreed to change its oil purchases or take additional steps to pressure Iran over its nuclear program.

Trade was another focus of Trump's meeting with Xi, with the president touting what he described as progress toward a more balanced economic relationship and signaling that he would seek additional purchases of American agricultural products.
Under what Trump called the "30-for-30" deal, he said the two countries had agreed to cut tariffs on $30 billion in trade.

Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump shake hands during a meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen. (Photo by Vyacheslav PROKOFYEV/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
"Our farmers have done very well, and I'll be asking you to do some more for our farmers," Trump said, adding that China had an "insatiable appetite" for American products.
The discussions came as Washington and Beijing continued to navigate disagreements over tariffs, rare earth minerals and access to advanced technology.

Trump also used the APEC summit to declare the United States the world leader in "superintelligence," making the assertion in Shenzhen, one of China's major technology hubs, as the two countries compete for dominance in artificial intelligence.

But the most consequential diplomatic development remained the historic trilateral meeting, which Trump described as an opportunity for the three powers to pursue cooperation despite their disagreements.
"We are really making history," Trump said.

title: $500M investment could bring AI robots to your workplace
summary: Genesis AI raised $500 million to expand its general-purpose robot Eno, which learns physical skills from workers wearing special electronic gloves.
story: Cognisee Founder & CEO Ahmer Inam highlights his company's innovative use of AI to close America's skilled labor gap. Cognisee captures the knowledge and experience of retiring workers, transforming them into digital mentors. This AI-powered training empowers new generations in critical sectors like manufacturing, aviation and healthcare, ensuring expertise is passed on without replacing human roles, making the workforce more efficient.

What if a robot could learn how to do your job simply by watching you work? That's what Genesis AI is working toward, and some of the biggest names in tech are betting big on it. The robotics company has raised $500 million to bring its general-purpose robot, Eno, into more workplaces. The investment values Genesis at $3.5 billion and puts some serious financial muscle behind its plans.

But what really caught my attention is how these robots learn. Genesis is developing technology that allows people to teach robots physical skills without having to program every movement. Workers wear special electronic gloves while doing their regular jobs. The gloves capture their hand movements and turn that information into training data that helps robots learn to perform similar tasks.

Eventually, Genesis wants these robots to handle complex work without someone constantly supervising them. The company plans to bring Eno to customer sites in 2027, starting with industrial workplaces. So how close are we to robots that can actually do our jobs, and what happens to the people teaching them? Let's take a closer look.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
AI BUILDS VIRTUAL HOMES WHERE ROBOTS LEARN FROM THEIR MISTAKES
Genesis AI has raised $500 million to expand development of Eno, a general-purpose robot designed to learn physical tasks by observing human workers. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Genesis AI raises $500 million to expand its robot workforce

Genesis AI announced a $500 million Series A funding round at a $3.5 billion post-money valuation. Premji Invest, Khosla Ventures and Eclipse co-led the investment. Other backers include NVIDIA, AMD Ventures, Samsung Next and Zoom. Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Zoom CEO Eric Yuan and Yahoo co-founder Jerry Yang are also among the investors. T. Rowe Price-advised accounts and several other major financial and technology firms participated. That's a significant vote of confidence in a company developing robots that can perform physical work across different environments.

Genesis plans to use the funding to expand robot training and improve its artificial intelligence. The company is also increasing production of Eno while hiring additional researchers and robotics engineers. "Our mission is to remove the physical limits on human ambition," said Zhou Xian, co-founder and CEO of Genesis AI. The company wants to move beyond robots programmed to repeat a single task. Its larger goal is to build machines that can adapt to changing conditions and eventually handle entire workflows.
How the Genesis AI robot Eno works

Eno takes a different approach from humanoid robots designed to closely resemble people. Genesis has focused on giving the machine useful physical capabilities rather than recreating every aspect of human appearance. The robot combines dexterous hands with a body designed for practical work. Its hands can handle tools and objects that require careful control, while its AI helps it respond to different physical tasks.

At the center of the technology is GENE, the company's AI foundation model, which acts as the robotic brain. The system helps robots interpret their surroundings and control precise physical movements. We previously covered Genesis AI's robotic brain and its ability to perform complex hand movements. Now, the company is working to bring that intelligence into Eno for commercial use. For now, Genesis has demonstrated several advanced skills using a test robot powered by GENE. Those capabilities are expected to move to Eno as development continues.
How special gloves teach Genesis AI robots human skills

How does a robot learn to handle delicate objects or perform tasks that require precise finger movements? We asked Genesis AI co-founder and president Théophile Gervet to explain how its electronic gloves make that possible. "The electronic gloves are worn while people are performing their regular work so we can collect massive amounts of real-world data about how humans perform physical tasks in order to train GENE, our robotic brain."

The gloves capture detailed finger movements and the pressure applied when handling different materials. Genesis designed its robotic hands to closely match human hands, creating what the company calls a 1:1:1 mapping between the human hand, glove and robotic hand. "This process enables Eno to learn complex physical skills without having to manually program every movement," Gervet explained.

Genesis also uses small cameras worn on workers' heads to record tasks from their point of view. "This lets GENE see exactly what someone sees as they perform a task, including how they use their hands and interact with their surroundings," Gervet said. The company also trains GENE using existing videos of people performing physical work. Together, these sources help the AI develop more complex physical skills.
How Genesis AI robots practice without being in the real world

Genesis has another training advantage. Its robots can practice inside Genesis World, a simulation platform that recreates physical environments. For example, a robot learning to play the piano can study movements collected from someone wearing the electronic gloves. It can then repeatedly practice those movements inside a virtual environment.

Gervet explained how the training process can speed up learning. "Also, instead of practicing at the piano for an hour or so a day like you and I might, the robot can train in our hyper-realistic simulation, Genesis World, helping it master its task, like playing the piano, much quicker than it would in the real world." That approach allows developers to test movements without relying entirely on expensive physical training sessions.
AUTONOMOUS EXCAVATORS ARE DIGGING WITH EMPTY CABS
Genesis AI uses electronic gloves and wearable cameras to collect human movement data, helping train robots to perform complex workplace tasks. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What tasks can Genesis AI robots perform today?

Genesis has demonstrated its GENE robotic brain performing several complex activities. These include preparing meals, handling laboratory equipment and assembling wire harnesses. Gervet also cited manipulating a Rubik's Cube as an example of a skill learned through human demonstrations. These activities require precise control of robotic hands.

However, there's an important detail here. These demonstrations currently use a test robot rather than Eno itself. "Today, GENE allows robots to tackle a wide variety of tasks including preparing a meal, lab pipetting, wire harnessing, packaging, and more. These tasks are currently being demonstrated in a test robot and will be exported over to Eno very soon," Gervet told us.

That means Genesis still needs to show how well Eno performs these skills during extended operation in actual workplaces. One investor says the technology has already shown encouraging progress. "What stood out to us was watching Genesis robots complete long, multi-step tasks on their own at the same speed a person would, with smooth and natural movement," said Vedant Agrawal, partner at Premji Invest.
When will Eno robots start working alongside people?

Genesis began proof-of-concept projects and customer pilots in 2026. Now, the company is preparing to bring what it learned into its next phase of commercial deployment. "We started proof of concepts and pilots with customers in 2026 and received valuable insight by working with the customers. Now we are taking these lessons learnt and heading to customer sites in 2027," Gervet told us. The first deployments will focus on manufacturing facilities, logistics operations and laboratories. Genesis has also announced a strategic partnership with LG CNS, LG's consulting and AI transformation business.

The companies plan to evaluate Genesis robots for manufacturing and logistics work at LG operations in the United States. Their partnership could eventually expand to additional industrial customers. Gervet confirmed the relationship and said, "We will share more on our work with them in the coming months." After industrial deployments, Genesis plans to expand into hospitality and healthcare. Home robots and outdoor applications are further down its development roadmap. However, the company has not announced a firm timeline for bringing Eno into people's homes.
Could workers be training their robotic replacements?

As Genesis works toward robots that can handle entire workflows independently, there's an important question about the employees helping train them. Could those same robots eventually take over some of their jobs? We asked Genesis how employees participate in its training program and who owns the data collected through the electronic gloves and cameras. The company says participation is voluntary and that people involved specifically agree to the work. "All employees who participate in data collection have chosen to opt in and have agreed and consented," Genesis told CyberGuy.

The company added that participants understand how the information is collected and that Genesis does not capture personally identifying information. It also says people receive clear information before providing consent. As for ownership, Genesis was direct: "We own the training data that we capture with our gloves and cameras."

That answers an important question about the program. However, the larger issue remains how this technology could eventually affect employment. Workers may voluntarily help train robots today, but those same machines could eventually perform some of their responsibilities without constant human supervision.
What challenges could slow down Genesis AI robots?

Teaching a robot to perform an impressive task under controlled conditions is one thing. Making that same robot work reliably every day inside a busy workplace is another. Industrial environments change constantly. Equipment moves, objects may end up in unexpected locations and people work nearby.

For general-purpose robots to become practical, they need to respond safely when something goes wrong. Genesis believes developing its hardware and AI together will help address those challenges. The company also controls its training systems and simulation technology, allowing engineers to improve different components together. But the biggest unanswered questions involve long-term performance.

Genesis has not provided detailed commercial pricing or independently verified reliability results for Eno across extended customer deployments. Gervet acknowledged the challenge when discussing the future of robotics. "The challenge is making sure these robots can operate reliably and safely in the real world, not just perform impressive demonstrations in controlled environments." Those are exactly the questions businesses will need answered before trusting robots with more responsibility.
What this means to you

You probably won't see an Eno robot rolling into your workplace tomorrow. However, this technology offers an early look at how physical jobs could change over the next several years. If you work in manufacturing or a laboratory, robots like Eno could eventually handle tasks that require constant repetition. That could reduce physically demanding work while changing the skills employers expect from their teams.

For employees, the bigger question is how companies will introduce these machines. Will robots work alongside existing teams, or will businesses eventually use them to reduce staffing? Genesis sees opportunities to make workplaces more productive, but the long-term impact on jobs remains uncertain.

For people outside those industries, the longer-term possibilities include robots that help with household chores or assist in healthcare settings. Those applications remain further away and will require additional safety testing.
HYUNDAI TO SEND 25,000 ATLAS ROBOTS TO THE US
Genesis AI plans to deploy its Eno robots at customer sites in 2027, beginning with manufacturing facilities, logistics operations and laboratories. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Kurt's key takeaways

There's something fascinating about the idea of teaching robots to do our jobs simply by putting on a pair of electronic gloves. But I can't help wondering what happens when those robots become capable of performing the same work without us. That's a conversation I think we need to start having now, before this technology becomes commonplace. The $500 million investment shows how much confidence major tech investors have in Genesis AI. The company has ambitious plans to bring Eno into workplaces, and we're getting closer to seeing how robots like these could change the way businesses operate. Genesis says people participating in its training program voluntarily opt in, which is important. But I think there's still a bigger conversation to have about what happens after these robots learn the job. If companies eventually use them to take over certain responsibilities, employees deserve to understand how that could affect their future.
Would you be comfortable wearing special gloves that teach a robot how to do your job if that same robot could eventually replace you? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan customer data leaked
summary: JPMorgan Chase says hackers accessed marketing data at third-party vendors as an extortion group leaks records tied to Visa and Mastercard customers.
story: Morgan Wright, former State Department antiterror advisor, joins the broadcast to analyze a massive cybersecurity breach affecting Chase, Visa and Mastercard. Wright explains how customer data was exposed in the leak and outlines critical safety measures individuals must take to protect their financial information amid a period of unprecedented global technology turmoil.

You trust your bank to protect your money. But how much do you know about the outside companies that also handle your personal information? That's a question worth asking after a ransomware group leaked customer data linked to Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase.

On Nov. 19, 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported that hackers had leaked information allegedly linked to thousands of customers of the three financial companies. The reported exposure involved third-party service providers that work with the financial companies. Now, customers are left wondering what information hackers obtained and whether they need to take action.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO?
JPMorgan Chase says hackers may have accessed customer names and email addresses held by outside vendors, but its banking services remain operational. (Photo by ANGELA WEISS/AFP via Getty Images)
What happened in the Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan data leak?

A cyber extortion group known as n0n claimed to have stolen information associated with the three financial companies. According to Reuters, the group posted claims on Nov. 16 about obtaining cardholder engagement records. These allegedly included extensive marketing activity associated with tens of thousands of email addresses. The group also posted claims involving Visa and Mastercard that same day.

The reported cyberattack involved outside service providers that handle information for financial institutions. Some of the records appear connected to customer marketing activities and cardholder benefit programs. However, several important questions remain unanswered. The companies have not publicly identified all the affected vendors, and investigators have yet to establish whether one compromised provider was responsible for all three reported exposures.
What JPMorgan Chase says about the cyberattack

JPMorgan Chase confirmed that third-party service providers were targeted in a cyberattack. In a statement to CyberGuy, a JPMorgan Chase spokesperson said, "Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses."

The bank says its services remain operational. It also plans to contact affected customers where appropriate and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring. Addressing the transaction processing delays that affected multiple banks earlier this week, the spokesperson added, "There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week."

According to Reuters, leaked records appeared to contain more than 16,000 JPMorgan Chase customer email addresses and 124 bank employee email addresses. Some entries also included phone numbers and postal codes. Reuters could not independently verify the authenticity of the records.
Mastercard confirms limited customer information was exposed

Mastercard also acknowledged an incident involving an outside provider. However, the company says the exposed information was limited to email addresses belonging to a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program. In a statement to CyberGuy, Mastercard said the incident involved non-payment information. "There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," Mastercard said.

The company also confirmed that the exposure has been contained. Its teams are working with the affected provider to support cardholders as needed. Mastercard has not publicly identified the benefit program involved or disclosed an exact number of affected customers. The company also has not indicated that payment-card numbers were exposed.
What Visa says about the reported customer data leak

Visa has responded to CyberGuy about the reported cybersecurity incident involving a third-party service provider in the Asia-Pacific region. The company says its own systems and payment information were unaffected.

In a statement, the company said, "Visa is aware of these claims. They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific. Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected. This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week."
However, Visa has not identified the service provider or disclosed how many customers may have been affected. The company also has not specified what non-payment information, if any, was exposed.
Could the data leak put your bank account at risk?

So far, the companies' statements point primarily to customer information held by outside service providers. Mastercard says its payment network remains secure, while Visa says payment-card numbers were unaffected. JPMorgan Chase has identified potentially exposed marketing data. There has been no verified indication that customer banking passwords were stolen or that hackers accessed funds through this incident.

However, stolen contact information can still create problems. Criminals may use names or email addresses to make phishing messages appear more convincing. You could receive an email claiming your bank detected suspicious activity related to the recent cyberattack. The message might direct you to a fake website designed to steal your login information. We've covered how convincing these scams can be in our article about fake bank security alerts that trick customers into sharing personal information.
9 WARNING SIGNS OF IDENTITY THEFT YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE

Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase are responding to a reported data leak involving third-party service providers that may have exposed customer contact information. (Photo Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
How to protect yourself after the Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan data leak
You do not need to assume your account has been compromised. However, there are several practical steps I recommend taking to reduce your exposure to follow-up scams.

Be cautious of unexpected emails or text messages claiming your Visa, Mastercard or JPMorgan Chase account needs immediate attention. Scammers may reference a real cyberattack to make their messages more convincing. They could also claim that your card will be suspended unless you verify your information. Don't click links or open attachments in suspicious messages. Instead, open your bank's official app or type its website address directly into your browser. You can also call the number printed on the back of your card. Using strong antivirus software can provide additional protection by helping detect malicious links and downloads before they cause damage. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at CyberGuy.com

A scammer may call pretending to be from your bank's fraud department. The caller might already know your name or email address and claim that a recent breach put your account at risk. The scammer may then ask you to read back a one-time verification code sent to your phone. That code could allow someone to access your account or approve an unauthorized transaction. Never share a verification code with someone who contacts you unexpectedly. Also, never transfer money to another account because a caller claims it will keep your funds safe. Legitimate bank representatives will not ask you to move your money to a supposedly safe account.

Enable transaction notifications through your bank or credit card app. These alerts can help you spot unfamiliar purchases without waiting for your monthly statement. Check your recent activity and report anything suspicious immediately. Even though the companies have not reported a compromise of their payment networks, monitoring your accounts remains a useful security habit.

Make sure your banking and primary email accounts use unique passwords. If you have reused passwords across accounts, replace them with strong alternatives. A password manager can help you generate and store them securely. Turn on multifactor authentication wherever available. If your bank supports passkeys or security keys, consider using them. An authenticator app is generally a stronger option than SMS codes, although it can still be vulnerable to certain phishing attacks. There is currently no verified evidence that passwords were exposed in this incident. These precautions can help protect your accounts against separate attacks. For more details, see our guide to whether bank text codes are enough to protect you.

JPMorgan Chase says it will contact affected customers where appropriate and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring. If you receive a breach notification, confirm that it came from your financial institution before clicking an enrollment link or sharing personal information. Credit monitoring can help you identify suspicious changes to your credit reports. However, it cannot stop someone from sending phishing emails or impersonating your bank. You should also be suspicious of anyone demanding payment to activate complimentary protection offered after a breach.

A credit freeze makes it harder for criminals to open new credit accounts in your name. You can place one for free through Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. You must contact each credit bureau separately. A freeze does not affect your credit score, and you can temporarily lift it when you need to apply for credit. If only your name and email address were exposed, a freeze may not be necessary because of this incident alone. However, it can provide broader protection, especially if a breach involves more sensitive identifiers such as a Social Security number.

An exposed email address becomes more useful to scammers when they can connect it with other personal details found online. Consider removing unnecessary information from public profiles and checking what data broker websites have collected about you. A personal data removal service can also help request the removal of information from participating people-search sites. These services cannot erase information already stolen in a cyberattack. However, reducing the amount of personal information publicly available may make it harder for criminals to build convincing profiles for targeted scams. You should also use your phone's spam filtering features and reputable antivirus software to help block suspicious messages or malicious downloads. If you clicked a suspicious banking link or shared personal information, take action quickly. What you do next depends on what happened.

Change your password. If you entered it on a suspicious website, update it immediately through your bank's official app or website. Change it anywhere else you've used the same password.Contact your bank. Shared a verification code with someone? Call your bank's fraud department right away and explain what happened.Protect your payment information. If you shared card details or spotted an unfamiliar transaction, ask your bank whether your card should be locked or replaced.Scan your device. Downloaded a suspicious file? Stop opening it and run a security scan using strong antivirus software.Report suspicious texts. Use your phone's spam reporting feature or forward the message to 7726 (SPAM).
Change your password. If you entered it on a suspicious website, update it immediately through your bank's official app or website. Change it anywhere else you've used the same password.
Contact your bank. Shared a verification code with someone? Call your bank's fraud department right away and explain what happened.
Protect your payment information. If you shared card details or spotted an unfamiliar transaction, ask your bank whether your card should be locked or replaced.
Scan your device. Downloaded a suspicious file? Stop opening it and run a security scan using strong antivirus software.
Report suspicious texts. Use your phone's spam reporting feature or forward the message to 7726 (SPAM).
You can also report suspected fraud through ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

A cyber extortion group says it stole customer information linked to Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase, raising concerns about phishing scams and data security. (Photo Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

I've always believed that protecting your financial information requires knowing who has access to it. This latest incident shows how complicated that has become. You can do everything right with your bank account, yet an outside company handling your personal information could still experience a cyberattack. Most of us have little say in which vendors our financial institutions use, and we rarely know how much information those companies collect. I appreciate that Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase provided statements about the incident. It's reassuring that payment services remain operational, but I'd like to see more transparency about the outside providers involved and exactly what customer information they were holding. Until we have those answers, I would pay close attention to unexpected messages claiming to be from a financial institution. If someone contacts you about a problem with your account, verify it yourself before taking action.

If your bank shares your personal information with outside companies, shouldn't you have a right to know exactly who has it? And would a data leak like this make you reconsider which financial institutions you trust? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Uber Parking could save you from circling the block
summary: Uber Parking launches in 15 U.S. cities after the SpotHero deal, offering upfront prices, Uber One credits, and a future role for robotaxis in garages.
story: Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi discusses the company's push to transform transportation, highlighting autonomous ride-sharing, air taxis and robotic food delivery on ‘Special Report.’

You finally make it downtown for dinner, but now comes the real challenge. Finding somewhere to park. You circle the block once, then again. Before you know it, you're late and getting frustrated. Sound familiar? Well, Uber thinks it has a solution. The company just launched Uber Parking, a new feature that lets you reserve a parking spot directly through the Uber app before you even leave home. Yes, the same company that built its business around getting you into someone else's car now wants to help when you drive your own. And there's another interesting twist. Uber has plans for those parking garages that involve robotaxis.

UBER LETS PARENTS WATCH TEEN RIDES LIVE
Uber's new parking feature lets drivers search for available spaces, compare prices and reserve parking directly through the app. (Uber)
Uber Parking lets you reserve a spot before you drive

On Nov. 9, Uber announced the launch of Uber Parking, bringing parking reservations directly into its app. The feature follows Uber's acquisition of SpotHero, a popular parking reservation service. Through that deal, Uber gained access to a network of more than 13,000 parking garages, lots and valet locations across more than 400 cities in the United States and Canada.

So, instead of driving around looking for parking, you can search for an available spot near your destination. You can also see the price upfront, making it easier to decide whether driving makes financial sense. For someone heading into the city for dinner or trying to get to an important appointment, that could save some aggravation. And if you've ever paid a small fortune to park somewhere, you'll probably appreciate being able to compare prices before arriving.
How to book parking using the Uber app
Uber has made the process pretty simple. You can book parking using the same app you already use to request a ride.
Here's how it works:

Enter your vehicle's make and model along with its license plate number.
Confirm your reservation and pay using an available payment method in your Uber Wallet.

Once you've booked, your digital parking pass appears inside the Uber app. Depending on the location, you'll either scan a QR code or enter through a system that recognizes your license plate. Uber also says you can extend reservations through the app if you need more time. Cancellation policies vary by parking facility. Some reservations qualify for a full refund if canceled before the scheduled start time. Always check the booking terms before paying.
One thing worth mentioning: Uber generally won't physically park your car for you. Unless you choose a valet location, you'll still be the one behind the wheel.

So, even if you're in one of the launch cities, you may not see the Parking icon immediately. First, make sure you're using the latest version of the Uber app. You can also visit SpotHero's website to search for parking in areas where the Uber feature is unavailable.
Uber One members can earn 10% back on parking

Here's a little bonus if you already pay for Uber One. Uber says eligible members can earn 10% back in Uber One credits on qualifying parking reservations once their parking session is complete. You can use those credits toward future eligible Uber rides or Uber Eats orders. For example, if you spend $30 on a qualifying parking reservation, you could earn $3 in Uber One credits.

That may not sound like a fortune. However, if you're regularly parking downtown, those credits could add up. Just keep in mind that the 10% reward only applies to eligible reservations. You also need an active Uber One membership to qualify and redeem the credits. And remember, these are Uber credits rather than cash back to your bank account. Before booking, compare the total parking price with other nearby options. A cheaper garage could still save you more money than the rewards you'd earn.
Why Uber wants parking garages for robotaxis

Uber also sees parking garages as part of its future robotaxi business. Think about it. When a driverless taxi drops someone off, what happens next? If another passenger needs a ride nearby, that's easy enough. But what happens when nobody needs the car? Does it keep driving around until another request comes in? That could mean more empty vehicles on already crowded streets. Uber is reportedly exploring ways to use parking facilities as waiting areas for autonomous vehicles. Instead of driving around without passengers, robotaxis could pull into nearby garages and wait for their next assignment.

Then, when someone requests a ride, the vehicle could head out to pick them up. Uber believes that approach could reduce unnecessary driving and help lower operating costs. There's another potential benefit. Keeping autonomous vehicles in nearby facilities could make it easier to have them ready when demand increases. However, this remains a developing plan. Uber has not announced that every SpotHero garage will accommodate robotaxis, and the company has not provided a timeline for a broad rollout of these facilities. For now, the immediate focus remains helping people find parking for their own cars.
Uber wants to be part of your trip even when you drive

There's something else worth paying attention to here. For years, Uber built its business around giving people an alternative to driving. Now, the company wants you opening its app even when you plan to take your own car. Let's say you're going downtown for dinner. You could check the price of an Uber ride. Then, you could compare that with the cost of driving and parking.

If driving looks cheaper, you can reserve a space through Uber. If taking a ride makes more sense, you can book that instead. Either way, Uber stays part of your plans. And as autonomous vehicles become more common, the company could eventually use that same parking network to support its robotaxi partners. It's an interesting strategy, especially as Uber looks for more ways to keep people using its app.
Uber Parking could help drivers spend less time circling busy streets by allowing them to reserve a garage space in advance. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What this means to you

The biggest benefit is pretty straightforward. You may be able to reserve parking before leaving home and spend less time driving around looking for an available spot. That could be especially useful when you're heading somewhere unfamiliar or trying to make a flight. However, there are a few things I'd recommend checking before you book.
Don't assume Uber offers the lowest rate. Check the final price against other parking options before paying. Also, make sure your reservation covers the time you'll actually need.

Some parking garages have height limits. If you drive a larger SUV or truck, check those restrictions before booking. Also, confirm the exact entrance address, which may differ from the garage's street address.

Some parking reservations can be canceled for free before they begin, but the rules vary by location. Review the specific garage's cancellation terms before booking. Once your reservation starts, Uber says it can no longer be canceled or refunded.

Some garages use QR codes for entry. That's convenient, but criminals have also placed fake QR codes on parking meters to trick drivers into visiting fraudulent payment websites. Use the parking pass provided directly through your Uber app rather than scanning an unfamiliar sticker. We've previously reported on how criminals use fake parking QR codes to steal money.

Even with a reservation, finding your car afterward can still be a headache. Fortunately, Google Maps and Apple Maps have tools that can help you remember where you parked. Our guide to finding your parked car with Maps explains how to set them up.
Kurt's key takeaways

I think Uber is onto something here. Who hasn't wasted time driving around looking for parking, especially when you're already running late? Being able to reserve a spot before leaving home sounds pretty convenient. Of course, I'd want to make sure I'm getting a good price. But what really caught my attention is Uber's plan to use parking garages for robotaxis. Having driverless cars park between rides makes sense, especially if it means fewer empty vehicles clogging up our streets. Still, I wonder what happens when those garages start filling up with robotaxis. Will there be enough room for the rest of us? That's something I'll be watching as this technology takes off.

Would you trust Uber to handle your parking reservations, or do you worry that parking garages could eventually become crowded with robotaxis, leaving fewer spaces for the rest of us? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Hackers use Microsoft Outlook security flaw to steal your login data
summary: Microsoft Outlook flaw CVE-2026-124194 lets a malicious .msg file expose NTLMv2 authentication data, and Microsoft confirms hackers already exploited it.
story: Cybersecurity researchers warn a fake Microsoft update site uses a look-alike URL and a familiar download button to deliver data-stealing malware. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

You probably know better than to enter your password on a suspicious website. But what if hackers could steal information tied to your Windows login without ever asking for your password? That's the concern behind a Microsoft Outlook security flaw that hackers are already exploiting. Attackers can trick someone into opening a malicious Outlook file that quietly exposes Windows authentication information. That information could help a criminal impersonate you and potentially gain access to systems you use.

Microsoft released a fix on Nov. 10. However, the company confirms hackers were exploiting the vulnerability before the update became available. If you use Outlook for work, this is one security update you should check right away.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE AI EVENT INVITES TARGET MICROSOFT AND GOOGLE LOGINS
Microsoft Outlook users could unknowingly expose Windows authentication information by opening a malicious message file, potentially allowing hackers to impersonate them. (Microsoft)
How hackers exploit the Microsoft Outlook security flaw

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-124194, involves how Outlook handles specially crafted message files. An attacker can create a malicious Outlook message file, such as one using the .msg format. The hacker then needs to convince someone to open that file in an affected version of Outlook. Once opened, the malicious file can cause Outlook to connect to a server controlled by the attacker. That connection happens without the usual warning about accessing external content. During the connection, Windows can reveal NTLMv2 authentication information. This data helps Windows verify your identity when connecting to certain network services.

The information differs from your actual password. However, hackers may be able to use it in a follow-up attack to impersonate you. For someone using Outlook at work, that could potentially expose company resources their account can access. The outcome depends on the network's security protections and whether the attacker can successfully misuse the authentication information. Here's what makes this especially concerning. The attack doesn't require you to type your password into a fake login page. Opening the malicious file can be enough if your computer can connect to the attacker's network location. Microsoft says simply viewing the message through Outlook's Preview Pane does not trigger this particular vulnerability. Someone must open the malicious file for the attack to work.
Microsoft confirms hackers are already exploiting the flaw

Microsoft included the Outlook fix in its November Patch Tuesday security updates. The company's core release addressed 1,093 vulnerabilities, including 63 rated critical. Interestingly, Microsoft classified this particular Outlook vulnerability as moderate, giving it a CVSS severity score of 6.5 out of 10. However, that rating tells only part of the story. Microsoft confirms attackers have already exploited the flaw. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) also added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Nov. 10. In other words, hackers are already taking advantage of this security weakness. Microsoft has not publicly identified who carried out the attacks or disclosed how many people were affected. The company also hasn't provided detailed information about the incidents. With hackers already exploiting the flaw, it's important to install the security update as soon as possible.
FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN
Microsoft released a security fix for the Outlook vulnerability, which users can install by selecting Update Now under Office's Update Options menu. (Microsoft)
Who is affected by the Outlook security vulnerability?
According to Microsoft's security advisory, the affected products include:

Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise: Affected versions of Outlook included with enterprise subscriptions.Microsoft Office LTSC 2021: Affected installations of Microsoft's long-term servicing edition.Microsoft Office LTSC 2024: Affected installations of the newer long-term servicing edition.
Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise: Affected versions of Outlook included with enterprise subscriptions.
Microsoft Office LTSC 2021: Affected installations of Microsoft's long-term servicing edition.
Microsoft Office LTSC 2024: Affected installations of the newer long-term servicing edition.

The vulnerability concerns affected desktop Office installations on Windows computers. Microsoft's advisory does not list Outlook.com in a web browser or the Outlook mobile apps as affected products. If your employer manages your Microsoft 365 software, your IT department may handle these updates. However, it's worth confirming that the security fix has been installed. For people who manage their own computers, here's how to check.
How to protect yourself from the Outlook security flaw
The most important thing you can do is update Microsoft Office. However, a few additional precautions can help reduce your exposure to suspicious files and account attacks.
Microsoft has released security updates addressing the vulnerability. You can manually check for updates in supported Windows versions of Office.

Open Microsoft Word or another installed Office application and create or open a document.Click File and select Account. In classic Outlook, the option may appear as Office Account.Under Product Information, select Update Options.Click Update Now and allow Microsoft to check for available updates.If prompted, save your work and allow Office to close any open applications, so the updates can finish installing.Wait for the "You're up to date!" or "Updates were installed" confirmation.
Open Microsoft Word or another installed Office application and create or open a document.
Click File and select Account. In classic Outlook, the option may appear as Office Account.
Under Product Information, select Update Options.
Click Update Now and allow Microsoft to check for available updates.
If prompted, save your work and allow Office to close any open applications, so the updates can finish installing.
Wait for the "You're up to date!" or "Updates were installed" confirmation.

If you don't see Update Now, you may need to select Enable Updates first. If the entire Update Options menu is missing, your employer may manage updates centrally. Contact your IT department rather than assuming the software has already been patched. You can also review Microsoft's official Office update instructions.
After installing the update, you can check which version of Office is running on your computer.

Open Microsoft Word or another installed Office application.Click File and select Account.Look under Product Information for the version and build information.Select About Word if you need to see the complete build number.
Open Microsoft Word or another installed Office application.
Click File and select Account.
Look under Product Information for the version and build information.
Select About Word if you need to see the complete build number.
For affected volume-licensed installations, Microsoft's November 10 security release includes these updated builds:
Office LTSC 2021: Build 14334.21048Office LTSC 2024: Build 17932.21140
Office LTSC 2021: Build 14334.21048
Office LTSC 2024: Build 17932.21140

These build numbers apply to the specified LTSC editions. They shouldn't be used to check other Office versions. If you're using Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, the correct build depends on your organization's update channel. You can check Microsoft's Office security release notes or contact your IT department to confirm the fix.
Although this vulnerability requires an Office fix, keeping Windows updated remains important.
On Windows 11:
Open Settings.Click Windows Update.Select Check for updates.Install available security updates.Restart your computer if prompted.
Open Settings.
Click Windows Update.
Select Check for updates.
Install available security updates.
Restart your computer if prompted.
Next, check whether Windows can receive updates for other Microsoft products.
From Windows Update, click Advanced options.Find Receive updates for other Microsoft products.Turn the setting On if available.
From Windows Update, click Advanced options.
Find Receive updates for other Microsoft products.
Turn the setting On if available.

This can help Windows deliver updates for supported Microsoft products. However, some Office installations receive updates through separate services or employer-managed systems. Remember that checking Windows Update alone may not confirm you've installed the specific Outlook fix. Check Office separately. It's also smart to back up important files before installing major operating system updates.
Outlook's built-in Report Phishing feature lets users flag suspicious emails without opening potentially dangerous attachments. (Microsoft)

A message file from an unfamiliar sender deserves extra caution, especially if you weren't expecting it. Watch for attachments ending in .msg, a common file format for saved Outlook messages. The format itself is legitimate. However, attackers can abuse it to deliver this exploit. If an email claims you need to open an attached message to review an invoice or urgent workplace request, verify it through another trusted channel. Even attachments appearing to come from coworkers deserve a second look when the request seems unusual.
If something looks suspicious, avoid opening the attachment. Instead, report the message using Outlook's built-in reporting tools when available.
In supported versions of Outlook:

Select the suspicious email in your inbox without opening its attachment.Look for Report or Report phishing in the toolbar.Choose Report phishing if that option appears.Follow the prompts to submit the report.
Select the suspicious email in your inbox without opening its attachment.
Look for Report or Report phishing in the toolbar.
Choose Report phishing if that option appears.
Follow the prompts to submit the report.

The exact menu location depends on your Outlook version and your employer's settings. If you're using a work account and don't see a reporting option, contact your IT department. Avoid forwarding the suspicious attachment to other coworkers.

Strong antivirus software can help identify suspicious attachments and malicious activity before they cause further damage. Look for protection that includes real-time scanning and behavior-based detection. These features may help catch threats that traditional virus signatures miss. However, antivirus software cannot replace Microsoft's security patch. Installing the Outlook update remains essential for closing this particular vulnerability. Multifactor authentication (MFA) adds another layer of account protection by requiring additional verification when you sign in. Enable it on your Microsoft account and other important services whenever available. Keep in mind that MFA may not stop attacks involving stolen Windows authentication information. That's another reason updating Outlook takes priority.
Know what to do if you opened a suspicious file
If you recently opened an unexpected Outlook message attachment, don't assume everything is fine because nothing unusual appeared on your screen. Here's what to do next.

Close the suspicious file: Stop interacting with the attachment. Don't reopen it or forward it to anyone else.Notify your IT department if it's a work computer: Report what happened right away. Your security team can investigate suspicious authentication activity and determine whether additional action is needed.Update Microsoft Office: Install the latest security updates to protect against further attempts to exploit the Outlook vulnerability.Run a security scan: Use your antivirus software to check for other suspicious activity or malware. Keep in mind that a clean scan cannot rule out stolen authentication information.Check your account activity: Review your Microsoft account for unfamiliar sign-ins or unexpected security changes. However, normal sign-in activity doesn't guarantee your authentication information wasn't exposed.Secure your personal accounts: If you suspect unauthorized access, change your password using a trusted device. Make sure multifactor authentication is enabled wherever available.
Close the suspicious file: Stop interacting with the attachment. Don't reopen it or forward it to anyone else.

Notify your IT department if it's a work computer: Report what happened right away. Your security team can investigate suspicious authentication activity and determine whether additional action is needed.
Update Microsoft Office: Install the latest security updates to protect against further attempts to exploit the Outlook vulnerability.
Run a security scan: Use your antivirus software to check for other suspicious activity or malware. Keep in mind that a clean scan cannot rule out stolen authentication information.

Check your account activity: Review your Microsoft account for unfamiliar sign-ins or unexpected security changes. However, normal sign-in activity doesn't guarantee your authentication information wasn't exposed.
Secure your personal accounts: If you suspect unauthorized access, change your password using a trusted device. Make sure multifactor authentication is enabled wherever available.

One important reminder: Changing your password alone may not address every potential exposure from this vulnerability. If you opened the attachment on a work computer, let your IT team determine whether additional security measures are necessary.
Why Microsoft's latest security update deserves attention

Microsoft's November security release covers far more than Outlook. It also fixes weaknesses that could allow attackers to gain additional privileges or remotely execute malicious code. For those of you using a Windows PC every day, the sheer number of vulnerabilities may sound overwhelming. However, not every flaw carries the same immediate risk. In this case, the Outlook weakness deserves your attention because Microsoft has confirmed active exploitation.

The larger concern is how easily a malicious file can take advantage of trusted software. Outlook is part of everyday communication for countless businesses, and opening saved email messages may seem harmless. This vulnerability shows why keeping Office updated deserves the same attention as updating Windows.
Kurt's key takeaways

What concerns me about this Outlook flaw is how little someone has to do to put their information at risk. You could receive what looks like a routine work attachment, open it and unknowingly expose information that helps a hacker impersonate you. There's no obvious warning telling you something went wrong. And by the time you realize it, the damage may already be done. I also find it troubling that Microsoft rated this vulnerability moderate even though attackers were already exploiting it. Most people aren't going to spend their day reviewing security ratings, and they shouldn't have to. They need software that protects them and updates that are easy to install. My advice is simple. If you use Outlook on a Windows computer, check for Office updates today. Don't assume your computer has already taken care of it.

Should Microsoft be doing more to prevent a single malicious Outlook file from exposing your login information, or do you think keeping your software updated is enough protection? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Former Secret Service investigator sounds alarm over AI scams as Americans grow increasingly anxious
summary: Former Secret Service cyberfraud investigator Jason Brown warns AI voice cloning scams could trick families into losing thousands of dollars this holiday season.
story: Jason Brown, a former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator, warns that AI-powered voice cloning and impersonation scams are making it increasingly difficult for Americans to distinguish real communications from fake ones.

A former Secret Service cyberfraud investigator warned that Americans are increasingly on edge following a wave of major technology disruptions, while artificial intelligence is making scams targeting families and consumers more sophisticated.

Jason Brown, a former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator and iCounter's director of customer advisory and counter fraud lead, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that Americans have reason to be increasingly cautious about technology.
"Everybody's on edge," Brown said.

"There's been a lot of stuff that has happened in the past week in particular that people are concerned about," he continued, citing recent technology outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and several financial institutions.
TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS
The more details a scam includes, the more likely it is built from your publicly available data. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Brown acknowledged that some incidents involved infrastructure problems while others remained under investigation.

With the holiday season approaching, Brown warned that AI has made it easier for criminals to create convincing fraudulent messages, eliminating many of the warning signs consumers previously relied on.
"AI has just made the criminal a lot more efficient and a little bit more effective," Brown said.

Spelling mistakes, poor grammar and awkward phrasing — once common indicators of fraudulent messages — are becoming less reliable as criminals use AI to generate more convincing communications, he explained.
AI VOICE SCAM TRAPS MOM IN 5-HOUR KIDNAPPING NIGHTMARE

Former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator Jason Brown warned that artificial intelligence is making scams more sophisticated and increasingly difficult for Americans to recognize. (Fox News Digital)
AI also allows criminals to impersonate familiar voices, potentially tricking victims into believing they are speaking with a family member in distress.
Brown described a scenario in which a scammer uses a short voice recording to impersonate someone's relative and demand thousands of dollars in gift cards.
"AI just makes them a lot more efficient and a lot less prone to errors," he said, warning that Americans must become more skeptical of suspicious messages.
"Unfortunately, we're at a point where everybody needs to have that level of distrust," he said.
As holiday shopping ramps up, Brown said scammers are likely to impersonate major delivery companies, including UPS, FedEx and the U.S. Postal Service.
FAKE E-ZPASS EMAIL THREATENS $100 FINE OVER UNPAID TOLL

Scammers may impersonate major delivery companies during the holiday shopping season, sending fraudulent messages claiming packages cannot be delivered without additional payment. (Ute Grabowsky/Photothek via Getty Images)
He warned that fraudulent messages may claim packages cannot be delivered until additional postage is paid, with scammers demanding payment through cryptocurrency or gift cards.
"If it comes from crypto, especially if it comes from gift cards, that's a red flag for sure," Brown said.

Beyond the emotional toll, Brown warned that increasingly sophisticated scams can result in significant financial losses. He cited FBI reporting that he said identified more than 22,000 AI-related fraud cases in 2025, with losses exceeding $890 million.
Brown noted that businesses are also vulnerable to schemes in which criminals impersonate trusted vendors and redirect legitimate payments into fraudulent accounts.
AGING MEANS LEARNING HOW TO PREVENT COSTLY SCAMS TARGETING OLDER AMERICANS

Former Secret Service investigator Jason Brown warned holiday shoppers to be cautious of suspicious delivery notifications appearing to come from UPS, FedEx or the U.S. Postal Service. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
The holiday season can create additional vulnerabilities as executives travel, employees take time off and temporary workers join company operations, he said.

Brown urged Americans to independently verify suspicious messages and take additional precautions when communicating with family members, including establishing a "safe word" to help confirm someone's identity during an unexpected call.

"Another thing that we always talk about with family members, set up a safe word ahead of time. Have that conversation now," he said, adding that even if a caller provides the correct word, people should still end the call and contact the person independently using a trusted number.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The biggest safety valve for anybody in a scam when it comes over the internet via your cell phone, over the computer is stop, think and then independently verify," he added.
