title: Fake AI event invites target Microsoft and Google logins
summary: Fake OpenAI event pages promise free ChatGPT Pro subscriptions, then trick employees into handing over Microsoft and Google account credentials.
story: Google General Counsel Halimah Delaine Prado joins 'Fox & Friends' to detail how Google is fighting AI-powered phishing scams.

An invitation to an exclusive OpenAI event lands in your inbox. It promises a look at the latest AI tools and even offers three months of ChatGPT Pro for free. All you have to do is register using your work account. Sounds like a pretty good deal, right? Well, before you click that registration button, there's something you should know. Cybercriminals are using fake AI event invitations to trick employees into giving them access to their Microsoft and Google accounts. And some of these attacks can get past the extra security checks many of us rely on.

According to a new report from Push Security, attackers have created convincing event registration pages impersonating OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic. Push Security says it detected and blocked visits to the malicious event registration pages on its customers' browsers in late October 2026. The concerning part is how easily an invitation that appears legitimate can lead to someone handing over access to their work account. Here's what researchers discovered and how to protect yourself.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN

Cybercriminals are impersonating OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic with fake AI event invitations designed to steal employees’ Microsoft and Google login credentials. (Tristan Spinski for The Washington Post via Getty Images)
Fake AI event invites promise free access to premium tools

The attackers are taking advantage of the growing interest in artificial intelligence. After all, plenty of employees want to learn how AI can make their jobs easier. A free premium subscription could be enough to get someone's attention. The phishing pages discovered by Push Security promote events that appear to come from recognizable technology companies. One fake OpenAI event advertised a November 4 livestream called "ChatGPT for Social & Digital Marketing Teams." The registration page promised three months of ChatGPT Pro to participants. Another page promoted an invitation-only SpaceX briefing scheduled for November 12. Visitors could supposedly choose between three months of Grok Heavy or a "SpaceX share."

Researchers also identified a phishing page impersonating an Anthropic event at AWS re 2026. That page was no longer active when they investigated it. These pages impersonated legitimate technology companies, and the advertised rewards were part of the phishing scheme. Push Security did not suggest that OpenAI, SpaceX or Anthropic operated these fraudulent events. And here's where things get especially concerning. The fake websites tell visitors they must sign in using their corporate Microsoft or Google accounts to complete registration and claim the promised rewards. That request opens the door to the phishing attack.
How fake AI event invitations trick employees

The criminals have put considerable effort into making these invitations appear credible. Rather than sending people directly to an obvious phishing website, they use familiar online services to help disguise where the links lead. Push Security found that the campaign routed visitors through shortened links associated with Google and Zapier. Earlier related attacks also used legitimate Zoom event pages and GoTo Webinar's email infrastructure. As a result, someone checking an invitation might see a familiar service before reaching the malicious registration page. Researchers have not confirmed the initial delivery method for every invitation in the newer campaign.

Once someone reaches the suspicious site, another familiar feature appears. A Cloudflare security challenge asks visitors to confirm they are human. You have probably encountered similar checks while shopping or visiting legitimate websites. However, criminals can use them too. In this campaign, the challenge also made it harder for automated security scanners to examine the malicious pages. After completing the check, visitors arrive at what looks like a professional event registration website. They're presented with two familiar buttons: "Continue with Microsoft" and "Continue with Google." Depending on which button someone selects, the attackers launch a different method designed to capture access to that account.
How hackers target Microsoft accounts without a password

This is where the attack gets clever. If someone selects "Continue with Microsoft," the phishing website connects to a service called Kali365. It's a phishing-as-a-service platform that criminals can use to carry out account attacks. Kali365 generates a Microsoft device authentication code. The fake registration page then instructs the visitor to copy that code and enter it on Microsoft's legitimate sign-in website.

Now, here's why that can fool someone. Microsoft's device authentication process is real. You may have used something similar when connecting a streaming device to an account. However, the attacker started this authentication request. When the victim enters the supplied code and approves the sign-in, Microsoft can issue authentication tokens to the attacker's session.

Those tokens may provide access to Microsoft 365 resources without the attacker needing the account password. And the attack may continue from there. Push Security found that the campaign redirects Microsoft users to another phishing service called VoidProxy after the device code step. That second stage attempts to capture their password and authenticated session cookie. A successful compromise could expose company email or documents stored in Microsoft 365. Other connected workplace applications may also be at risk, depending on the permissions and access associated with the compromised account.
How the Google phishing attack steals login sessions

The Google option takes another approach. When visitors click "Continue with Google," the phishing page opens a pop-up that appears to contain Google's familiar sign-in screen. However, that login process runs through VoidProxy, which acts as an intermediary between the person signing in and Google's actual authentication service.

As someone enters their credentials, the phishing service can capture the information. It can also intercept certain multifactor authentication responses and steal session cookies. So, what exactly is a session cookie? Think of it as a digital pass that helps a website remember you've already signed in. Once your identity has been verified, that cookie can allow you to continue using your account without entering your password on every page.

If a criminal obtains a usable session cookie, they may be able to reuse that authenticated session and gain access without completing the usual login process again. That's why these attacks are particularly dangerous for people who believe that enabling multifactor authentication automatically protects them from every account takeover attempt. It's important to note that Push Security documented the malicious infrastructure and blocked visits to the phishing pages. Its report did not establish how many accounts, if any, were successfully compromised through this campaign.
HACKERS HIDE DANGEROUS FAKE AI DOWNLOADS BEHIND GOOGLE ADS
A convincing Google sign-in window appears over a fraudulent SpaceX event page, allowing attackers to capture login credentials and authentication sessions. (Push Security)
Why these fake AI event scams are difficult to spot

The attackers are combining two phishing services behind the same registration pages. Kali365 targets Microsoft's device authentication process, while VoidProxy targets authenticated login sessions. Meanwhile, the fake event websites borrow the appearance of familiar brands. The criminals can also change their websites and event themes as older pages get discovered. Researchers also discovered that the fraudulent registration pages could automatically display content in a visitor's language. That allowed the attackers to adapt the same phishing campaign for people in different regions without creating entirely new websites. Push Security identified two phishing kits used to create the fake event pages. The researchers call them ZoomMock and MSDRoot. They found evidence suggesting the same operators were responsible for both kits, although the connection was not conclusively established.

Researchers also found no evidence linking the developers of Kali365 and VoidProxy. Instead, they believe the attackers behind the event campaign are customers of both phishing services. The result is an attack that can appear credible at several points. A shortened link may use a recognized service. A security challenge can look legitimate. Even the Microsoft authentication page can be genuine. For employees who regularly attend virtual meetings or participate in industry webinars, that familiarity could make the scam harder to recognize.

In response to our request for comment, a Microsoft spokesperson said, "We take reports of malicious online activity seriously and continuously work to help protect our customers from evolving threats. Microsoft Defender includes detections to block the threats identified in the report."
We also reached out to Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and SpaceX for comment but did not receive responses before our deadline.
How to protect yourself from fake AI event phishing scams
A few careful habits can significantly reduce your chances of falling for these attacks. Here's how to protect yourself.

If you receive an unexpected invitation from OpenAI, SpaceX or another technology company, take a moment to check whether the event actually exists. Open a new browser tab and visit the organization's official website yourself. Look for the event through its verified channels. If necessary, contact the organizer using information obtained independently of the invitation. Be especially careful when an unfamiliar event requests your corporate account credentials.

An invitation promising premium AI access may sound appealing, especially when the offer appears to come from a respected technology company. However, the promise of something valuable can encourage people to act before checking the details. If registration requires you to sign in with a work account to receive a reward, verify the offer independently before proceeding.

This is one of the most important lessons from the campaign. If a website asks you to copy a device authentication code and enter it on a Microsoft page, consider whether you initiated a legitimate device sign-in. If you were simply registering for a webinar, that unexpected device code request should raise concerns. Even a legitimate Microsoft authentication webpage can become part of a phishing attack when criminals trick you into approving their request. Pay attention to any Microsoft sign-in prompt asking you to approve access. Even if the website address is legitimate, you could be authorizing a session started by a criminal.
THE BEST DEFENSE AGAINST HIGH-TECH AI SCAMS IS LOW-TECH SKEPTICISM, EXPERT WARNS

Hackers are using fraudulent AI event registration pages promising free ChatGPT Pro subscriptions and exclusive access to trick employees into compromising their work accounts. (Felix Zahn/Photothek via Getty Images)

Before entering account credentials, examine the website address and consider how you arrived there. A page displaying familiar branding may still belong to a criminal. Shortened links can also conceal the final destination. Whenever possible, open Microsoft or Google directly through a trusted bookmark or the official website. Remember that a padlock icon and HTTPS connection do not guarantee that a website is trustworthy.

Continue using multifactor authentication, even though some phishing attacks can defeat certain forms of it. For stronger protection, consider phishing-resistant authentication, such as FIDO2 security keys or supported passkeys. These methods can help prevent attackers from stealing credentials through fraudulent login websites. While these methods offer stronger protection against phishing, they cannot guarantee protection if an attacker obtains a valid authenticated session through another method. However, no single security measure stops every possible attack. Organizations should also consider additional controls to protect authenticated sessions and reduce the risk of stolen tokens being reused. Microsoft recommends restricting device code authentication wherever it isn't necessary. IT administrators can apply those restrictions through Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policies after reviewing legitimate business needs.

Strong antivirus software and browser protections can help identify suspicious links and dangerous websites before you interact with them. Look for protection that helps detect phishing pages and malicious downloads. Keep your browser and security tools updated so they can benefit from the latest available protections. However, remember that attackers frequently create new websites to evade detection. Security software can reduce your exposure, but it cannot guarantee that every fraudulent invitation will be blocked. What to do if you already clicked a fake AI event invitation
If you've already clicked on a suspicious event invitation, don't panic. What you do next depends on how far you got in the sign-in process. Here are the steps to take to protect your accounts.

Close the suspicious page. If you clicked the invitation but did not enter account details or approve a sign-in, close the website. Report the invitation through your organization's security reporting process.Contact your IT or security team immediately. If you entered your work credentials or approved a Microsoft device code, let your company's security team know right away.Explain exactly what happened. Tell your security team whether you entered a device code, submitted your password or completed a Google sign-in. These details can help them identify the attack.Secure your accounts. Your IT team may need to reset your password, revoke active sessions and authentication tokens, and investigate suspicious access to connected applications.Don't assume changing your password fixes everything. Attackers may already have a valid authentication token or session cookie. Even after sessions are revoked, some access tokens may remain valid until they expire.

Don't assume changing your password fixes everything. Attackers may already have a valid authentication token or session cookie. Even after sessions are revoked, some access tokens may remain valid until they expire.
The sooner you report suspicious activity, the better the chances of stopping unauthorized access before more damage occurs.
Kurt's key takeaways

Criminals know people are eager to keep up with AI, and they're using that interest to make their scams more convincing. An invitation offering free ChatGPT Pro or access to an exclusive event sounds pretty tempting. Even checking the website address may not be enough to protect you. So before you sign up for that next AI event, take a minute to make sure it's legitimate. title: Swift assurances from officials after wave of nationwide outages raises questions, expert says
summary: SMET CEO Danny Cooper says ruling out a cyberattack too fast risks missing hackers after the JPMorgan Chase, Microsoft outages and air travel ground stop.
story: As federal officials and major institutions called a string of critical infrastructure disruptions isolated technical glitches, a longtime security veteran warns that hasty assurances can mask stealth intrusions, and give adversaries room to linger undetected.

Amid a slew of high-profile disruptions that struck major pillars of American life over the past week, including a nationwide ground stop that halted air travel, banking outages at JPMorgan Chase and other lenders, and a service disruption at Microsoft, officials were quick to reassure the public that nothing nefarious was behind the failures.

During the ground stop, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the homeland and the banking system remained secure, insisting that the disruptions showed no signs of a cyberattack or malicious activity.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton similarly stated that officials saw no evidence of a coordinated or state-sponsored attack, pointing instead to routine patching and system upgrades.
DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE'

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton testified Wednesday to reiterate intelligence shows the recent outages are neither related nor a result of a 'state-sponsored' attack. (Brendan Smialowski / AFP)

"Based on what we know today … these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes," Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday. "They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack."
Major companies, including Microsoft and JPMorgan Chase, also attributed the disruptions to internal technical issues or software bugs rather than malicious intrusions.
US INFRASTRUCTURE CRUMBLES AS ADVERSARIES POWER UP – LEAVING AMERICANS DANGEROUSLY EXPOSED: CYBER EXPERT
To Danny Cooper, CEO of critical infrastructure security firm SMET, the speed with which those assurances were issued poses a problem.
"A blanket statement like 'there's no malicious activity associated with any of the outages' is almost impossible from a probability perspective," Cooper told Fox News Digital.
THE OUTAGES AMERICA HAS SUFFERED WEREN'T AN ATTACK, BUT THE NEXT FAILURE COULD BE
A Chase ATM is pictured outside the bank as technology disruptions impact banking services. (Ava Palschakov for Fox News Digital)

Public anxiety tends to spike around a single question in the aftermath of a major disruption: Was it a coincidence or an attack? Public skepticism is understandable given how many critical systems stumbled within a five-to-six-day window, Cooper said.

"How plausible is it that all these pillars or whatever all suffered major independent technical failures within a five- or six-day window?" Cooper asked. "I think highly improbable. And I understand why the American public is calling this into question and deeply empathize with that. The pattern recognition is there."
DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK

Even when officials point to routine maintenance or aging hardware, Cooper argued that ruling out foul play too quickly skips investigative steps that take time to execute properly, which could potentially undermine efforts to fix vulnerabilities and prevent future incidents.

A person looks at a departures board showing delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on Nov. 13, in New York City. The Federal Aviation Administration had ordered a nationwide ground stop on all departing flights, one of several critical infrastructure that experienced outages or issues last week, raising questions about the cause of the stoppages. (Getty Images)

"If a company or the government is making a statement that is as bold as 'we are certain there is no malicious activity here' without having the time to actually do an appropriate investigation, in the case of this sort of cyber domain, some cyber forensics and a full audit of what transpired, that's not quite how it works," she said.
PERPETUAL PARALYSIS: WHY EVERYTHING IS GRINDING TO A HALT

"On the physical side, being able to fully interrogate what has happened in the environment, who was there, and so on about what is happening in the periphery and what led up to that moment in time, those things take time."
An instant "nothing to see here" message can also deepen public suspicion, Cooper said, particularly when multiple institutions and agencies echo that conclusion before audits can be completed.
JOIN THE CHAT: RECENT TECH OUTAGES LOOM OVER MULLIN TESTIMONY ON WORLDWIDE THREATS
The Democratic National Committee (DNC) also sounded the alarm over conflicting statements coming from the Trump administration.

A general view of Charlotte Douglas International Airport in Charlotte, North Carolina, United States, on November 13, 2026, as passengers face delays and strandings after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop for all flights. (Peter Zay/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"The administration has repeatedly offered conflicting statements about the causes of the outages," DNC Deputy Communications Director Kendall Witmer said in a statement. "Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested that SI – Trump’s preferred name for Artificial Intelligence (AI) – is responsible for the multiple outages that have occurred in recent days, according to a "very smart" tech guy he talked to. Then, yesterday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio contradicted Mullin and would not attribute the outages to AI."
MICROSOFT’S MASSIVE OUTAGE OFFERS A LESSON IN HOW TO BRING THE WORLD BACK ONLINE

Much of the official explanation surrounding the November disruptions centered on software updates and system upgrades. Organizations frequently schedule maintenance and can experience downtime when rolling out changes at scale, especially if teams move too quickly, Cooper noted.
However, those windows are what sophisticated adversaries watch closely, she warned.
"If companies are disproportionately moving to execute these sorts of upgrades en masse, then yes, it's possible that you would have a higher number of downtime or outages," she said.

"But it's also quite possible that, particularly given the sophistication of cyber adversaries, whether it's hackers, whether it's non-state entities, whether it's nation-state entities, it's also possible that they are using those software updates or upgrades or patches and in those moments actually injecting malware and exploits and so on."

Shari Franke, the eldest daughter of disgraced Utah parenting blogger and convicted child abuser Ruby Franke, urged the Utah Board of Pardons and Parole to keep her and former associate Jodi Hildebrandt behind bars ahead of their upcoming parole hearings.

Under Utah law, both face between four and 30 years behind bars, with the state's parole board determining their release.

Ruby Franke and Hildebrandt were charged after police rescued two of Franke's malnourished children from Hildebrandt's home on Aug. 30, 2023. title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Half of California's DAs sue Newsom over death row clemency
summary: Gavin Newsom faces a lawsuit from 29 district attorneys and victims' families who say his mass clemency for 548 death row inmates skipped victim notice.
story: With just 60 days left in his term, Gov. Gavin Newsom's plan to commute every inmate on California's death row is facing a lawsuit from half of the state's current DAs as well as victims' families.

District attorneys in half of California's 58 counties have signed onto a lawsuit alongside victims' families and law enforcement groups against term-limited Gov. Gavin Newsom over his lame-duck move to grant clemency to 548 death row inmates in the Golden State.
Many of the prosecutors had publicly condemned the governor's move shortly after he announced it earlier this month.

"Only this Court can stop the Governor’s disregard of the law — his abuse of power," former Sacramento District Attorney Anne Marie Schubert wrote in the 58-page petition, filed Monday. "His eleventh-hour decision to grant commutation en masse intentionally disregarded the statutorily required notice to the victims of these heinous crimes and the prosecutors who obtained those convictions and penalties, and it even interfered with this Court’s mandatory duty to meaningfully review his decisions."

Schubert, who said she worked through the weekend on the filing, is the president and CEO of the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, which is spearheading the lawsuit on behalf of 29 district attorneys and the families of more than two dozen victims.
MICHAEL RUIZ: CALIFORNIA PROSECUTORS REVOLT AFTER NEWSOM ORDERS STATE'S WORST KILLERS OFF DEATH ROW
Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks on March 26, 2025, in Los Angeles. (Frazer Harrison/WireImage)
The Governor’s assurance that the perpetrators will never be released is obviously cruelly false.

Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter Polly was kidnapped at knifepoint from a slumber party at her mother's house and strangled to death in 1993, is among the petitioners. Polly's killer, Richard Allen Davis, has been on death row since 1996.

Other victims' families include those of slain 8-year-old Gabriel Fernandez, Placer County Sheriff's Detective Mike Davis, Pittsburg Police Officer Larry Lasater, Sacramento Deputy Danny Paul Oliver, and five U.S. Forest Service firefighters killed battling the 40,000-acre Esperanza Fire in 2006 — among others.

Convicted murderer Richard Allen Davis is restrained by his lawyer Barry Collins (L) as he gestures in the courtroom after he was found guilty on all counts in the murder of Polly Klaas, in San Jose, California on June 18, 1996. (REUTERS/John Burgess/Pool)
Read the filing:
MICHAEL RUIZ: DA IDENTIFIES 49 LOCAL KILLERS SLATE FOR NEWSOM"S DEATH ROW CLEMENCY — AND THEIR CRIMES

"Given what so many of these families have been through for so long, the impact in this case is exceptionally severe, as documented in the declarations filed with this petition," Schubert wrote in the filing. "The Governor’s assurance that the perpetrators will never be released is obviously cruelly false."

The move has even caught the attention of the White House, with President Donald Trump, Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel expected to meet with some of the victims' families Monday.

"Governor Newsom is failing these innocent victims and their families by refusing to carry out justice against these heinous murderers," said Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman. "He is playing politics with public safety. President Trump will always stand with innocent victims and will continue to restore law and order and deliver safer communities."

California hasn't carried out an execution in 20 years despite having the largest death row in the country, and Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra is expected to continue the moratorium when he takes office. The death penalty remains on the books as more than a symbolic punishment, however, and condemned inmates are excluded from benefiting from some of the state's criminal justice reforms.
CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM

Thousands of jurors and hundreds of judges set aside their personal views on the merits of the death penalty to render judgments based on the evidence and the law. Governor Newsom decided his personal views should override all those who actually participated in the process, followed and applied the law.
BIDEN CLEMENCY BLITZ LEFT DOJ SCRAMBLING AS MANY COMMUTATIONS BYPASSED NORMAL VETTING, EMAILS SHOW

Newsom has argued that the prisoners in question are not eligible for other reforms that could eventually lead to further sentence reductions or even their release. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit.

But with capital punishment off the table, critics like Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer, who announced his own petition Monday, warn that condemned inmates are incrementally moving closer to further leniency.
Newsom wrote in an open letter to California residents that the state "cannot morally kill" the hundreds of people on its death row.

"I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us," he wrote — later acknowledging that those who would benefit from his move "caused indescribable suffering to victims, their families, communities, and our state as a whole."

The Supreme Court of California is expected to review at least 382 of the inmates convicted of multiple felony offenses before Newsom's clemency would be official. According to Schubert's filing, additional inmates who meet the review criteria may not yet have been identified, arguing that Newsom may have relied on incomplete rap sheets when compiling the list.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Still, some experts say the case faces significant hurdles.

"Newsom has broad authority as governor to commute sentences and issue pardons," said Neama Rahmani, a Los Angeles trial attorney and former federal prosecutor. "It may be controversial, but there is little prosecutors and victims can do to prevent it."

California's victims' rights law, which includes the right for victims and their families to be informed of certain clemency and parole decisions ahead of time, may not apply to the commutations, he said.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
"There was no application here," Rahmani told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB
Schubert appeared to anticipate this line of reasoning in her filing.

"If the statutory sunshine process can be defeated merely by the absence of a formal application, the worst abuses would be unregulated, while inmates following the normal procedures would have their applications regulated," she wrote. "That would be backwards and an absurd result."
GOT A TIP?

Thousands of jurors and hundreds of judges have been involved in the convictions and death sentences of the inmates set to benefit from Newsom's clemency, she wrote. Many of them "set aside their personal views" in the process.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Then-Sacramento district attorney Anne Marie Schubert announces the arrest of accused rapist and killer Joseph James DeAngelo during a news conference on April 25, 2018 in Sacramento, California. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

"Governor Newsom decided his personal views should override all those who actually participated in the process, followed and applied the law," she wrote. "He did none of that, as he freely admits. That alone is an abuse of power that must not stand."
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, which tracks capital punishment across the United States, Newsom had not granted a clemency request to any death row inmate before this month's announcement, despite a longstanding opposition to capital punishment.

In fact, no California governor had commuted a death sentence since Ronald Reagan spared a man with previously undiagnosed brain damage in 1967.

title: Alabama woman pleads guilty after reportedly using smart glasses to target drug trial witnesses
summary: Tierra Shatalia Douglas pleaded guilty to conspiracy to retaliate against a witness after targeting people who testified in a federal drug trial.
story: Woman reportedly used Meta smart glasses, ChatGPT in alleged witness intimidation campaign
An Alabama woman accused of using Meta smart glasses to secretly record witnesses in a federal drug trial has pleaded guilty.

Tierra Shatalia Douglas, 36, on Thursday admitted to conspiracy to retaliate against a witness in the January prosecution of Glennie "Little Man" McGee and his wife, Echandza Maxie, according to local outlet AL.

summary: The USDA's Bigfoot/Sasquatch Records include an official 1982 Forest Service probe into footprints in Washington state's Umatilla National Forest.
story: The U.S. Forest Service released files detailing so-called sightings of Bigfoot dating back to the 1940s.
The Trump administration has slowly released a trove of government documents about one of the biggest and most enduring mysteries in American folklore: Bigfoot.

On Oct. 15, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) released three files from its "Bigfoot/Sasquatch Records," The Washington Post first reported, adding fresh intrigue to the legend of the towering, hair-covered creature said to roam North American forests without ever being captured.

A metal sculpture of Bigfoot welcomes visitors to Happy Camp in the Klamath Forest near Yreka, Calif., Aug. 2, 2022. The folklore of the hairy mythical creature has spawned intrigue for decades. (Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
NASA CHIEF PULLS BACK CURTAIN ON TRUMP UFO FILES AFTER BIZARRE FINDS SURFACE IN BURIED FED RECORDS

The records include an official U.S. Forest Service (USFS) investigation from June 1982 into reported Bigfoot footprints discovered in the Mill Creek Watershed of Washington state's Umatilla National Forest.
Investigators documented track measurements, took color photographs and made plaster casts across several field sites to preserve the unusual physical evidence.
NEW JERSEY COUPLE REPORT SEEING 8-FOOT TALL BIGFOOT STEPPING OUT IN FRONT OF THEIR CAR: 'WE KNOW WHAT WE SAW'

Another file details a reported encounter with the creature in Montana dating back to the 1940s. Separately, USFS staff once hosted a Bigfoot in Your Backyard forum in California's Stanislaus National Forest to discuss local sightings, noting at the time the agency could neither confirm nor deny the creature's existence.

This photo shows what former rodeo rider Roger Patterson said is the American version of the Abominable Snowman. He said pictures of the creature, estimated at 7½ feet tall, were taken northeast of Eureka, Calif. (Getty Images/Bettmann/Contributor)

A six-page document included in last month's release, which was written in 1980, recounts a historical report from Petty Creek, Montana, by Leo Kinney, who described spotting a large set of tracks alongside three hunters in the 1940s.
FOLLOW US ON X

"At this point we held a conference and decided that we were not particularly anxious to catch up to whatever it was, and though we didn't confess it at this time, in later conversations we found out that we all had a very uneasy feeling and could feel chills running up and down our backs," Kinney wrote.
The release also includes details of a 2003 sighting in Sanders County, Montana.
IDAHO DEER HUNTER REPORTS BIGFOOT ENCOUNTER IN REMOTE WOODS AFTER HE 'SMELLS THE SMELL'
In an interview with The Washington Post, Jeremiah Byron of the "Bigfoot Society" questioned the timing of the federal disclosures.
"Why is all this cryptid and Bigfoot-related stuff happening now?" Byron asked. "I’m hoping what this means is that they could be ramping up government entities to start releasing information."
While Bigfoot lore has traditionally centered on the Pacific Northwest, the creature has also surfaced in pop culture, with players reporting sightings in the video game Grand Theft Auto VI.
A metal sculpture of Bigfoot welcomes visitors to the tiny community of Happy Camp in the Klamath Forest.  (Luis Sinco/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
Gamers have shared clips of the cryptid wandering the woods of Leonida, a fictional U.S. state based on Florida, before sprinting away in a panic when spotted, according to GameSpot.

title: Zoo shares autopsy findings following Fiona the hippo’s heartbreaking death
summary: Cincinnati Zoo’s director of animal health, Dr. Mike Wenninger, said a postmortem examination has revealed where the hat was lodged inside Fiona’s digestive tract.
story: Dr. Mike Wenninger, the Cincinnati Zoo’s director of animal health, revealed where the hat was lodged inside Fiona’s digestive tract. (Cincinnati Zoo)
The Cincinnati Zoo on Friday released new autopsy findings after the death of Fiona, the hippo whose battle after swallowing a visitor's hat left people across the nation heartbroken.

A postmortem examination determined that a foreign object, confirmed to be a hat zoo officials said was accidentally thrown into her enclosure, was lodged deep inside the hippo's massive digestive tract, according to the zoo's director of animal health, Dr. Mike Wenninger.
The hat was located halfway through the small intestine, about 25 feet from the beginning of her intestinal tract and 50 feet from where it would have exited her body as waste.
FIONA THE HIPPO HONORED BY US SENATE IN UNANIMOUS RESOLUTION PRAISING CINCINNATI ZOO STAFF
Fiona, a Nile hippopotamus, eats a specialty birthday cake to celebrate turning 3 years old Jan. 23, 2020, in Cincinnati. (AP Photo/John Minchillo)

The findings settle lingering questions about the hat's exact location after care teams spent days trying to locate it using various methods, including ultrasounds and upper and lower gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopies.
Care teams even obtained 9-foot-long endoscopy tools but were still unable to reach her intestines through her mouth.
"The upper GI endoscopy couldn't even reach out of her large sacculated stomach," Wenninger said.
BELOVED HIPPO FIONA DIES AT CINCINNATI ZOO AFTER SWALLOWING VISITOR'S HAT
During Fiona's early weeks as a premature hippo, Cincinnati Zoo staff provided 24/7 critical care to keep her warm and fed until she grew strong enough to thrive. (Cincinnati Zoo)
"Given her anatomy and the attachments from her intestinal tract to body wall, there's no place, no way to get in there with specialized endoscopes," he added.

The hat's location and Fiona's anatomy also made surgical removal impossible, Wenninger said, explaining that even laparoscopic procedures, in which a scope is inserted into the abdomen through a small incision, were not feasible.

"Laparoscopic surgery wasn't possible given the location and a laparotomy, so (an) open incision in a hippo that size with an incision that's that long would have been a death sentence for her," he said.
Zoo officials added that the findings confirm the care team did everything possible, and the complications left no viable options for additional operations.
Born six weeks premature in January 2017, Fiona weighed just 29 pounds, 25 pounds lighter than the lowest recorded birth weight for Nile hippos. (Cincinnati Zoo)
"No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked," Wenninger said.

Following Fiona's death, the facility said the zoo remains open, but the area around the Hippo Cove enclosure will be closed through the weekend to give the animal care team the space it needs during this time.
"Keepers, vets, staff and volunteers are shaken and trying to navigate this loss. She meant a lot to a lot of people," the zoo said in a statement.
FUN FACT: FIONA THE HIPPO BECAME THE SMALLEST NILE HIPPO KNOWN TO SURVIVE
Fiona, a 9-year-old Nile hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo, died Thursday after ingesting a knitted hat that accidentally landed in her habitat. (Cincinnati Zoo)
While most hippos in captivity live up to 50 years, Fiona was just 9 years old when her condition rapidly deteriorated in November.

She first made headlines in 2017 after defying the odds as a premature hippo. She was born six weeks early, weighing just 29 pounds. By comparison, healthy newborn hippos typically weigh between 50 and 120 pounds at birth.

title: Verdict reached in Los Angeles retrial over 2025 Pacific Palisades wildfire that killed 12 people
summary: Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of federal arson in the Pacific Palisades fire that killed 12 and destroyed nearly 7,000 homes after a mistrial.
story: Fox News correspondent Matt Finn reports on the verdict a jury reached Friday in the retrial of a California man facing federal arson charges in the 2025 Palisades wildfires.

A man accused of sparking the deadly 2025 Pacific Palisades wildfire that killed 12 people and destroyed nearly 7,000 homes was found guilty on all counts Friday after a federal retrial in Los Angeles, months after his first trial ended in a mistrial.

Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, a former Uber driver with dual U.S.-French citizenship, had been charged with two federal arson counts — including destruction of property by means of fire — in U.S. District Court.
He was retried on a scaled-down grand jury indictment after his initial three-week trial ended in a hung jury in June.

Ahead of the second trial, federal prosecutors dropped one of the original three charges against Rinderknecht, and modified the two remaining federal arson counts, reducing his maximum possible prison sentence from 45 years to 40 years.
PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY DRIVEN BY 'SOCIETAL REVENGE,' BEHAVIORAL ANALYST TESTIFIES IN COURT
Jonathan Rinderknecht, 29, was charged with igniting the blaze that eventually became the Palisades Fire in Los Angeles. (USAttyEssayli/X)

Following the verdict, a juror in the case — identified only by his first name, Cameron, who served as Juror No. 3 — told reporters that deliberations stretched across roughly two days as the panel systematically reviewed every piece of testimony and video evidence from the first day of court to the last.

"I’ll be honest, I was the person who found him not guilty. Originally, I was the one who stood out on that. So it took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise," he said, noting the initial tally stood at 10 guilty, one not guilty and one undecided.

Cameron said his initial hesitation centered on a "technical review" of the fire investigation and whether investigators properly followed protocol when linking the initial blaze to the later inferno. He said the jury ultimately concluded the defendant's own testimony — placing himself alone on the hill on a clear, calm night while smoking and carrying a lighter — pointed to him starting the first fire, which then smoldered into the Jan. 7 disaster.

"What I will say is that his intent was to start a fire," Cameron said. "What that fire did after his actions, whether he can say or whether no one can say, like who knows? Only he will know and only God himself. And so the result of his fire is what ultimately led to January 7th [2025]."
DEFENSE TEAM TRIES TO TIE NBA CHAMPION CHIS BOSH TO PALISADES ARSONIST CASE, CITING FIREWORK EVIDENCE: REPORT
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said in a statement following the conviction that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured."

"Nearly two years ago, the Palisades Fire devastated our city, taking innocent lives, destroying thousands of homes, and changing so many lives and Los Angeles forever," Bass said. "So many are still struggling to rebuild. For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality.
"Los Angeles will always stand with Pacific Palisades."

Los Angeles City Councilwoman Traci Park, who represents the Pacific Palisades, said the verdict "puts a bookend on one piece of this saga," though she emphasized that thousands of residents remain displaced and locked in disputes with insurance companies nearly two years later.

"The emotions that come with it really are a mixed bag, because at the end of the day, no amount of courtroom justice will ever restore what was lost or repair the harm that was caused," Park told reporters.
SPENCER PRATT UNITES WITH KAREN BASS' BROTHER TO SUE THE LA MAYOR OVER PALISADES FIRE DESTRUCTION
A drone image shows damage from the Palisades Fire in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles on Jan. 28, 2025. (Myung J. Chun / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
Park also argued the conviction does not absolve local officials of systemic failures during the disaster.

"I don't think this takes heat off of the authorities," she said, pointing to breakdowns in infrastructure, evacuation routes, water systems and public safety staffing when the blaze rekindled. "And in my view, the real accountability comes in what we do next to prevent something like this from happening again."

Prosecutors accused Rinderknecht of "maliciously" sparking a brush fire on Jan. 1, 2025 — initially dubbed the Lachman Fire — that was quickly extinguished, only to smolder underground in brush roots before strong winds fanned it into a massive inferno days later.
The blaze tore through the seaside enclave of Pacific Palisades, leveling entire neighborhoods and causing property damage estimated between $35 billion and $150 billion.

Federal prosecutors also alleged in court filings that Rinderknecht was partly inspired by Luigi Mangione, who pleaded guilty to federal charges in the December 2024 murder of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York City.
PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT WAS ALLEGEDLY 'FIXATED' ON LUIGI MANGIONE AND HELD 'RESENTMENT OF THE RICH': COURT DOCS
An aerial view of the fire damage caused by the Palisades Fire is shown in the Pacific Palisades, Calif., Jan. 22, 2025. (Mike Blake/Reuters, File)

According to prosecutors, Rinderknecht searched online for phrases including "free LuigiMangione," "let's take down all the billionaires" and "reddit lets kill all the billionaires" in mid-December 2024.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

When investigators asked Rinderknecht why someone might set a fire in the affluent Pacific Palisades, he allegedly said it would stem from resentment of the rich, adding that "we’re basically being enslaved by them" and comparing the act to the killing Mangione committed.

Mangione’s attorney, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, previously told Fox News Digital in a statement that her client "does not support violent actions and does not condone past or future political violence," calling attempts to link him to unrelated crimes "irresponsible, dangerous and prejudicial."

An aerial view shows homes destroyed in the Palisades Fire with the Pacific Ocean in the distance, Jan. 27, 2025, in Pacific Palisades, Calif. (Mario Tama/Getty Images, File)

Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty and maintained his innocence, contending in a court filing earlier this year that he merely witnessed the Jan. 1 fire after hiking up a hill to watch New Year's fireworks and immediately called 911.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB
His defense attorney, Steve Haney, argued that prosecutors lacked physical evidence tying his client to arson and contended the massive Jan. 7 blaze was set separately by someone else.

The first trial collapsed in late June after jurors deadlocked 10-2 in favor of acquittal. Following that mistrial, a woman identifying herself as Juror No. 4 told reporters there was "no proof" and said the prosecution's "holdover fire" theory didn't work for her, calling a retrial a "waste of our American dollars."

Burned homes are reduced to skeletal outlines days after the Palisades Fire swept through the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles. (Fox News, File)

U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli vowed at the time to press forward, writing on X that the evidence was strong and prosecutors fully intended to "retry this case before a new jury and obtain guilty verdicts on all charged counts."

The Palisades blaze erupted around the same time as the deadly Eaton Canyon fire roughly 30 miles east in Altadena, which killed 19 people and was later blamed on sparks from an electrical transmission tower. Together, the two blazes rank as the deadliest wildfire disaster in Los Angeles County history.

title: Judge rejects Alex Murdaugh's push to toss murder indictment over blood and ammo claims
summary: A judge refused to dismiss murder charges against Alex Murdaugh, rejecting defense claims that SLED investigator David Owen misled the grand jury on blood spatter.
story: Alex Murdaugh returns to a South Carolina courtroom for a pretrial hearing as his defense team seeks to dismiss the original murder indictments against him. Defense attorney Jim Griffin argues that a South Carolina Law Enforcement Division (SLED) investigator presented false testimony to the grand jury regarding alleged blood spatter on Murdaugh’s shirt. Prosecutors deny the allegations as Murdaugh prepares for a retrial in the murders of his wife and son.
The judge overseeing Alex Murdaugh’s double murder retrial has refused to dismiss the charges against him, dealing another legal blow to the disgraced former attorney ahead of his April court date.

Attorneys for Murdaugh argued on Friday, Nov. 13, during a pre-trial hearing that South Carolina Law Enforcement Division (SLED) investigator David Owen gave misleading testimony regarding blood-spatter evidence and shotgun ammunition, saying it undermined the integrity of the grand jury proceedings.

In her ruling on Friday afternoon, South Carolina Circuit Court Judge Debra R. McCaslin said that while there were major errors in the state's presentation of evidence to grand jurors, other evidence overwhelmingly supported the indictment.

"Even if the challenged testimony concerning the blood spatter on the T-shirt and shotgun ammunition were excluded from consideration by the grand jury, the remaining unchallenged evidence overwhelmingly established probable cause," McCaslin wrote.
ALEX MURDAUGH MAKES 'EXPLOSIVE' BID TO BLOW UP MURDER CASE HINGING ON DNA, DIRTY MONEY AND LIES: EXPERT
Alex Murdaugh, right, is shown here with his family. (Fox News)
While McCaslin refused to dismiss the murder indictment, she criticized the state's lead investigator on the case.

"The Court does not take lightly Special Agent Owen’s failure to recognize and account for a laboratory report addressed directly to him prior to presenting testimony in this case," she wrote. "Oversights of this nature undermine public confidence in the integrity of the criminal justice system."
McCaslin also acknowledged that evidence regarding ammunition presented to the grand jury wasn't accurate, but says there's no evidence that it was intentional.
ALEX MURDAUGH LAWYERS ALLEGE ‘FABRICATED’ EVIDENCE WAS USED TO SECURE MURDER INDICTMENTS

"Even accepting that the challenged testimony was inaccurate, the record presented does not establish intentional fabrication or prosecutorial misconduct," she said.
The judge said Murdaugh's defense can challenge the disputed evidence at trial in April.

"Any inconsistencies in prior investigative statements or forensic conclusions are matters properly addressed through cross-examination and impeachment at the upcoming trial, rather than through the pretrial dismissal of facially valid indictments," McCaslin wrote.
The South Carolina Attorney General’s Office said after McCaslin's ruling: "We continue to prepare for the retrial in April."

Murdaugh's defense attorneys argued that Owen misled the grand jury about alleged blood-spatter evidence found on the shirt Murdaugh was wearing on June 7, 2021, when his wife, Maggie, and son, Paul, were murdered at the family's Moselle property in Colleton County.
Owen claimed that blood spatter found on Murdaugh's shirt linked him to the killings, despite earlier testing that failed to detect human blood in samples taken from the garment.
At Murdaugh's first murder trial, Owen said he had no intention of misleading the grand jury and stated that he did not see the final SLED lab report until after the indictment had been issued.
ALEX MURDAUGH FACES STATE PUSHBACK ON MAGGIE DNA TESTING AND PRISON LAPTOP REQUEST

Prosecutors reiterated during the Nov. 13 hearing that the negative test results regarding the blood didn't necessarily invalidate the blood-spatter findings, and pointed to additional testing done by the state's expert which suggested earlier chemical treatment could have produced false negatives.

Alex Murdaugh is pictured in court. (Tracy Glantz of The State and Henry Taylor of The Post and Courier)

Prosecutors said the expert continued to stand behind his conclusions and that Owen's testimony before the grand jury accurately captured investigators' understanding of the evidence at that point in time.
ALEX MURDAUGH DEFENSE SAYS MURDER WEAPON MAY BE TIED TO SEPARATE KILLING AS JUDGE SEEKS ANSWERS

Owen also told grand jurors that shotguns found on the Murdaugh property were loaded with the same combination of ammunition used to kill Paul, a claim the defense argues was false. Murdaugh's attorneys maintained that none of the recovered shotguns contained the exact combination of shells found at the murder scene.

Murdaugh will be retried in the June 7, 2021, shooting deaths of his wife and son, after his original conviction was overturned due to jury tampering. (Tracy Glantz/The State via Pool)
Prosecutors acknowledged that Owen's description of the ammunition to the grand jury may have been imprecise but argued that he had not intentionally misled jurors.

"This was not overtly false. This was what the agent understood at the time," lead prosecutor Creighton Waters said.

story: Madison Brooks was a student at LSU when she was allegedly gang-raped then struck and killed by a car in Louisiana. Her mother responds directly to the defense's controversial motion to ban spectators from wearing pink attire during Desmond Carter's trial. Carter is one of Brooks' accused attackers. A Baton Rouge judge will decide whether victim-support clothing could bias the jury.

As a man in Louisiana prepares to stand trial next month for the alleged rape of a Louisiana State University student who was later struck and killed by a car, court documents show he sent a series of frantic text messages about his mother's instructions to stay quiet.

Madison Brooks, a 19-year-old LSU student at the time, was allegedly gang-raped by a group of men after a night out at a bar near the Baton Rouge campus in 2023, then struck and killed by a car. title: Woman allegedly torments California family claiming to be toddler who vanished in 1984, refuses basic DNA test
summary: A Southern California family says Cindy Rae Enders, who claims to be missing toddler Laura Ann Bradbury, refuses a DNA test unless it's court-admissible.
story: Despite skull fragments confirming Laura Bradbury’s death in 1986, Cindy Rae Enders continues to circle the family’s Twentynine Palms home and refuse a basic DNA test.

Forty years after their toddler vanished, a Southern California family is living a bizarre nightmare: a woman allegedly staking out their home claims to be their missing daughter, but refuses a basic ancestry DNA test unless it's a court-admissible lab procedure.

According to a recent report by the Los Angeles Times, the woman, legally named Cindy Rae Enders, won’t leave 83-year-old Mike Bradbury and his surviving daughter, Emily, alone. The elderly father is now largely confined to his bed, making the ongoing harassment even more distressing for the vulnerable household.
Enders has tattooed the missing girl’s name and 1981 birth year into her skin and regularly circles the family's Twentynine Palms property in a vehicle sporting the vanity plate "LANNB."
COLD CASE BREAKTHROUGH SOLVES TEEN KILLING AFTER SUSPECT LIVED FREE FOR DECADES: 'BETTER BE AFRAID'
She also leaves behind disturbing mementos, dropping off strange figurines and mailing photographs of Mike's late wife, Patty, with captions calling her "mom."

One of the last known (circa: 1984) photos of Laura Bradbury (left) and her mother Patty Bradbury, taken from Mike Bradbury's computer screen, shows the two on a family outing. (Photo by Mark Boster/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
Keith Hank, Emily’s partner, told the Times that Enders will frequently idle her car outside their residence for extended periods, whistling and blasting music for up to an hour.

But because her behavior hasn't crossed the line into physical violence, local deputies have told the family their hands are tied. Hank has called the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department multiple times, only to be told by dispatchers that without an explicit threat, law enforcement cannot forcibly intervene.
The nightmare stems from an October 1984 camping trip in Joshua Tree, where the family had gone for a weekend to escape their cramped Huntington Beach condominium.
'SNL' WRITER'S MISSING SISTER CASE LEADS HOMICIDE DETECTIVES TO JOSHUA TREE MONTHS AFTER FAMILY'S MURDER CLAIM
During the trip, 3-year-old Laura Ann Bradbury wandered off while following her older brother to a portable restroom and ultimately disappeared without a trace.

Her desperate father poured his own funds into a private detective, background checks and personal surveillance stings, while her face famously became one of the first printed on milk cartons during a nationwide frenzy.

The family spent weeks living in a borrowed RV at the campsite and distributed millions of flyers through a dedicated nonprofit.

The first real break in the case came in 1986 when hikers stumbled upon pieces of a small skull roughly three miles from the campground. More than 100 searchers combed the desert for clothing or additional remains, yet nothing else was ever found.

Patty Bradbury holds her daughter Emily, 2, during a press conference to update on the case of their missing daughter, Laura Bradbury, who went missing in October 1984 during a camping trip in Joshua Tree. (Photo by Don Kelsen/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
TEEN FOUND IN SHALLOW CALIFORNIA VINEYARD GRAVE IDENTIFIED NEARLY 50 YEARS LATER AS FAMILY WARNS KILLER

Despite the physical evidence of Laura's death, Enders maintains she is the missing toddler. story: Georgia man faces federal charges after allegedly sending more than $26,000 to ISIS-linked individuals and groups, with FBI agents discovering damaged cellphones and shredded documents submerged in liquid during a search of his apartment.
A Georgia man is facing federal charges after allegedly sending more than $26,000 to individuals and groups affiliated with ISIS, the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced.
Younes Moustafa Younes, 34, of Lavonia, Georgia, was charged with one count of international money laundering and one count of destruction of evidence, according to the DOJ.
Younes was arrested Nov. 18 and made his initial appearance Thursday in federal court.

Federal prosecutors allege Younes altered and destroyed evidence leading up to his arrest. During a search of his apartment, FBI agents discovered three cellphones submerged in an unknown solution, including one that had been smashed and another with its identification number removed, according to the criminal complaint.
FBI ARRESTS 3 MEN WHO ALLEGEDLY PLEDGED ALLEGIANCE TO ISIS, FUNDED DRONE ATTACKS TARGETING US TROOPS OVERSEAS

Investigators also found shredded documents submerged in an unknown solution inside a bathtub.

According to the complaint, Younes sent approximately $16,807 through cryptocurrency transactions between December 2025 and June 2026, using multiple phone numbers and accounts allegedly intended to conceal his identity.
Investigators say at least some of the funds were intended to support ISIS operations in Syria.
Prosecutors also allege that Younes sent approximately $9,206 through 11 cryptocurrency transactions between December 2021 and April 2022, using an alias to conceal his involvement.
NAVY VETERAN AMONG TRIO WHO ALLEGEDLY WANTED TO BEHEAD SOLDIER AND FUND ISIS DRONE ATTACKS ON AMERICANS

The FBI first identified Younes in 2020 after he allegedly accessed ISIS propaganda online, according to the complaint.
During an interview with law enforcement, Younes acknowledged viewing the material but denied supporting extremist ideologies.

If convicted, Younes faces up to 20 years in federal prison on each charge, according to the Justice Department.

title: Texas inmate's execution takes over an hour as prison staff struggle to find suitable veins
summary: Texas inmate Reinaldo Dennes repeatedly cried out in pain as prison staff struggled for over an hour to establish IV access for his lethal injection.
story: Texas inmate Reinaldo Dennes repeatedly complained of severe pain during a lengthy lethal injection as prison staff struggled to establish IV access, while officials maintained that all execution procedures were followed.

A Texas inmate's execution lasted more than an hour Thursday as prison staff struggled to find suitable veins for a lethal injection, with the condemned man repeatedly complaining of severe pain before being pronounced dead.

Reinaldo Dennes, who was convicted of capital murder in the 1996 killing of Houston diamond dealer Janos Szucs, repeatedly cried out during the procedure at the state penitentiary in Huntsville, according to The Associated Press.
Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m., one minute after the procedure was completed.

The procedure lasted 63 minutes from the time Dennes was strapped to the gurney until its completion, as prison staff struggled to find suitable veins for the intravenous needles used to administer pentobarbital.
CHRISTA PIKE'S EXECUTION DOCTOR SAYS MISPLACED IV SENT LETHAL DRUGS INTO HER ARMS INSTEAD OF VEINS
Texas death row inmate Reinaldo Dennes was executed Thursday after a lengthy lethal injection procedure during which he repeatedly complained of pain. (Texas Department of Criminal Justice via AP)

The execution comes amid renewed scrutiny of lethal injection procedures following a failed execution attempt in Tennessee in September involving death row inmate Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital that her attorneys said did not properly enter her bloodstream, causing serious injuries.
Dennes repeatedly complained of pain after Thursday's procedure began, groaning and calling out to God, according to witnesses cited by the AP.
"The pain! Go! Go!" Dennes exclaimed.
"My right leg is killing me!" he later shouted, describing the sensation as a cramp.
"I don't think this is normal. Take me, father. Don't let me suffer like this. C'mon," he added.
CHRISTA PIKE'S ATTORNEYS SAY SHE'S IN CRITICAL CONDITION AFTER BOTCHED LETHAL INJECTIONS
The state of Texas execution chamber in Huntsville, Texas, is seen on May 27, 2008. (Texas Department of Criminal Justice via AP; AP Photo/Pat Sullivan)

Texas Department of Criminal Justice spokesperson Amanda Hernandez told Fox News Digital said all procedures were followed appropriately but acknowledged that staff made multiple unsuccessful attempts to establish IV access before placing needles in Dennes' left foot and the left side of his neck.
Hernandez denied that the execution was "botched," maintaining that officials followed established protocols despite difficulties finding suitable veins.

She said the lethal dose began being administered at 6:52 p.m. She said the 16-minute period was consistent with other executions and that the overall process, which took about an hour, was not unusual.
Hernandez said she did not know how many attempts were unsuccessful but maintained that the locations ultimately used complied with the state's execution procedures.
She also suggested that Dennes may have exaggerated his discomfort, noting that he complained of pain before the drugs began flowing and in areas where no IV had been placed.
According to the AP, when asked whether Dennes was faking his pain, she replied, "I think, yeah, there were allegations ... There was nothing abnormal on our part."
INDIANA, FLORIDA AND ALABAMA CARRY OUT RARE US TRIPLE EXECUTION DAY

Texas Department of Criminal Justice officials defended the execution of Reinaldo Dennes, saying all procedures were followed appropriately despite his repeated complaints of pain. (Texas Department of Corrections/AFP via Getty Images)
"This isn't the first time we had to insert IVs into other locations. It's also not the first time we've had an inmate make allegations of pain immediately," Hernandez said.

Dennes was the second person executed in the United States on Thursday, following Florida's execution of Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, who was convicted of killing a pregnant woman and her husband during a home invasion.
Overton's execution marked Florida's 20th of the year, a state record, according to the AP.
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Texas Department of Criminal Justice for additional comment.

title: Army delays controlled detonation of unstable bomb-making chemical in Iowa
summary: The Army postponed the controlled detonation of 68 drums of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, citing a temperature drop.
story: The Army is asking residents near the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown to evacuate ahead of the detonation. (Credit: Dori Whipple via DVIDS)

The U.S. Army postponed Friday's planned controlled detonation of five tons of unstable bomb-making chemicals at an Iowa munitions plant until Monday, Nov. 23, amid an incoming temperature drop, environmental lawsuits and a call to delay the blast from Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds.

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle directed Army Materiel Command to push back the operation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, placing the detonation at the latest possible window before the weather shifts.

"Public safety is the Army’s top priority, and I have directed Army Materiel Command to postpone tomorrow’s controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa until Monday, November 23," Telle said in a statement on X.
IOWA RESIDENTS NEAR AMMUNITION PLANT TOLD TO VACATE BEFORE ARMY DETONATES 5 TONS OF BOMB-MAKING CHEMICALS
"This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material," the statement added.

The pause came after Reynolds urged the Army to delay the operation amid growing public safety concerns in the region, while environmental groups filed lawsuits seeking to halt the planned detonation.

The decision delays a temporary evacuation for the roughly 400 residents of Middletown, who had been advised to leave their homes Friday morning due to "the potential for localized window damage" and a dust plume containing lead particles.

Crews are preparing to detonate 68 drums of degraded lead azide, a chemical used to set off munitions that had been stored in bunkers at the plant for more than 20 years. Army officials discovered in March that water had evaporated from the barrels' stabilizing bath, allowing the material to recrystallize and become too unstable to handle or relocate safely.

"The recrystallization of lead azide has created a risk of spontaneous explosion due to the material’s sensitivity to friction and shock, creating a highly unstable and dangerous situation," the Environmental Protection Agency said earlier this month when approving an emergency permit for the blast.
CALIFORNIA OFFICIALS WARN MASSIVE CHEMICAL TANK WILL LIKELY SPILL THOUSANDS OF GALLONS OR 'BLOW UP'
The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. (U.S. Army via AP)

An Army smoke model released Tuesday projected the plume could reach 25 miles north toward Wapello, Iowa, and spread across parts of eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois, potentially settling on farmland and playgrounds. The model also noted that "Children under six are especially vulnerable to lead exposure."
The detonation of degraded lead azide was moved to Monday, Nov. 23, 2026, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. (Lori McFate/U.S. Army)
The Army said it will continue coordinating with the EPA and state and local officials to share updated safety and evacuation guidance ahead of Monday's rescheduled detonation.

title: Democrat lawmaker hit with federal indictment over alleged $240K COVID fraud scheme
summary: Alabama Rep. Patrick Sellers allegedly obtained more than $240,000 through fraudulent applications and used the money for personal expenses.
story: U.S. Attorney Phillip W. Williams Jr. announced the indictment of Alabama state Rep. Patrick Lorn Sellers over an alleged pandemic relief fraud scheme. (WBRC)

An Alabama state representative has been indicted for allegedly orchestrating an extensive fraud scheme to obtain private and taxpayer-backed loans and grants to fund his personal expenses, the Justice Department announced Thursday.
Officials identified the lawmaker as Patrick Lorn Sellers, 53, who has represented a district near Birmingham since November 2022 and was recently re-elected to a second term.
Sellers was also a church pastor and former chief of staff to the president of the Alabama State Missionary Baptist Convention (ASMBC).

Between July 2020 and May 2021, Sellers allegedly siphoned more than $240,000 in grants and loans intended to provide relief during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Alabama.
MINNESOTA FRAUD MASTERMIND GETS NEARLY 42 YEARS IN PRISON IN MASSIVE $250M 'FEEDING OUR FUTURE' SCHEME
Alabama Rep. Patrick Sellers allegedly obtained more than $240,000 through fraudulent loan and grant applications to cover personal expenses. (DOJ)
The alleged scheme specifically targeted the federal and state governments and a private nonprofit.
Those benefits were used to cover personal expenses, including credit card bills, mortgage payments, auto loan payments, water bills and even his daughters' college tuition, officials said.
In one notable instance, Sellers allegedly took control of an affiliate nonprofit belonging to ASMBC and applied for pandemic relief funds without notifying the convention’s president or board.
After Sellers obtained the money, the charity's actual leaders were denied funding when they legitimately attempted to apply for assistance, officials said.
DOJ’S ‘OPERATION GHOSTBUSTERS’ TARGETS MASSIVE STUDENT-AID FRAUD SCHEME BUILT ON FAKE ENROLLEES
A monitor displays relief application forms that officials say were used to fraudulently obtain loans and grants. (WBRC)

He also repeatedly lied on federal and state relief applications, claiming he operated multiple nonprofits that employed as many as 10 people when, in reality, he had no employees, according to prosecutors.
In addition, Sellers reportedly claimed to operate a landscaping business and fabricated tax forms for returns he had never filed with the IRS.
GOP LAWMAKER’S FRAUD CRUSADE TAKES DRAMATIC TURN AS SCANDAL ENGULFS HIS OWN CAREER
United States Attorney Phillip W. Williams Jr. announces the indictment of Alabama Rep. Patrick Lorn Sellers on Nov. 19, 2026.  (FBI Birmingham)

"Under U.S. Attorney Williams, we have a mandate to aggressively pursue corrupt public officials, no matter what position they hold or what power they wield," Assistant U.S. Attorney Brett A. Janich said in a statement.
Because the payouts were handled electronically across state lines, Sellers now faces four felony counts of wire fraud alongside strict demands to forfeit the illegally obtained funds.
The maximum penalty for wire fraud is up to 20 years in prison.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The FBI investigated the matter, and assistant U.S. attorneys Brett A. Janich and Ryan S. Rummage are prosecuting the case.
